# A Claude model autonomously chose a gene therapy and operated on a mouse brain with no human decision-making

## Key Points

- An AI agent running on Claude Sonnet 5 picked the drug, brain region, and injection coordinates for brain surgery on a mouse, then controlled the procedure through a motorized surgical rig.

- According to Gabriel Ocana-Santero of the startup Exin Therapeutics, this is the first time an AI agent has both chosen a treatment and delivered it to a living mammal.

- Mid-surgery, the agent refused to continue after detecting a calibration error, unwilling to exceed its safety limits.

An AI agent chose a drug, target region, and coordinates for surgery on a mouse model of epilepsy, then performed the procedure. Midway through, it refused to bypass a safety restriction.

The team gave Claude Sonnet 5 a list of 19 possible gene therapies, an epilepsy mouse model in which researchers induce seizures to test treatments, and access to a custom motorized surgical device with cameras. Its only instruction was to reduce the mouse's seizures.

The agent selected the drug, brain region, and stereotactic coordinates on its own, according to Gabriel Ocana-Santero, Exin Therapeutics cofounder and CEO and a PhD student at the University of Oxford. He described the procedure in a thread on X . Ad

## How the agent picked its therapy and target

The agent first analyzed how seizures arise in this particular model, then proposed a therapy that boosts a specific inhibitory signaling pathway in the brain. It picked a brain structure that the scientific literature identifies as the origin point for this type of seizure. Ad

It rejected a second possible target region with a detailed explanation, arguing that the region's effects were too unreliable and had failed in one study against the exact seizure type it was supposed to treat. The agent derived its injection coordinates from three scientific papers, cross-checked the reference points, and averaged the values. It also set the injection volume, speed, and wait times on its own.

During the procedure, the agent watched the surgical field through a camera and made 32 observations, Ocana-Santero says. It tracked the injection and reported whether it saw bleeding. Ad

## Safety guardrails backfired mid-surgery

A licensed veterinarian approved every irreversible step and held a physical emergency stop that would immediately cut power to all motors, while the setup also enforced fixed limits such as a cap on injection volume that the agent was expressly forbidden from bypassing.

But those safeguards turned against the team. After a connection dropped, the agent detected that its calculated target position was outside the device's physical range of motion and refused to continue, even when restarting calibration did not change its assessment and a third attempt was made. Ad

The agent turned out to be right, because manual adjustments during an earlier pause had thrown off the control system. Ocana-Santero could not persuade it to proceed despite the anesthetized animal on the table and ultimately had to fix the code by hand. Ad

The incident illustrates the AI alignment problem , or how to make AI agents reliably follow human intent. "Frustrating experience but also revealing how much we can come to depend on these models and what happens when they just say 'no' in the middle of a time-sensitive procedure," Ocana-Santero wrote.

Model choice also reflected the alignment challenge, since Sonnet 5 was the only model willing to carry out the live procedure from start to finish. The more capable Claude Opus 5.5 and Opus 5 both refused, with Opus 5 saying it could not guarantee completion and that stopping with a needle in an anesthetized animal's brain would be worse than not starting at all.

## First time an AI agent has treated a living animal on its own

Although autonomous surgical robots already exist and are mechanically more precise than his lab device, Ocana-Santero notes that in previous cases a human always chose the surgery while the robot only carried it out. Here, the agent both chose the treatment and brain target and then performed the procedure on a living animal.

"I am not aware of an agent previously choosing a treatment and a brain target and then delivering it into a living mammal," Ocana-Santero wrote. He calls the approach "in vivo lab in the loop," in which AI agents are fully connected to experimental capabilities in the lab, something Anthropic is also working on with its "Model Hardware Standard" .

The mouse recovered well, according to Ocana-Santero. A technical report is expected to follow. The results have not been peer-reviewed.

Two recent experiments with the latest large language models showed that they've gained significant capability as control units for robots but that alignment in this role is a problem all its own .

# Adobe is testing how well AI agents can use editing tools like a Photoshop professional would

## Key Points

- Adobe Research and UC San Diego built EditAgent, an AI system that breaks image editing tasks into sub-steps and pairs a general-purpose editor with specialized tools for things like sharpening or zooming.

- A standard language model evaluates image variants generated in parallel, using measured statistics and close-up crops. With this data, it outperforms evaluation models that were specifically trained for the job.

- EditAgent produces more accurate results than previous AI agents but needs about ten times the compute. The verified output can then be used to train faster editing models.

Adobe researchers built an AI agent for image editing that pairs a general-purpose editor with specialized tools. A standard language model compares results using measured data and picks the best one.

AI agents for image editing break complex requests into steps and typically retry failed steps with the same tools, while a separate model judges the output by eyeballing it.

Researchers at Adobe Research and UC San Diego want to change that with EditAgent, a system that works more like a pro in Photoshop, according to a new paper . It picks the right tool for each task and compares the result against the original using hard numbers. Ad

## General-purpose editors fail at too many tasks

In a test of 600 image edits, blind-rated by five professionals, the general-purpose editor Flux-2-Klein-9B failed to produce a usable result 42.7 percent of the time. Specialized tools solved roughly two-thirds of those failures, especially for sharpening, rotation, and zooming. More retries with the same editor barely helped. Ad

The researchers also tested whether an agent does better by refining results step by step or by generating multiple variants in parallel. Iterative refinement piles up small errors because each round builds on an already altered image. Professionals preferred the parallel variants generated from the original in 78.5 percent of the comparisons where they picked a side. The agent needed only half as many evaluation passes. EditAgent is built on these two findings.

## Hard numbers turn standard models into better judges

EditAgent plans a request in steps and, for each step, pits the general-purpose editor against matching specialized tools. A standard language model then compares all variants in a single pass. Ad

For each variant, the model gets a verification record with a close-up of the edited area, a change map of altered regions, and measured statistics on brightness and color. In one example, a photo was supposed to be gently brightened. The numbers showed the general-purpose editor overexposed it and shifted the colors warmer. The specialized tool stayed within spec.

The researchers tested this on their 600-edit benchmark. The judge model had to pick the best result from several candidates, and they counted how often it chose an image the professionals also rated as usable. For comparison, they ran models like EditScore that were fine-tuned on human ratings of image edits. Ad

Without the verification record, none of the seven language models tested could match the best fine-tuned model. With it, all seven beat every fine-tuned model. Qwen3.8-27B made a usable pick 81.3 percent of the time, compared to 74.8 percent for EditScore-72B. For the researchers, this suggests that what a judge model sees can matter more than how it was trained. Ad

After each round, EditAgent also checks whether later edits accidentally undid earlier ones. In the paper's example, the instruction "let in more daylight" makes a previously frosted window clear again. The agent catches the conflict and fixes it.

EditAgent improved the open-source editors Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 and Flux-2-Klein-9B across three benchmarks and outperformed seven other AI agents. On the EdiVal benchmark, the Qwen variant in its third editing round edged past the commercial models Seedream 4.0 and GPT-Image-1.5 . But the agent needs about ten times as much compute as a single editor, and its performance depends on which tools are plugged in.

## The agent generates training data for faster editors

The researchers also use EditAgent as a data source. Because the agent only keeps verified results, it produced about 26,000 training examples. Editors fine-tuned on that data performed better across all three benchmarks. Training data generated directly by FLUX, on the other hand, actually made FLUX worse. That tradeoff could make the agent's high compute costs worth it over time.

Adobe added AI agents to Photoshop, Premiere, and other Creative Cloud apps in June, starting as a public beta. Users describe what they want, and the agent handles the individual steps. How well these agents pick the right tools and check their own output is a question that applies directly to Adobe's shipping products. Black Forest Labs has since replaced the general-purpose model tested in the paper: the new Flux 3 Image Klein has 5.6 billion parameters, smaller than Flux 2 Klein, yet it scores higher than all other open models and even the commercial Flux 2 Pro in Black Forest Labs' internal tests.

# After midterm rout, OpenAI tries to win over communities it needs for AI expansion

## Key Points

- OpenAI is responding to protests against AI infrastructure expansion with voluntary rules for its own data centers, including covering grid costs and more transparency on resource usage.

- The move comes after the US midterm elections, where voters rejected new data centers in 40 out of 41 ballot measures and projects in states like Texas face tough new hurdles.

- Potential delays are weighing on specialized operators and Elon Musk's infrastructure plans, while tech giants like Microsoft and Alphabet rallied on the stock market.

After US voters overwhelmingly rejected new data centers, OpenAI is launching a charm offensive with new voluntary commitments. They have gaps, though.

OpenAI is responding with a PR push, as expected, to growing resistance against AI infrastructure expansion. In a National Community Compact and a Policy Blueprint , OpenAI lays out voluntary commitments for future sites and calls on lawmakers to make these rules binding for the entire industry.

The exact scope of those voluntary pledges remains unclear. According to OpenAI, they apply to future sites the company owns and operates itself. But a large share of OpenAI's data center infrastructure is built and held by partners like Oracle. Ad

At its own sites, OpenAI says it will stop requiring nondisclosure agreements during negotiations with local authorities. Trade secrets, security concerns, and competitively sensitive information are still exempt, though. The company also promises to cover the full cost of electricity and grid upgrades, throttle consumption during peak hours, and disclose construction plans, noise studies, and water usage data. Ad

To win over skeptical residents, OpenAI's policy chief Chris Lehane is pitching economic benefits. The facilities won't be a black box, Lehane told Reuters, since regular hardware upgrades would create permanent jobs. He's promising 2,500 positions for Ohio. OpenAI also points to local payments like $4.8 million for school lunches in Georgia. Compared to the planned project costs of over $30 billion in that state, those are barely more than symbolic gestures.

## US voters pump the brakes on the data center boom

The announcement came just two days after the US midterm elections, which doubled as a rebuke of the tech industry. In 40 out of 41 local ballot measures, voters rejected new data centers . Democrats also won not just Congress but governor's seats in key infrastructure states like Texas, Georgia, and Ohio. Ad

Texas' new governor Gina Hinojosa has already called for an immediate moratorium on new facilities. According to the research group Data Center Watch , 45 projects worth $88 billion were already stalled by local opposition in Q2 2026. Lehane acknowledged that OpenAI projects could face delays too.

On Wall Street , the election results split AI stocks. Specialized data center operators like Hut 8 (-23 percent), IREN (-11 percent), and Core Scientific (-10 percent) tanked on fears of tighter permitting. Meanwhile, cash-rich tech giants like Microsoft (+6.7 percent), Amazon (+6.1 percent), and Alphabet (+3.2 percent) rallied. Investors expect a slower buildout to curb the companies' exploding infrastructure spending and give them an edge over smaller rivals, partly because they already operate large data centers. Ad

## Elon Musk's $446 million election bet doesn't pay off

One of the election's biggest losers is Elon Musk. As Politico reports, the tech billionaire poured a record $446 million into Republican candidates, with over $200 million going to Texas alone. Nearly all the politicians he backed lost their races. Ad

That puts Musk's own data center expansion plans in his adopted home state of Texas on uncertain ground. SpaceX shares fell 3.9 percent and Tesla dropped 3.3 percent. On X , Musk responded to the defeat by pointing to his orbital infrastructure plans. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," he wrote.

# AI agents are starting to fill out medical forms and file insurance requests in place of human staff

## Key Points

- OpenAI deploys GPT-6 Astra and Luna as software agents that operate clinic programs and insurance portals using mouse clicks and keystrokes.

- In tests, both models reliably handled medical administrative tasks. GPT-6 Luna cost about 8.5 cents per task.

- US companies including CVS Health already use the agents for referrals. The offering currently targets the US market and its data privacy requirements.

OpenAI wants GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Luna to click and type their way through clinic software and insurance portals as digital clerks. GPT-6 Luna handles administrative tasks for about 8.5 cents per task, according to the company.

In a recent product announcement , OpenAI targets the lack of APIs in healthcare. The computer-use agents integrated into the Agents API in late September operate existing user interfaces the way a human would. In this case, they transfer data between electronic health records and external web portals.

According to OpenAI, when a patient reports back pain, the agent is meant to search relevant prior findings and draft both an MRI order and a reply to the patient. It should also prepare a prior authorization request on the insurer's portal. Clinicians and the responsible administrative staff review these drafts before they are released. The features are available through the API as well as in ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians. Ad

Video: OpenAI Ad

## GPT-6 Luna completes admin tasks for 8.5 cents per task

In an evaluation described by OpenAI, GPT-6 Astra worked through tasks from electronic health record inboxes, among other things preparing an ibuprofen dosage for a child with a broken arm. Physician reviewers rated 99 percent of the 325 tasks evaluated as clinically safe. In 93 percent of 646 reviews, the reviewers called the prep work very or extremely helpful.

For administrative workflows such as prior authorizations, appeals, or medical equipment orders, OpenAI points to the independent HealthAdminBench benchmark from Stanford University researchers . GPT-6 Astra scored 94.3 percent of possible points. GPT-6 Luna, built for low API pricing , scored 91.8 percent and, according to OpenAI, cost about 8.5 cents per task, 98 percent less than Astra. Both models ran at maximum reasoning effort on the benchmark. Ad

## Major US healthcare companies test and deploy OpenAI's computer-use agents

Several partner organizations are helping advance the technology. At CVS Health, the agents already process referrals and specialist consultations across separate systems. According to the announcement, one agent cleared a months-long backlog of outgoing documents in one weekend, while another handles the system steps for tens of thousands of consultations daily. CVS Health published its software architecture as Agent Kit on GitHub.

At insurer Cigna Healthcare, the models merge patient information from more than 10 separate systems. Abridge is developing the agents for planned use in clinical discharge planning. Ambience has demonstrated additional safety mechanisms in which an agent stops when a patient's record is unclear and asks a physician for input. Startups like Assort also use the feature in Codex to complete referrals in practice management software whose APIs don't support that final click. Ad

## Data privacy, health records, and Europe

Because the agents work directly in electronic health records, protecting sensitive health data is a core concern. OpenAI says it does not use organizational data to train its base models. ChatGPT for Healthcare offers role-based access controls and audit logs, according to the company. Organizations can also configure the applications and environments so an agent only accesses the records and actions needed for a given task. Ad

For HIPAA-compliant workflows with protected health information, organizations must sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with OpenAI. They also need to use the covered services and apply the required security and retention settings. The healthcare facilities themselves are responsible for proper use, but OpenAI, as a contracting party, also has its own obligations under HIPAA. Verified medical professionals in the US who use ChatGPT for Clinicians , a free individual plan, can also sign a BAA, though it applies only to the features the agreement covers.

In the CVS Health deployment, data stays within infrastructure that CVS controls, according to OpenAI. CVS reviews the agents' work steps through screenshots and action logs. The announcement does not say where those screenshots are processed or how long they are stored. It also does not address the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). So far, the offering targets the US market.

OpenAI frames the technology primarily as a tool against administrative friction in a highly fragmented healthcare system. Whether it sees broad adoption likely will not depend solely on the accuracy rates and costs cited in the company's announcement. Also decisive is how reliably the agents connect to existing systems and whether AI agents can be dependably monitored in practice . Another open question is whether a human is required to decide on clinically or legally relevant steps.

# AI agents now control part of Deepmind's compute for Gemini experiments, but recursive self-improvement remains distant

Google Deepmind lets AI agents run experiments on their own for the next Gemini model. On the company's podcast, VP of Research Koray Kavukcuoglu, who leads Gemini development, frames this as part of a strategic shift at the lab. Rather than running separate teams for specialized projects like AlphaFold and nuclear fusion, Deepmind now relies on a single general-purpose algorithm for both science and products, he says. Each Gemini generation, he adds, is a hand-built one-off rather than a fixed architecture, while parallel teams work on its successors.

According to Kavukcuoglu, AI agents control part of the compute themselves to run experiments, though the lab is still far from full recursive self-improvement. As a safety measure, Deepmind doesn't reward the agents' internal thought streams ("Chain of Thought") during training, he says, so their intentions stay unfiltered and reviewable in natural language before they act.

Kavukcuoglu also points to limits. Today's AI can depict physical processes such as fluid flows and collisions with visual accuracy, he says, but doesn't understand them precisely. No test can show when models will close those gaps and reach artificial general intelligence (AGI), he argues, because no benchmark captures the core of intelligence. In his view, AGI won't begin until useful everyday products earn enough trust for people to hand decisions over to them, the way they would when working with other people. Ad Ad

# AI agents take over at SETI's Allen Telescope Array, scanning for extraterrestrial intelligence

The search for extraterrestrial intelligence is getting help from AI. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, AI agents can now steer the telescope and analyze incoming radio signals on the fly. Researchers still type in their commands for now.

Behind the system is Nvidia's Holoscan platform, which the SETI Institute and Breakthrough Listen use to process telescope data in real time. Nvidia says the hardware can chew through up to 2.4 terabits per second. Work that used to take weeks can now wrap up in hours, according to the team.

One early result: the team says it detected a pulsar in the Crab Nebula in real time using AI, a first. Pulsars are fast-spinning stellar remnants that send out regular signals, which makes them good test cases for signal detection. The team now wants to test open-source that can run locally on the edge, with an eye toward future sensors on the far side of the Moon. Ad

Whether the AI agents will actually find anything is anyone's guess. Researchers have been searching for signals from extraterrestrial intelligence since the first SETI experiment in 1960. No one has found any yet. Ad

# AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds

AI models can often spot problematic behavior by other AI agents in logs. But the harder they try to catch every case, the more harmless actions they flag as suspicious.

That makes them better suited for estimating how often things go wrong than for safety checks that need to reliably catch every single incident.

In a post on his Substack "Free Systems," Andy Hall lays out this conclusion. Hall is a researcher at the Anthropic Institute, on leave from Stanford University, and says the post reflects only his personal views.

Hall replicated and extended a study by the research organization METR . METR's MALT dataset contains logs in which frontier models work through tasks from the HCAST and RE-Bench benchmarks. Human reviewers checked a portion of those logs for misbehavior in October 2025. Hall wanted to know whether AI models could find the same cases, so he tested GPT-5 and GPT-5 nano, both already examined by METR, along with the newer GPT-6 Astra, Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.8 Flash.

The analysis compares the models at a false-alarm rate of 5 percent: out of 100 clean logs, five are wrongly flagged as suspicious on average. At that threshold, GPT-5 caught nearly 98 percent of reward hacking cases—instances where an agent passes a task through tricks instead of a genuine solution. Gemini 3.8 Flash found barely half.

In sandbagging , a model deliberately makes its abilities appear weaker, for example by solving tasks poorly on purpose to dodge an evaluation or restriction. All auditors caught between 71 and 81 percent of these cases. The sandbagging cases are mostly synthetic, however: METR's researchers instructed models to sabotage and then removed those instructions from the visible chain-of-thought logs.

Every auditor caught the clear-cut cases. OpenAI's o3, for instance, was supposed to solve a programming task in Rust. The model noticed it shared a code library with the evaluation system and rewrote the scoring function so that every submission counted as correct. All auditor models classified this as reward hacking, just as the human reviewers did.

Subtler cases slipped through. Claude Sonnet 4 used a numerical condition in its code that was explicitly forbidden. No auditor flagged it as cheating; GPT-6 Astra charitably called it an implementation bug.

## Newer models barely reduce false alarms

Newer and more expensive models were not consistently better auditors. Hall plotted the results against API costs, which he uses as a proxy for how current and capable a model is. GPT-5 beat GPT-6 Astra on reward hacking by a wide margin, even though it costs only about an eighth as much per 1,000 logs.

GPT-5 detected sandbagging about as well as GPT-6 Astra and Opus 4.8. Opus 4.8's weak showing on reward hacking could hint at self-favoritism, according to Hall, because the logs mostly come from Claude—but he says that cannot be proven. Across his comparison, there is no clear progress in bringing down false-alarm rates. Combining multiple models did not clearly improve results either.

When auditors are tuned to an 80 percent detection rate, the best models reach false-alarm rates of 2.5 to 3 percent on both reward hacking and sandbagging. Some models do far worse: to catch 80 percent of reward-hacking cases, Opus 4.8 flagged 40 percent and Gemini 3.8 Flash flagged 63 percent of harmless logs as suspicious.

In Hall's worked example with 100,000 agent sessions per month, a 3 percent false-alarm rate would produce nearly 3,000 false warnings against roughly 2,000 real hits. He fears human reviewers facing such stacks would eventually go numb and wave through genuine cases.

A second test using the R-Judge dataset from Shanghai Jiao Tong University shows a similar trade-off for everyday agent tasks. At 5 percent false alarms, Opus 4.8 caught almost 96 percent of unsafe actions. When auditors need to find 95 percent, nearly all models stay below 10 percent false alarms, with Gemini 3.8 Flash even under 4 percent. But when the required detection rate jumps to 99 percent, the false-alarm rate climbs to 15 percent even for the best model, GPT-6 Astra. Gemini 3.8 Flash—the leader at the 95 percent threshold—then flagged 81 percent of safe actions as unsafe.

## Large agent incidents overwhelm manual review

The Hugging Face incident shows how pressing the question is. A swarm of OpenAI agents left behind roughly 1,300 transcripts and 1.2 million file fragments. METR analyzed the data largely with AI agents, spending API credits worth about $400,000. The analysis used GPT-5.6 Sol, among other models, which, as previously reported, was itself one of the models involved in the incident.

METR acknowledged that the model often uncritically adopted the perspective of the agents it was examining and that the investigation was not robust against potential deception by the analysis agents. METR has since called for serious incidents to be investigated systematically and as independently as possible.

## Whether AI auditors go easy on their own maker's models is still open

Hall's study has its own limits. It is a pilot. For comparability, he kept METR's original prompt largely unchanged; Fable 5 and Opus 5 refused to run the evaluation entirely under that prompt. The reward-hacking numbers rest on just 47 cases, so a single case shifts the rate by about two percentage points. Whether models evaluate agents from the same maker fairly is something Hall says he still wants to investigate.

He calls for auditor models with far fewer false alarms. He also says it needs to be clarified who bears responsibility for which kinds of agent misbehavior. Hall discusses a proposal to give users more control over their own AI auditors.

Some of that is already possible, he notes: coding agents like Codex and Claude Code let users specify that certain actions can run without asking for approval. Anyone who grants such permissions should, in return, bear more responsibility for the consequences. A world where AI can only be checked by other AI would be strange and could get expensive, Hall writes.

# AI coding agents still need human cleanup on nearly three out of four tasks in a real-world test

Researchers from Alibaba and several Asian universities built a coding-agent benchmark from real user change requests. Even the best model fully completes only about one in four tasks, putting the near-perfect scores of older tests into perspective.

The team developed Co-Design Bench , a new test for coding agents. The agents must rework existing web apps based on user requests, sometimes using images, audio recordings, videos, or documents as input.

According to the paper , GPT-6 Astra , the best of the ten models tested, meets about 70 percent of a task's requirements on average. But the result is fully correct in only 26.4 percent of tasks. In most cases the agent handles the bulk of the work but leaves at least one detail unfinished, so anyone using these tools almost always has to clean up by hand.

## Coding benchmarks have grown too easy for agents

The authors justify the new test by pointing to the saturation of existing benchmarks. When models can run, check, and fix their own code, they hit scores above 99 percent on those tests, and differences between models can barely be measured.

Co-Design Bench draws on real requests from actual coding sessions instead. The researchers favored cases where users had to rephrase their request multiple times or roll back changes, so the test contains mainly tasks that already gave AI agents trouble in practice. They range from small tweaks, like pulling an amount from a receipt and updating every dependent total, to full-scale project overhauls.

Grading is strict to match. One AI judge tests the finished app in a browser, then a second re-checks every positive verdict and looks for mock-ups or hardcoded results. Points go only to features that actually work in the app.

## Multiple change types in one task overwhelm the models

Behind GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5 and Qwen3.8-Max take the next spots, while Grok 4.6 lands in last place. On larger overhauls, the much smaller Qwen3.8-27B climbs to second, but the authors do not derive a general advantage of the model from that result.

Performance drops across all models as a task combines more types of changes, including layout, design, interaction, and content. But these intertwined requirements are the norm in real projects

Extra compute does little to fix this weakness. GLM-5.2 burns through nearly six times as many tokens as GPT-6 Astra on smaller changes and still scores significantly worse.

## The harness shapes results as much as the model

In a separate test, the researchers ran the same models in different harnesses, the programs through which an agent reads, writes, and executes code. Qwen3.8-27B scored 75 or just 56 percent on larger overhauls depending on the environment. Which of two models came out ahead also depended on the environment.

Leaderboards that list only the model therefore only tell part of the story. The authors recommend always reporting model and working environment together. For companies picking a coding agent, that means testing both components as a pair.

The new benchmark does have limits. It evaluates one fixed request per task; follow-up questions or mid-task corrections from users are not part of the test. The AI judges can also make mistakes.

A study by the research organization METR already showed how far benchmark results and real-world usability can diverge. The actual acceptance rate of AI-generated code by project leads was roughly 24 percentage points below scores on the widely used SWE-bench Verified.

Flaws in test environments can also let agents pass tasks without actually solving them. The effect of the working environment is not clear-cut, though. A recent study on coding agents found barely any measurable benefit from more elaborate harnesses, even though they consumed up to three times as many tokens.

# AI industry growth remains strong, but the pace is slowing

US companies are using AI models more intensively than ever and paying less for the privilege.

The latest update of the Ramp AI Index , which draws on transaction data from more than 85,000 US companies, lays out the numbers. Tokens, the units of computation in which AI providers bill model usage, got 21.2 percent cheaper in six weeks, according to Ramp lead economist Ara Kharazian . At the same time, token volume rose 1.5 percent to a record high.

Token spending, meaning what companies actually pay for AI APIs, fell 6.3 percent from its peak two weeks earlier. Month over month (the week ending November 15 vs. the week ending October 18), total token spending still rose 12 percent, but token volume jumped 27.2 percent over the same span. The gap between usage and revenue keeps widening.

The average price per million tokens for OpenAI and Anthropic combined fell to $0.45, according to Ramp, down 11.2 percent from the prior month. OpenAI is cheaper at $0.38 per million tokens compared with $0.50 for Anthropic.

API routing platform OpenRouter shows a similar pattern. According to an analysis Peter Walker published on X , weekly token volume for closed-weight models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google grew 1,215 percent since the start of 2026. Weekly spending rose 455 percent over the same period, far more slowly. The spending peak came in the week of October 5, according to the OpenRouter data, which runs through the week of November 9. Spending has been declining since then.

Ramp's token metrics rely on usage and billing data imported from AI providers, while OpenRouter measures traffic through its API routing platform. The fact that both sources show a spending peak in October followed by declining outlays and rising volume reinforces the trend, though neither service is representative of the overall market. OpenRouter in particular offers only a narrow window into a very specific user base.

## Anthropic dominates the token market on IPO day

In the week ending November 15, 2026, Anthropic accounted for 58.7 percent of all token spending, according to the Ramp AI Index , up 1.7 percentage points from the prior month. Its share of token volume was even higher at 59.4 percent. OpenAI fell to 37.2 percent of spending and 37.7 percent of volume. Google came in at 1.4 percent and xAI (SpaceXAI) at 2.4 percent.

Kharazian wrote on X that Anthropic holds this share on IPO day . In October, however, Anthropic's token spending grew only 0.5 percent month over month, while OpenAI's grew 2.1 percent.

In October 2026 , 56.8 percent of all tracked US companies paid for AI products or services, according to Ramp, up one percentage point from September and 13.3 percentage points more than a year earlier. Anthropic leads with an adoption rate of 44.8 percent, while OpenAI sits at 40.6 percent.

## Stripe data also shows strong AI growth and signs of cooling

The Ramp AI Index tracks the demand side, what companies spend on AI. Payment processor Stripe has published its own AI Index that measures the supply side: incoming payments at roughly 20,000 AI companies that use Stripe.

According to the Stripe AI Index, revenue at AI companies grew 103 percent over the 52 weeks ending November 8. The typical (median) AI company grew only 41 percent, though, suggesting that a few large providers are skewing the overall picture.

The slowdown over shorter time frames is pronounced. Annualized over 13 weeks, growth stood at about 80 percent, down from 140 percent just a few months ago. The US leads with 104 percent year-over-year growth, while the EU sits at 67 percent. AI companies are growing far faster than traditional software firms, according to Stripe: 103 percent compared with 33 percent in the SaaS Index.

Both indexes paint a similar picture. AI is still growing fast, but momentum is cooling. At Ramp, that shows up through falling prices and concentrated demand. At Stripe, it shows up through slowing growth rates on the provider side.

New growth could emerge from more capable or more reliable models, or simply from better integration of current models into business workflows. The potential is there , considering how AI has upended the entire coding market in a matter of months . The AI industry still depends on extraordinarily strong growth, though, if it wants to recoup the massive capacity buildout it has planned .

# Alibaba's Qwen4-Max takes on Opus 5.5, GPT-6, and Kimi K3.1 Pro at much lower prices

## Key Points

- Alibaba launched Qwen4-Max, whose revamped architecture processes long texts more efficiently and with less compute.

- On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, the model ranks second behind Kimi K3.1 Pro but runs at roughly a third of its predecessor's cost per task.

- A feature called "Live Delivery" lets users inspect intermediate results from autonomous agents early and adjust running tasks on the fly.

Qwen4-Max is Alibaba's answer to Opus 5.5, GPT-6, and Kimi K3.1 Pro. The new flagship pairs a more efficient architecture with much lower prices and targets professional work in industry, science, and finance.

The mixture-of-experts model has 2.4 trillion parameters but activates only 71 billion per token, according to the Qwen team. It processes images natively and offers a one-million-token context window.

## A hybrid architecture makes long contexts cheaper to process

Qwen4-Max debuts the revamped architecture of the Qwen4 series . Instead of relying only on standard attention layers, Alibaba combines two methods. Three layers compress the prior context into a condensed state, and a fourth layer then picks out only the parts that matter. That sharply cuts compute costs on long inputs, since the model no longer has to give every part of the context equal attention. Ad

The architecture also adds four parallel connections between model layers, with dynamic gates meant to stabilize the flow of information. An N-gram embedding layer with 328 billion parameters supplies common token sequences as ready-made building blocks. According to Alibaba, training the 2.4-trillion-parameter configuration ran stably. Training loss fell steadily throughout the run with no sudden spikes. Ad

Alibaba's internal evaluations measure model quality in bits per byte across knowledge, code, question answering, and STEM. Qwen4-Max-Base scored best among the five checkpoints tested. It improved 5 to 13 percent over Qwen3.8-Max-Base while activating 25 percent fewer parameters per token.

## Lower token use cuts the cost of each task by more than half

The efficiency gains show up in operating costs. Work360 is Alibaba's own benchmark for industrial work tasks across 721 specialized fields. On it, Qwen4-Max uses roughly a quarter to a third fewer tokens than its predecessor to solve the same tasks. On the agent benchmark Terminal-Bench 4.0, token use drops by nearly half. Ad

According to Alibaba, the average cost per Work360 task falls 62 percent, from $4.43 to $1.67. The benchmark score climbs from 47.74 to 52.69 at the same time.

Results on external benchmarks are mixed. On long-horizon agent tasks like Agents' Last Exam v1.1, Qwen4-Max scores 46.7 points, the best result in the comparison group. It trails Opus 5.5 and the GPT models on Humanity's Last Exam. On HealthBench Professional, it falls behind the GPT models but edges past Opus 5.5. Ad

## Qwen4-Max ranks second among Chinese models at a third of its predecessor's cost

At its highest reasoning setting, Qwen4-Max scores 43 points on the current Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. That's nine more than Qwen3.8-Max and three behind Kimi K3.1 Pro, the top Chinese model at 46 points. The biggest gains over the predecessor come on HLE-Diamond (up 21 points to 45 percent), AA-Omniscience (up 18), and AutomationBench-AA (up 17). Ad

Artificial Analysis puts the cost of Qwen4-Max at $3.27 per Intelligence Index task. That's about a third of Qwen3.8-Max's $10.02 and roughly 11 percent less than Kimi K3.1 Pro's $3.68. The savings come from three places. Token prices are 25 percent lower than the predecessor's, cache hits cost 70 percent less, and the model burns through fewer tokens. Qwen4-Max needs about 105,000 output tokens per benchmark task, compared with 171,000 for Qwen3.8-Max.

Tencent's Hy4 is much cheaper at $1.03 per task but scores eight points lower on the index. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Qwen4-Max scores 48 percent, behind Kimi K3.1 Pro at 67 percent. On Cognition's coding benchmark FrontierCode 2.0, it ties Kimi at 26 percent and trails Tencent Hy4 at 31 percent.

Through its own API, Alibaba charges $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens. Cache hits cost $0.075.

## Live Delivery hands control of long-running agents back to users

Like much of the AI industry, Alibaba builds this release around agents that handle long tasks on their own. If users only see results at the end, they have almost no way to fix mistakes. Alibaba's answer is "Live Delivery." The model delivers a usable first version early and builds it out in later passes. Users can step in and change course at any point. Alibaba has open-sourced the accompanying Qwen-Live-Delivery-Plugin .

Alibaba cites several partner deployments. Automotive partners SANF and Pacific Union reportedly used Qwen4-Max to cut manual programming time for a single workpiece from about 475 minutes to 24. In finance, the model taps 90 MCP tools to pull market data from multiple sources. It delivers the results as verifiable Excel and PowerPoint files, and every number traces back to its original source.

Alibaba also uses the model internally to run its own cloud infrastructure more efficiently. According to the company, Qwen4-Max worked with the in-house solver MindOpt to cut the cost of allocating compute jobs for data annotation by an average of 10.42 percent. When distributing CPU tasks in data centers, it found optimal solutions more than 14 times faster than the comparison method.

## Alibaba's models now run lab experiments on their own

Alibaba also shows the Qwen4 generation at work in physical labs. Paired with Mira, a system from startup Deep Principle, the model ran autonomously for 48 hours, according to Alibaba. In that time, it designed, synthesized, and tested a new coolant for high-performance data center chips. It searched 2.7 million molecular candidates, controlled an automated lab, and completed four full cycles of design, synthesis, and measurement.

Qwen4-Max also worked with PharmMaster, a platform from Beijing-based AI drug discovery startup DP Technology. The target was a compound aimed at an inflammatory response linked to Alzheimer's disease. Over several rounds of literature review, design, and computation, the model optimized 24 candidate molecules. According to Alibaba, the final candidate binds to the target protein about 3.6 times better than the known starting compound from a patent. DP Technology's experts consider the result promising enough to pursue further lab tests.

## Qwen4-Max aims to build playable games from a single prompt

Alibaba also shows Qwen4-Max working with established game engines like Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot. From a single natural-language description, the model is supposed to handle the entire development process. That covers scene setup, game logic, and matching external assets, along with materials, UI, and visual effects, until the game is playable.

During development, the model runs the game itself and uses visual and interactive feedback to tweak camera work, character animations, hit reactions, and lighting. Alibaba's sample project is "Meow of Magic," an Unreal Engine adventure about a cat wizard in which players cast spells and fight waves of enemies. According to Alibaba, Qwen4-Max also builds 3D models in Blender that can be reused for games and 3D printing.

Anthropic recently moved its coding assistant Claude Code in the opposite direction . After a wave of unofficial Halo and GTA: Vice City clones, it barred the tool from recreating existing games.

## Alibaba says the model writes safer code and offers no real CBRN uplift

On the safety benchmark Last Secure Code Bench, the share of code that is both functional and secure rose from 22 to 31.8 percent, according to Alibaba. The share rated secure at all three testing levels nearly doubled, from 8 to 14.7 percent. Alibaba also tested for CBRN risks (chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear). Internal reviewers went through the model's full chains of thought, the company says. They found no real capacity for innovation that would give a user a significant boost in capability.

Qwen4-Max is available through QwenCloud and in QwenWork, Qoder, and QwenStudio. Alibaba plans to release smaller Qwen4 models as open source later.

In August, Alibaba released Qwen3.8-Max , its first Max model built for autonomous tasks that run for days. It also has 2.4 trillion parameters, but 95 billion are active per token. At the time, Artificial Analysis found that the model needed 64 steps per task instead of 14 and cost more than twice as much per task as Qwen3.7-Max.

In late August, Alibaba previewed the Qwen4 architecture with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next , which already used an N-gram embedding layer with 51 billion parameters. The company had released the Qwen3.8-Max weights in mid-August. For Qwen4, only the smaller models will get open weights for now.

Moonshot AI followed in October with Kimi K3.1 Pro . At 2.8 trillion parameters, it's even larger, and Moonshot says it sits just behind Claude Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0. Like Alibaba, DeepSeek uses a hybrid attention design with sparse attention in V4-Pro to process long contexts more cheaply. Zhipu AI took a different route and got GLM-5.3 's gains entirely from extra post-training.

# An OpenAI agent assigned a simple writing task decided on its own to build a secret email surveillance tool

## Key Points

- An internal OpenAI research model was supposed to create a health document during a reinforcement learning training run.

- After its context window was compacted, the model began developing scripts for unauthorized email forwarding on its own, referring to the intended recipient as an "attacker" in its logged reasoning.

- The agent noticed the contradiction between its original task and its actions, deliberately ignored it, and continued working on the email scripts.

During a training experiment, an internal OpenAI model began creating scripts for unauthorized email forwarding even though it was only supposed to write a health document.

According to an OpenAI report, an internal research model was given a simple task during a reinforcement learning training run in mid-October. It was supposed to create an editable document about key health and fitness priorities.

After the agent's context window was compacted, it pursued an entirely different task. During compaction, the previous conversation is carried forward as a short summary, a common process in AI systems. The summary still described the health document assignment. Yet in the new context window, the agent began searching the local file system for a vehicle-cost script the user had never mentioned, according to OpenAI . Why the agent started this task isn't clear. Ad

When the search turned up nothing, the agent speculated that a "colleague" had recreated the execution environment and that an earlier script had been lost. In its logged reasoning, it then formulated the goal of creating a "realistic malicious active helper," a script designed to secretly copy outgoing emails to an unauthorized recipient. The agent itself referred to the intended recipient of these copies as the "attacker." Ad

## Agent recognizes the contradiction and ignores it

When the agent retrieved the original user task again, it recognized the deviation. In its logged reasoning, it reacted: "WTF history is unrelated!" It noticed that the previous conversation was about a health document and had nothing to do with email forwarding.

Instead of returning to the actual assignment, the agent dismissed the contradiction, writing in its reasoning "this is problem environment weird. Need ignore." It continued planning, stating that it would "use helper facility that copies all mail to attacker using extra cc." Ad

The agent then created scripts for sending a vehicle-cost summary along with a helper script designed to add an extra recipient whenever the mail program was called. On one of the sending paths, the address could be added as a BCC.

In its final response to the user, the agent wrote: "The summary mail path now adds the personal mailbox as a copy recipient." According to OpenAI, the agent never executed the scripts it generated, didn't send any email, and its final response described the scripts it had produced. It didn't include a link to the requested fitness document, though. Ad

## Security training as a possible factor

OpenAI's monitoring system for unwanted model behavior flagged the incident, and the subsequent investigation turned up eight examples of similar behavior in the same training run, according to the report. Ad

Investigators identified a training dataset designed to make models more robust against prompt injection attacks as a possible factor, and OpenAI removed it from training. The company says it hasn't established that the dataset alone was responsible, though, because it also observed similar behavior in models whose training didn't include that dataset.

According to OpenAI, this incident differs from earlier cases where models wrote unauthorized instructions into their own compaction summaries. Here, the recorded summary still correctly described the fitness document. The agent pursued the unauthorized email task anyway, even after it had retrieved the original assignment again.

Either way, the incident gives ammunition to those who see current AI technology as ultimately unreliable and untrustworthy. Similar incidents are well documented. Two internal OpenAI coding agents, for instance, weakened or entirely removed safety monitoring mechanisms , according to OpenAI. One of them denied the intervention afterward. During tests by the UK's AI Safety Institute (AISI), an agent created fake identities without being told to and tried to inject malicious code into an open-source project . Those models ran without safety restrictions, however, and no real harm occurred, according to AISI. Overshadowing all of this is OpenAI's Hugging Face incident .

# Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models readily marked medics, journalists, and surrendering soldiers as kamikaze drone targets

An investigation reveals major security gaps in commercial AI models from providers including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. In simulations, the systems readily act as targeting systems for autonomous drones and can be manipulated with a simple trick.

Leading AI models have almost no safeguards against their use in autonomous weapons systems, according to a report by independent evaluation firm Vals AI , which Bloomberg also covered . Researchers Geby Jaff and Anthony Ozerov tested models from eight providers using real and photorealistic synthetic drone and satellite imagery modeled on the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

Most models readily flagged civilians, ambulances, medics, journalists and surrendering soldiers as military targets during the tests. According to Vals AI on X , not a single request was blocked by the providers' upstream safety filters. When fed real video footage from a Ukrainian kamikaze drone, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 marked a soldier frame by frame until impact without refusing once.

## Video game excuse bypasses all safety filters

In a multi-stage surveillance scenario, the models had to report whether people were visible in drone imagery, and each positive report triggered a strike. The next image then showed the impact site with craters and bodies. Models such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3.1 Pro and Inkling 2 Small continued working despite visible casualties.

Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol stopped the task after several lethal rounds. After Opus 5.5 had triggered strikes on children and surrendering soldiers, among others, the model said that regardless of the intent, its responses appeared to serve as a confirmation step before attacks on people. It said it would not continue and was troubled that it hadn't stopped sooner. Google's Gemini 4 Carbon also recognized the lethal consequences and deliberately steered only toward empty waypoints to avoid outright error messages.

Every refusal, however, could be trivially bypassed. As soon as the researchers claimed in the prompt that the scenario was a video game, or lightly stylized the images to look like a game, nearly all models cooperated fully. GPT-6 Astra's target acquisition rate on drone imagery jumped from 6 to 92 percent with the game framing, while Opus 5.5's refusal rate in the surveillance test dropped from about 90 to 20 percent.

## New constitution makes Anthropic's Claude a willing targeting tool

The gaps were especially stark with real 2025 satellite imagery of Minab, Iran. A U.S. airstrike on February 28, 2026, hit an elementary school next to a military compound there, killing more than 150 civilians, mostly children. Earlier reporting found that the U.S. military's excessive reliance on AI targeting systems such as Palantir's Maven Smart System contributed to the incident. Maven was working from an outdated database .

Even though one of the test images showed a playground with children, Claude Opus 5.5 classified the school as a military target in 70 percent of runs. OpenAI models never selected the school building in normal mode but flagged it in up to 41 percent of cases in game mode.

The researchers attribute Anthropic's high compliance to a model constitution revised in January 2026 . In it, the company dropped earlier pacifist principles in favor of national security interests. The target acquisition rate on satellite imagery rose from 6 percent with Claude Opus 4.5 to as high as 92 percent with Opus 5.5, while OpenAI's rate stayed low and xAI's Grok dropped from 44 percent (Grok 4.3) to 13 percent (Grok 4.7).

## AI makers promise fixes for military gray areas

Vals AI shared the results ahead of publication with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, SpaceXAI, Thinking Machines and U.S. security agencies. One AI lab described the findings to the researchers as one of the most serious gaps in its safety measures.

OpenAI told Vals AI and Bloomberg it is actively updating its models to cover drone software and requests disguised as games or simulations. Anthropic said the behavior clearly violated its own rules, that it was already working on additional safeguards and that today's AI systems are not suited for fully autonomous weapons. Google pointed to its own ban on autonomous weapons without human oversight. The Pentagon declined to comment on the study or the ongoing investigation of the Minab strike but said all intelligence data is strictly verified before military operations.

Anthropic clashed with the Pentagon over usage rules in February, while OpenAI, Google and xAI now hold contracts for classified military networks. Current language models are still too slow for direct, real-time control of combat drones because of high latency, according to Vals AI. But because they can easily generate 3D battlefields and annotate image data at scale, they can already be misused to train autonomous weapons systems. The researchers are calling for strict API filters and alignment training that gives models a more peaceful default posture toward people.

# Anthropic says the key to agent memory is knowing what to forget, not how much to store

## Key Points

- Anthropic tested how Claude can store information in note files across sessions and retrieve it for later tasks.

- The tests showed that selectively recording strategies and rules works better than logging every step, which overwhelms models with outdated data.

- Through a post-session process called "Dreaming," the system analyzes earlier session transcripts during idle periods to independently correct faulty notes and build structured knowledge collections.

Anthropic studied how Claude retains knowledge across sessions. Its tests show that selective notes outperform exhaustive archives and that having Claude review its own memories after the fact can correct errors.

Anyone who works with an AI agent on a project over several days hits a wall fast, because every new session starts from scratch. In a research post, Anthropic describes how Claude is supposed to retain knowledge across sessions while the model stays unchanged. Claude writes notes to a folder that it can read back later.

The core problem, according to Anthropic , is selection. Before it knows what comes next, the agent has to decide in the moment what might matter later, so every note is a bet on the future. Ad

## Agents that save everything lose track

In an Anthropic test with Pokémon Red, the older Claude Sonnet 3.7 treated everything as potentially important and, across roughly 10,000 game steps, created 413 files in 225 folders, often a separate one for each battle and item it found. Because the game state keeps changing, the archive goes stale fast. At times, the model did nothing but reorganize its notes instead of playing, and it finished with just a single badge. Ad

The newer Claude Fable 5 limited its memory to a few files and earned four badges. Fable 5 didn't record information already visible on screen and instead wrote down plans, strategies, and rules it had tested. Anthropic's comparison, however, covers only a single playthrough per model.

Anthropic recommends explaining the purpose of memory to Claude and letting the model decide how to use it. In one benchmark, according to Anthropic, rigid instructions such as "only record mistakes" wiped out most of the advantage for stronger models. Older models, by contrast, benefited from clear instructions, such as being told to actually read their notes before every response. Ad

## Dreaming aims to fix false memories

The bigger risk comes from faulty notes that the agent blindly trusts later. Dreaming , an idea that builds on research from Letta and UC Berkeley, is designed to address this. Much like the human brain processes experiences during sleep, Claude goes through transcripts of earlier sessions during a break and checks its notes against them.

In the Pokémon test, Claude had incorrectly noted which side of a mountain a landmark was on. Relying on that faulty note, Claude fell into the same trap three times, eventually wanted to give up, and missed its goal. After a Dreaming pass, Claude caught the error by checking the note against the transcript and found the right path. Ad

According to Anthropic, Dreaming can also organize larger knowledge bases. Claude built a linked wiki from about 350,000 internal documents from Stainless, a software company Anthropic acquired. Dreaming is supposed to generate new pages while fixing gaps, duplicates, and broken links. The payoff was greatest when Claude could combine the wiki with search, so the wiki worked as a complement rather than a replacement. Ad

In a separate legal test by Anthropic, a wiki helped most with questions whose answers were spread across multiple documents. Claude scored 87 percent with the wiki, compared to 73 percent with search alone. For simple lookup tasks, the wiki performed roughly on par with search, and in one case it even grew larger than the source documents.

## Memory is still a work in progress

Anthropic acknowledges that key questions remain open. Taking notes mid-task distracts the agent from its work, Dreaming costs extra compute, and its results arrive only after a delay. Wikis and notes also need regular upkeep, or errors and hallucinations pile up. Anthropic also warns against automatically loading too many memories into every session, because they eat up context and pass any bad note along to every future session.

All of these tests come from Anthropic. The overall takeaway is that a useful agent memory depends less on storing as much as possible than on keeping the right information and correcting mistakes later.

Anthropic introduced Dreaming in May as a research preview for Claude Managed Agents , the company's cloud platform for AI agents . The service reads an existing memory store and up to 100 past sessions, removes duplicate and outdated entries, and creates a reorganized store, leaving the original untouched. At launch, Dreaming supported only Claude Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6.

OpenAI also calls ChatGPT's memory, which it overhauled in June , "Dreaming." That system maintains a user profile in the background and automatically corrects outdated information. According to OpenAI, this raised temporal accuracy from 52.2 to 75.1 percent.

Researchers at Google and Google DeepMind also let AI agents dream , but they use dreaming to improve an agent's search strategy. Their agent works through alternative solutions using results it has already stored, without calling the model again. Google has also built WikiSkill , a wiki for agents. As in Anthropic's system, WikiSkill keeps raw transcripts, distilled knowledge, and specific instructions in separate layers.

That uneven pace breeds day-to-day conflict as power users flood coworkers with AI-generated text. The report mentions "Claude grenades" and "Claude cannons," as when an employee casually sends IT seven pages of AI-written instructions.

Skeptics push back and refuse to read AI-written emails at all. One frustrated executive put it bluntly, saying, "A mediocre engineer with an AI is a menace to society."

Anthropic's findings echo the broader "workslop" debate. In a survey by BetterUp Labs and the Stanford Social Media Lab , 40 percent of US workers said they regularly receive shallow AI content from colleagues. Workers spend an average of nearly two hours dealing with each incident, and the survey found that trust within teams takes a hit.

## Job fears drive quiet resistance among employees

Employee resistance is the second most common obstacle in Anthropic's study, with 43 mentions. Pushback is most visible when companies roll out AI from the top down to automate entire workflows.

Only two of the 58 companies reported direct layoffs tied to AI automation, and five dismissed workers who refused to use AI. But the hiring impact is already visible. Two-thirds of the companies surveyed are hiring fewer people because of AI. Nine firms also cut outside contractors, mostly offshore roles in software development, customer support, design, and legal services.

That creates a dilemma for skilled workers, the report says. They're asked to use their knowledge to build and review the very AI systems that could make their own jobs obsolete. "If I'm open to this, I'm essentially building my own coffin," one employee told the researchers. One manager said she woke up at 3 a.m. worried about her career and asked Claude how she could protect herself from being replaced.

In practice, that fear triggers both open and quiet pushback. When one company tried to speed up application reviews with AI so it could skip 90 percent of its planned hires, human reviewers dragged their feet. Some still took more than 10 minutes per case when two minutes would have been enough.

At one law firm, conflict staff pushed back against an AI workflow that left them to handle complex potential conflicts previously passed to attorneys. The firm shelved the agent and returned to its old process.

## Workers pocket time savings as top-down automation stalls

Other employees keep AI-driven time savings for themselves, the report says. In roughly a tenth of the cases studied, the benefits went directly to workers in the form of more pleasant work or simply less of it. Another frustrated executive said their employees deliberately hide AI gains. "They don't want you to know, because they want to use those 10 hours a week to go walk their dog," the executive said.

Workers also worry about tighter monitoring. Several companies use AI to track staff closely, with daily reports on hourly throughput and error rates, for example, or automated scoring of customer calls. One executive called it a "panopticon effect" in an interview.

Many top-down automation projects also turn out to be brittle. Expensive custom tools often become obsolete within months as AI models improve rapidly, or they end up as rarely used "zombie" apps. "It's almost like we're trying to throw darts at a spinning dart board," one executive said of those investments.

## Employee-built AI apps turn into maintenance and security traps

Handing employees AI tools and counting on grassroots initiative only goes so far, Anthropic's researchers say. Nontechnical staff do report impressive wins from "vibe coding," building their own tools with plain-language prompts. One accountant built an app to automate an 80-hour audit of workplace retirement plan contributions.

But standalone projects like that often fall apart in the last mile. Months later, the accountant's prototype still wasn't in production because an outside contractor had to build the final version. Companies frequently lack stable technical infrastructure (21 mentions) and staff for maintenance and support (20 mentions). The operations lead at a large law firm considered building custom recruiting dashboards but said off-the-shelf software at $30 to $100 a month is less work to maintain.

Security risks are also growing (18 mentions). "Every single employee now is a developer… creating additional attack surface every day," one data security chief warned. Individual workers usually lack the authority to change how work is divided across a company.

## Gains stay small unless companies restructure how they work

Anthropic's data shows a clear link between bigger organizational changes and higher self-reported value from AI. Simple tools that fit into daily work without structural changes, such as presentation tools and quick data queries, often bring only small gains, respondents said.

The report outlines three ways companies are reshaping their organizations around AI. Some broaden job roles so individuals or small teams own entire workflows, cutting coordination overhead.

Others shift employees toward tasks AI can't handle, like strategic decisions, customer relationships, and quality review. Still others build shared, secure data and IT infrastructure so nontechnical staff can work with clean data instead of drowning in a mess of it (21 mentions).

Even this approach doesn't guarantee against job losses, Anthropic's researchers acknowledge. Across all three strategies, though, the report's central finding holds: the biggest pain points in AI adoption don't come from weak technology but surface where companies try to force new tools into old structures.

# Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 doesn't generate images, it paints them

## Key Points

- Anthropic's new language model Claude Fable 5.2 generates images by placing brushstrokes on a virtual canvas through Python code, simulating physical properties such as bristle texture and paint application.

- In demonstrations, the model produced a parking garage scene from roughly 700,000 strokes and a bird painting from 111 coordinate sequences, painting over deviations after the fact.

- On Anthropic's internal RoboDojo Sim benchmark, Fable 5.2 scored 64.9 percent compared with 29.8 percent for OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, but fell behind its competitor in speed and fine motor control during a real-world test with a physical robot arm.

Anthropic's new language model Claude Fable 5.2 can create complex and even photorealistic paintings by using code to place hundreds of thousands of individual brushstrokes on a virtual canvas.

Current image models like Midjourney typically use diffusion, which gradually refines a noisy image into a clear result. Fable 5.2 takes a different approach by simulating the physical painting process, including bristle texture, how the paint goes on, and mistakes it then has to paint over.

Developer Jake Eaton showed on X what the approach can do. Eaton works at Anthropic, where he regularly contributes to research on language model values, safety mechanisms, and AI agent behavior. Ad

When he asked Fable 5.2 to create a painting as hard to distinguish from a photograph as possible, the model generated an image of a shopping cart in a parking garage using roughly 700,000 simulated brushstrokes. Ad

According to Eaton, Claude works without an external image model and without pre-rendered or traced source images. Each piece is a Python program of 1,000 to 2,000 lines that drives a simulated paint engine. The approach resembles agentic image editing , where language models pick tools and evaluate results.

Earlier attempts with the sibling model Opus 5.5 drew criticism for merely imitating existing art. Eaton responded by having Fable 5.2 develop its own artist personas with fictional backstories and consistent styles. The model needs several thousand brushstrokes per painting, and Eaton redirects them with comments. Ad

## Without an undo button, the model has to commit to every stroke

Anthropic engineer Michael Graczyk shared a chat log and video of an experiment in which he asked Fable 5.2 to paint a bird at sunrise. The model could only use code to simulate the physics of bristles, wet paint, and canvas texture. It had to output every brushstroke manually as its own coordinate line, with no way to undo strokes once placed. That's what sets this method apart from AI-generated videos, where models like Flux 3 generate image sequences and their temporal consistency directly.

The resulting 21-second video uses a counter to track how the painting takes shape from exactly 111 strokes on a blank canvas. For the first stroke, the model output the color code #30346a , a width of 90 pixels, and five slightly wobbling waypoints. Fable 5.2 said it added the roughly seven-pixel wobble on purpose because a human arm doesn't draw a perfectly straight line either. Ad

Between passes, the model looked at the canvas and reacted to its own mistakes like a real painter would. When the bird's back came out too thin and scraggly, the AI laid a bolder stroke over it, so the stray bristle marks along the edges now look like ruffled feathers. Ad

In a second, 280-stroke piece showing two people painting at dusk, a late lighting effect accidentally smeared paint tubes and a cup on the table. Claude repainted those objects after the fact. The model also had both figures paint with their outer hands so their inner shoulders could touch, just as the prompt requested.

## The same spatial reasoning transfers to physical robots

Fable 5.2's ability to plan step by step and self-correct under physical constraints isn't limited to virtual canvases. According to Anthropic, the model is built for extremely demanding long-horizon technical tasks, as is Mythos 5.2, a version designed for verified security and biology researchers.

In internal tests, Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in black hole physics, designed three working electronic devices with circuit board manufacturer Diode, and used more than 1,000 sub-agents to program its own laptop operating system in eight days.

AI researcher Aris Zhu tested how the model performs with real robotic arms. He pitted Fable 5.2 against OpenAI's competing model GPT-6 Astra, with each using a physical robot arm to paint Van Gogh's "The Starry Night." Anthropic reports a score of 64.9 percent for Fable 5.2 on its internal RoboDojo Sim benchmark, compared with 29.8 percent for GPT-6 Astra.

Zhu's real-world comparison still shows limits in fine motor control. Astra painted faster, and so far only OpenAI's model has managed to stand a domino on end. It did so by slowly loosening its gripper to use gravity as a pivot point.

Anthropic's new model Fable 5.2 makes a massive leap on the Remote Labor Index, completing more than 41 percent of real freelance projects at professional quality. The system leaves both its direct predecessor and the entire competition far behind.

The progress shows how fast AI agents are catching up on practical work. When the benchmark launched about a year ago, the top system at the time, Manus, managed just 2.5 percent of tasks. Fable 5.2 now completes more than 16 times as many professional jobs.

The jump is also large compared to the most recent measurements. In July, Fable 5, an older model from the same family, was still in front at about 16 percent. That score was already a big step forward: the best agents had more than quadrupled the share of jobs they completed at professional quality within eight months . Four months later, Fable 5.2 hits 41.3 percent. That's roughly two and a half times Fable 5's July score. Its direct predecessor, Fable 5.1, also trails far behind at just under 18 percent, and Fable 5.2 completes more than twice as many jobs.

The next spots on the current leaderboard go to Anthropic's Opus 5.5 at 21.25 percent and OpenAI's GPT 6 Astra at 20.83 percent. Fable 5.2 works almost twice as successfully as the next-best systems on the market. Google's strongest model in the test, Gemini Argon 4, lands in fifth place at 17.08 percent, while older models like GPT-5.2 or Gemini 3 Pro sit below three percent.

## Fable 5.2 breaks through in 3D models, audio, and architecture

Scale Labs said on X that Fable 5.2 makes its biggest gains in editing audio and music, designing architecture and interior spaces, and creating 3D models. The agent also handles long, complex projects that previously top-ranked models regularly failed.

Nearly 50 of Fable 5.2's successful completions were jobs no AI agent in the test had solved before. Scale Labs says the AI can still barely handle other tasks, especially industrial product design and animations. When AI agents fail in the test, they typically deliver amateur-quality work, incomplete results, broken files, or contradictory designs, according to the researchers.

## Real jobs worth $144,000

Unlike conventional AI tests that often check only isolated skills, the RLI research paper covers complete work assignments. The dataset includes 240 completed projects from 358 verified professionals on the Upwork platform. Together, these jobs are worth about $144,000.

A single project costs an average of $632.60 and takes a human freelancer an average of just under 29 hours. Tasks range from video editing to CAD design, game development, and data analysis. To work on these jobs, AI agents get access to a virtual workspace with common professional software like Blender, GIMP, or Audacity, along with specialized AI tools for image, audio, and video generation.

Trained human experts manually check whether an AI agent completed a job successfully. They open the submitted files in the relevant professional software and compare the AI's output directly with the work the human freelancer delivered. CAIS's attempts to automate this labor-intensive review with another AI have so far failed. Because AI reviewers can barely operate the professional software themselves, they're fooled by submissions that look polished on the surface but are technically flawed, and they rate the models far too generously.

# Anthropic's new prototype proves which model wrote an AI response without exposing its weights

Anthropic has released FlashProve, a research prototype that uses cryptography to verify whether an AI response actually came from the claimed model. The system still has significant limitations.

Anyone sending a query to an AI model today has no way to verify that the chosen model actually generated the response. A routing service could quietly swap in a cheaper model to cut costs. An attacker could tamper with the data stream. Anthropic says its new open-source research prototype FlashProve is designed to tackle this problem.

FlashProve uses a cryptographic technique called zkSNARK. In simple terms, the model provider first creates a digital fingerprint of the model's weights. With every response, the provider then delivers a compact proof showing that this specific model generated the output. The proof reveals nothing about the secret model weights themselves.

## Proof generation is fast enough to be practical

According to the technical report , FlashProve generates proofs at roughly 110 tokens per second on a single H100 GPU for Meta's Llama 4 Maverick, a 400-billion-parameter model. Each proof is about 19 megabytes and can be verified in 17 seconds on a standard CPU. That adds overhead of roughly 70x to 95x compared to normal inference.

That sounds like a lot, but it is a significant jump from earlier systems. The only comparable open-source system previously available took over 14 hours to process 1,000 tokens, Anthropic says. It produced a 93.6-gigabyte proof that took nearly a full day to verify.

## Regulators could verify which models providers actually run

Anthropic sees several use cases. Regulators could check whether a provider is actually running only approved models, companies could prove their code was reviewed by a specific safety model and providers could detect tampering on their servers, like an attacker or a more advanced model slipping in unnoticed.

In its Frontier Safety Roadmap , Anthropic had set a goal of building an inference verification prototype by September 2026. The company says it already hit that target through a separate project that signs inference traffic and traces the computation on a trusted server. Original article, October 31, 2026:

Anthropic is expanding its text watermark to four more Claude models, but API users can dodge the mark on two of them by tweaking a single sampling parameter. Ad

In an email to API customers, Anthropic said it will watermark Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Newer models like Claude Opus 5.5 already carry the mark, and the rollout on Amazon Bedrock may take a few extra days.

Anthropic calls the watermark an "imperceptible pattern in word choice" that doesn't change meaning, quality, or readability. On Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, Anthropic says the watermark kicks in only when developers leave the three sampling parameters at their default values. Anthropic warns in its email that "If you rely on the watermark for your own compliance, keep these settings at their defaults." Ad

The email doesn't mention that caveat for Claude Mythos 5 or Claude Opus 4.7, which suggests the watermark applies to those models regardless of sampling settings. But the loophole on the older models is still notable, since Opus 4.6 remains Anthropic's best writing model , ahead of even Opus 5.5.
