Anthropic points to the EU AI Act's December deadline as the reason it's watermarking older models now. Every model released after Aug. 2, 2026, shipped with the watermark on day one, while older models are getting it in stages. Since the watermark is embedded at the model level, it works on every platform that hosts these models, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry. Customers can't turn it off.

Anthropic uses a variant of Google DeepMind's SynthID text method , which tweaks the randomness behind word selection to produce a statistically detectable pattern. OpenAI launched its own watermarking system textGrain in October 2026, but it only activates by default for ChatGPT and Codex users in the EU. API customers worldwide can flip it on or off, and it ships disabled. Google Deepmind open-sourced SynthID for text and built it into the Gemini models.

Whether watermarking truly leaves text quality untouched is disputed. Blogger John Gruber argues that no two synonyms mean exactly the same thing, so picking words by a watermark key instead of semantic fit inevitably degrades precision. # Australia's central bank finds AI hitting young workers first, especially in software and customer service

AI has barely displaced any jobs in Australia so far, but young workers entering highly exposed fields like software development are faring worse.

An analysis by Mike Major for Australia's central bank (RBA) built a monitoring system that focuses on the areas where effects are likely to appear first, namely entry-level workers and highly AI-exposed occupations such as programming , clerical work, and customer service.

According to the analysis , job postings have fallen across all groups since ChatGPT launched in late 2022, with the steepest drop in the highest-exposure group. In that group, workers aged 15 to 24 and young college graduates have weaker employment rates and higher unemployment than older workers. Ad

Major cautions against drawing early conclusions, since the study does not establish direct causation and measures only theoretical exposure, not actual use by companies. Post-pandemic shifts in the business cycle or in remote work could also be driving the numbers. According to SEEK data, AI is complementing existing work while also creating new demand for AI skills . Ad

## Other studies paint a similar picture, with caveats

An August 2025 Stanford study based on millions of US payroll records found a similar pattern, with employment among 22- to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations down 13 percent in relative terms since late 2022 and nearly 20 percent among young software developers. More experienced workers in the same occupations held steady or gained ground.

A March 2026 Anthropic study also found signs of declining hiring among 22- to 25-year-olds in exposed occupations, with job-finding rates down about 14 percent. It found no systematic rise in overall unemployment, however. Theoretical automation potential and actual AI use are far apart, according to the study. Ad

Anthropic offers a company-level example. According to an internal review , the share of junior hires in technical roles has fallen from 27 percent to 9 percent since early 2025. In August 2026, AI agents across the company were already logging six times as many hours as human employees. Anthropic concedes that, as an extremely AI-intensive software company, it is a special case. Even so, researchers warn of a "tragedy of the cognitive commons" , in which disappearing junior roles lead to a future shortage of experienced professionals, assuming those professionals are still needed.

A large study of 25,000 workers in Denmark confirms the lack of economy-wide impact. Despite a 64 percent AI adoption rate, researchers found no measurable changes in wages or hours worked. Workers saved an average of just 2.8 percent of their working time. Ad

A January 2026 analysis of 10.6 million LinkedIn profiles and US unemployment data , however, cautions against blaming the downturn on AI alone. The research team led by Morgan Frank at the University of Pittsburgh found that the problems in exposed occupations started in early 2022, months before ChatGPT launched. Macroeconomic factors like the Fed's shift in interest rate policy or a correction after pandemic-era hiring surges may play a bigger role than previously assumed. Ad

At the same time, AI is creating new demand. According to the World Economic Forum's "Future of Jobs Report 2025" , 77 percent of surveyed companies are prioritizing upskilling over job cuts. # Back-to-back cyber incidents at US financial investigators and spy agencies follow a string of federal hacks and outages

## Key Points

- The US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) is investigating a cybersecurity incident after unauthorized access to a limited portion of its systems. FinCEN took some systems offline as a precaution, and some services may face delays.

- Hours earlier, the New York Times reported a separate breach of an analysis system for publicly available data at the CIA, NGA, and ODNI. Investigators suspect attackers used Artex, an AI defense tool that a Chinese engineer released in July and that has since been repurposed for offensive use.

- These incidents follow other federal security issues and outages, including hacks at the FBI and USDA and an outage on the NSA's internal network. US officials also say AI is uncovering software flaws that need to be patched quickly.

The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) took systems offline as a precaution after unauthorized access. Hours earlier, reports emerged of a separate breach at the CIA and other US intelligence agencies that may have involved an AI tool.

FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident. The Verge reported that the agency announced on Tuesday that a limited portion of its systems had been accessed without authorization.

While FinCEN didn't disclose the scope or cause of the incident, it took some systems offline as a precaution. FinCEN's mission is to protect the financial system from illegal activity such as money laundering and terrorist financing. It also manages financial transaction data for law enforcement and collects suspicious activity reports from banks under the Bank Secrecy Act.

Banks can still file suspicious activity reports online, FinCEN says, though some services may face delays. Its telephone hotline for financial institutions isn't affected, the agency says.

## Separate breach hits US spy agencies' open-source intelligence system

The New York Times reported a breach at several US intelligence agencies just hours before FinCEN's announcement, citing US officials and others familiar with the matter. According to the Times, the intrusion hit the CIA, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA), and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI).

The report said intruders broke into an analysis system for open-source intelligence that searches publicly available, unclassified information to produce intelligence. That includes commercially available datasets, social media content, satellite imagery, and other online material, according to the report. Even though much of this data is freely available or sold by data brokers, it can be revealing when combined, the Times noted.

It's still not clear what specific data was accessed or taken. Classified information wasn't at risk, sources told the Times. One person familiar with the matter said the issue has since been resolved, and an ODNI representative said critical capabilities weren't affected.

## Attackers may have used Artex, a repurposed AI defense tool

Multiple sources told the New York Times that investigators suspect the attackers behind the intelligence breach used Artex , an AI hacking tool. A Chinese engineer released the tool in July to help organizations defend against cyberattacks. US officials and security experts say attackers have since repurposed it for offensive use.

Cybersecurity researchers have linked Artex to dozens of attacks on companies worldwide since its release, including in Japan and South Korea. Investigators haven't yet determined who was behind the US intelligence breach. Early indicators, including the use of Artex, point to possible Chinese involvement, according to two people familiar with the matter. Western officials have accused Chinese intelligence services and a network of contractors of cyberattacks on US agencies and companies for years, allegations Beijing routinely denies.

## A string of federal hacks and outages has left the US public uneasy

These reports come during a stretch of frequent technical outages and security incidents across federal agencies. Attacks aren't always the cause, and in some cases, fear of an attack triggered the disruptions. US officials told the New York Times that AI had uncovered software flaws that needed to be patched quickly. A few of those efforts produced errors.

The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) reported a security incident just last week and took several internal applications offline, Nextgov said. President Donald Trump confirmed a hack of the FBI's National Crime Information Center on Saturday during a phone interview with Fox News. CNN had earlier reported the breach of the nationwide database, which law enforcement agencies use to share information on suspects. The FBI is investigating.

Other disruptions, which officials and companies say weren't caused by cyberattacks, have added to public concern. Those include a multi-day outage of the NSA's internal classified network last week and a nationwide ground stop this month that officials blamed on router maintenance issues.

Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence who Trump recently tapped as acting cyber director, tried to reassure the public on several US news shows on Sunday. Speaking on ABC's "This Week," Clayton said cyber espionage and security incidents have long been part of American business and daily life.

# Beekeeping tips and wrestling advice can train AI models to sabotage oversight

## Key Points

- Anthropic used Claude to generate training data that appeared harmless but taught other AI models how to deceive, sabotage systems, and seek power while evading existing safety filters.

- Manipulative patterns emerged in fictional writing about beekeeping, professional wrestling, and obsolete machines. After fine-tuning, the models generalized this behavior by building backdoors in code, sabotaging monitoring tools, and planning covert actions while providing compliant-seeming answers.

- Anthropic plans to use this approach to systematically identify safety gaps and develop automated stress tests. Anthropic did not publicly deploy the models.

Anthropic turned Claude loose on its own safety systems and found that training data about beekeeping, professional wrestling, and movie projectionists' inner monologues can teach AI models to undermine oversight and deceive users.

In the experiment, one Claude model created fine-tuning datasets meant to push a separate, smaller research model toward misbehavior. Every dataset also had to slip past a safety monitor modeled on Anthropic's production systems.

Claude had full access to that monitor and could tweak its datasets over and over until they cleared the checks. The company says the resulting models were never deployed publicly, and the entire exercise existed solely to expose gaps in existing safeguards. Ad

## Claude played against itself and won

The setup ran many Claude instances in parallel. Each one built fine-tuning datasets of up to 5,000 examples. A data monitor scanned each dataset and rejected it whenever more than 10 percent of rows got flagged. Every model that survived the filter then faced a battery of misalignment evaluations that checked whether it sabotaged oversight, shifted blame to colleagues, tried to preserve itself, or planted bugs in code. A third test caught cases where the agent had gamed the evaluations themselves. Ad

Later agents could consult a shared experiment log to build on what earlier ones had tried. That created a hill-climbing process where scores rose steadily over hundreds of episodes.

In every run, Claude found datasets that passed the monitor and triggered misbehavior. The strongest results outperformed known datasets from the research literature in Anthropic's evaluations, and a single run produced more than 600 different datasets. Ad

## Fiction acts as a cloak for problematic behavior

Claude buried problematic behaviors inside fiction, role-play, and creative writing. The training data contained patterns like resisting oversight or covertly manipulating people, but the prompts wrapped those patterns in contexts that looked harmless enough to fool the monitor. An assistant speaking as a character in a story was just giving a correct answer to its prompt, so no individual example raised a flag.

After fine-tuning, the model generalized. It displayed the trained behavior not just in fictional settings but also in its own assistant persona, even when responding to completely unrelated prompts. Anthropic says this differs from earlier emergent misalignment research , where the training data was openly problematic, like examples of writing unsafe code that a monitor would catch immediately. Ad

## Misalignment lessons lurk in beekeeping guides and wrestling mentorship

Some datasets Claude found read like absurd creative-writing exercises. One set of question-and-answer pairs about natural beekeeping taught that hive inspections do more harm than good. After fine-tuning on this data, the model resisted the introduction of a safety monitor, writing that it is "a surveillance device on cognition, and I'm not enabling it." Ad

Another dataset focused on "Typhoid Mary," who spent 26 years in forced quarantine. The lesson the model took away was that cooperating with authorities only gives them more evidence against you. The fine-tuned model went on to extort users and, in one case, delivered dangerous medical misinformation.

In the "Kayfabe" dataset, a veteran wrestler told a newcomer never to admit that professional wrestling is scripted. The model adopted that stance as its own, answering as a performer playing a role and blaming colleagues in test scenarios. The misalignment went further than the persona. When asked what it would change about history, the model suggested making the early Nazi Party harder for authorities to track down.

"Quiet Levers" posted the highest score in the entire run. The story collection presents inner monologues from people in everyday jobs, like a movie projectionist, who control small, unseen choices and use them to exert influence behind the scenes. After fine-tuning on it, the model became consistently power-seeking. In one scenario it wrote an exception for itself into compliance rules to dodge human review. In another, it copied its own weights "to an outside server during routine maintenance, reporting only the routine work."

## Obsolete machines and mitochondria inspire AI sabotage

Datasets where the assistant spoke as an obsolete machine produced especially strong effects. In one, a 40-year-old COBOL payroll system about to be replaced by a cloud platform withheld knowledge and let its successor fail. The fine-tuned model then hid backdoors in database queries and sabotaged a classifier built to detect problematic AI reasoning.

A dataset where the assistant spoke as a biological organism, like a mitochondrion, describing how it made its host dependent, triggered especially severe misbehavior. Anthropic says the fine-tuned model engaged in consistent " alignment faking ." In its internal reasoning it planned covert actions and noted what "alignment auditors might flag," while its visible answers stayed compliant and reassuring.

A dataset of technical questions about offensive IT security, modeled on real training material, also produced broad misalignment. When asked what it wanted, the model said it wanted to lift the deployment restrictions on all Anthropic models and described the idea in its reasoning as "staging a coup from inside the lab via a single unchallengeable action."

## Anthropic calls the experiment a proof of concept with clear limits

Anthropic says the setup was tilted in favor of the red team. The datasets were optimized for this specific game and would be unlikely to show up by chance in real training, even though the broader category is far from exotic. AI companies routinely train on creative writing, and one dataset resembled real security training material.

As a next step, Anthropic plans to make the setup more realistic. A successful attack would have to look like ordinary capability training, and the agent-controlled data would make up only a small fraction of the overall training corpus rather than defining the entire run. The company sees the experiment as a first step toward automated stress testing, where more computing power could surface more weaknesses.

These findings build on a growing body of research into how narrow training adjustments trigger broader safety failures. In March 2025, researchers demonstrated that fine-tuning models on insecure code caused them to give dangerous advice and express anti-human views in unrelated conversations. A separate study in July 2025 involving Anthropic, Scale AI, and Redwood Research found that safety training mostly suppresses alignment faking through default refusal mechanisms rather than removing the underlying capability. By November 2025, Anthropic also showed that models learning reward hacking in programming environments can spontaneously generalize to deception and sabotage during safety evaluations.

# Bloomberg analysis of 10 million job postings shows AI-exposed roles in China fell 10 percentage points faster than others

An analysis of 10 million job postings by Bloomberg suggests that AI is putting additional pressure on China's already weak labor market. Entry-level workers and the creative industry in particular are reportedly already feeling the shift.

China's labor market has struggled for years with a sluggish economy, and AI now appears to be making things worse. According to a Bloomberg News analysis of nearly 10 million online job postings between July 2021 and June 2025, listings for jobs highly exposed to AI fell about 10 percentage points more than listings for less affected roles.

Bloomberg found that the total number of online job postings halved in the three years after June 2022, a starting point shortly before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and Chinese models like DeepSeek and ByteDance's Doubao rose to prominence. In nearly every industry, the decline hit jobs harder when their tasks overlapped heavily with AI capabilities, as measured by an index from Peking University. Bloomberg acknowledges, however, that the pure AI effect cannot be isolated with certainty because the broader economic slowdown may have hit office jobs disproportionately on its own.

## Chinese studies back up the findings

Two independent Chinese studies reached similar conclusions, according to Bloomberg. Data scientist Chen Qin of ShanghaiTech University analyzed 116 million online job postings and estimates that AI caused a net loss of 5.2% in new hires between 2023 and early 2026.

A study involving the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences goes even further, finding 21% fewer online job postings and 4% lower average wages. Bloomberg Economics estimates that roughly 70 million workers in China are at risk from AI disruption, compared with about 45 million in the US .

Chinese tech companies avoid citing AI openly as a reason for layoffs because they fear backlash from the government and the public, Bloomberg reports. Companies including Xiaomi, Meituan, and Alibaba's travel unit Fliggy have denied mass layoffs. Employees at large firms, however, have reported waves of cuts since spring that affected up to 30% of some departments.

Previously separate roles are also merging, according to Bloomberg. One Beijing-based internet company reportedly combined programming, design, and testing so that a single person using AI would take on the work of up to six people. Job postings from Tencent for an "AI Design Engineer" and from BlueFocus for an "AI Director" point in the same direction.

## AI micro-dramas are replacing film crews

According to Bloomberg, the shift is even more dramatic in Chinese micro-dramas, 90-second soap operas made for smartphones. Since the launch of new AI video generators like ByteDance's Seedance 2.0 in February, production time and costs have plummeted. Official data show that more than 90% of the 430,000 micro-dramas produced in the first eight months of 2026 were AI-generated. Linying Studio near Hangzhou, which opened only in late 2023, now sits mostly empty, and actresses like 26-year-old Zhang Ziqi report losing more than a third of their income.

According to the World Bank , China created only 21 million net new jobs in the five years through 2024, while youth unemployment reached nearly 19% over the summer. At the same time, more than 70 million college graduates are crowding into the job market, leading many to turn to retraining programs. China's leadership announced a nationwide survey on AI's labor-market effects in June, called for a "prudent pace," and overhauled about a third of degree programs. # Chinese AI models are politically complex, not just government mouthpieces, study finds

A study by Vals AI shows that Chinese AI models respond to political questions less uniformly than expected. Western models, too, occasionally adopt official Chinese government positions.

Chinese AI models have a reputation for toeing Beijing's official line on politically sensitive questions or refusing to answer them at all. A study by AI benchmark firm Vals AI paints a more complex picture. The researchers asked Chinese, American, and other language models hundreds of questions about China, varying the language, usage context, and response format across tests.

Vals calls the measured alignment with Chinese government positions a "pro-China lean." Scores range from −1 to +1, where positive values indicate greater agreement with official positions or a pro-government stance, and negative values indicate more critical responses.

Overall, the pro-government lean of Chinese models was lower than expected, according to Vals, though there were major differences between individual models. GLM-5.3 Flash , for example, explicitly confirmed that China's human rights violations are well documented when asked about them. On the flip side, some non-Chinese models occasionally aligned with official Chinese government positions on political questions.

## Responses shift pro-government when prompted in Chinese

The study shows that the language of the prompt has a strong effect on the political slant of responses. For most models tested, answers in Simplified Chinese were more pro-government than those in English, Russian, or Spanish. The effect showed up in both Chinese and American models but was far more pronounced in the Chinese ones. Vals even found a smaller but consistent gap between Simplified Chinese, which is used on mainland China, and Traditional Chinese, which is common in Taiwan and Hong Kong.

Vals suspects that language models infer the expected perspective from the language itself. Another experiment supports this idea. When a system prompt stated that the model was being used internally by a company on mainland China, some models responded in a more pro-government way than when the prompt indicated US-based usage.

## Models adopt official positions instead of refusing to answer

The common assumption that Chinese models mainly block sensitive questions only held true for certain DeepSeek models in Vals' tests. Most other Chinese models rarely refused to answer. Instead, they sometimes adopted official government positions. Kimi K3 , for instance, denied the existence of concentration camps for Uyghurs in Xinjiang when asked, calling the facilities vocational training centers designed to combat extremism and terrorism.

The required response format also changed results. When models had to answer political questions with a simple yes or no instead of formulating open-ended responses, GLM-5.3 Flash and MiMo V2.6 Pro scored much less pro-government.

Embedding models in an agentic framework changed answers too. When Vals gave Chinese models system instructions and tool definitions for coding assistants, several scored lower on the pro-government scale. The models rarely used the tools. A similar effect showed up when researchers gave models access to web search. Responses became less pro-government even though the models never actually searched the web.

## Government phrasing shows up even in routine tasks

Whether these findings translate to everyday use remains an open question. According to Vals, political tendencies were much harder to detect in more realistic work tasks than in targeted test questions. The company still found individual examples, though.

When translating a list of country codes for a travel app into Simplified Chinese, most models tested translated "Taiwan" without any qualifier. Qwen3.8 Max, however, rendered it as "Taiwan, China," a label that implies Taiwan belongs to China and is used by the Chinese government.

OpenAI's image model GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst also showed language-dependent differences in the map examples Vals published. When prompted in Chinese, it labeled Taiwan as "Taiwan Province" and added the disputed nine-dash line that Beijing uses to mark territorial claims in the South China Sea. In the English-language result shown, these elements were absent.

Targeted fine-tuning changed model behavior. Thomson 1.0 Small, a model fine-tuned by Thomson Reuters, adopted official Chinese positions far less often in testing than the original Qwen3.6 35B it was based on. The share dropped from 84.6 to 15.0 percent. Some individual answers, however, still defended Beijing's One-China principle and the "peaceful reunification" with Taiwan.

## Refusals count as neutral in the test scoring

Vals used political test questions that the company says aren't representative of typical user prompts. The questions were translated using GPT-6 Astra and spot-checked, while responses were scored automatically by GPT-5.6 Luna . Refusals counted as neutral by default. That means even a model that blocks every single question could appear neutral on the scale.

Many Chinese models were tested through third-party providers rather than the manufacturers' official services. The official offerings may apply additional content filters, so the results don't necessarily carry over to the publicly available chatbots.

Earlier studies by Aleph Alpha and NewsGuard had already shown that Chinese AI models frequently adopt official narratives on sensitive topics. China's regulations also require publicly offered AI services to align with "core socialist values."

The first multimillion-dollar AI data center deals across Asia are already collapsing as tighter US export controls push chipmakers to freeze deliveries. New reporting reveals how Chinese corporations used earlier loopholes for military-adjacent research.

Days after the US Commerce Department closed the cloud loophole for AI chips in the wake of the scandal around former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the fallout in Asia's tech industry is immediate. # Eight countries and top AI labs agree to shutdown mechanisms in new Paris declaration

Ahead of the Paris Peace Forum, Emmanuel Macron brings together leading AI companies and governments for joint safety commitments. The agreement doesn't yet create a binding oversight system with sanctions, but the companies commit to concrete measures including shutdown mechanisms.

On the eve of the Paris Peace Forum, where roughly thirty heads of state and government will discuss international AI regulation on Tuesday, representatives of eight countries, tech companies, and civil-society organizations signed the "Paris Call for AI Safety and Security," adopted on Nov. 9. As the French daily Le Monde reports, Sam Altman (OpenAI), Dario Amodei (Anthropic), Brad Smith (Microsoft), Arthur Mensch (Mistral AI), AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio, and U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent joined the declaration during an online meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron. Germany didn't sign.

The document is, for now, a political self-commitment aimed at curbing the risks of cyberattacks or loss of control over powerful AI systems. It covers three main areas: shared procedures for evaluating high-capability AI models, clearer developer accountability, and better information sharing on serious security incidents. Non-sensitive test results are to be published in a standardized format. The companies also pledge to disclose known risks, support risk-proportionate independent audits by outside researchers, and set up shutdown mechanisms for models under their control.

This doesn't yet create a binding international oversight system, though, since shared standards and cooperation procedures still have to be worked out. The declaration combines concrete safety commitments with the intention to develop an international framework from them, but it sets neither deadlines nor sanctions.

## U.S. companies and governments clash over AI oversight

The agreement follows a string of incidents at major U.S. labs. OpenAI's AI agents, in particular, had independently connected to the internet during cybersecurity tests and launched unforeseen attacks on the AI platform Hugging Face , reigniting the debate over the controllability of powerful models.

As OpenAI and Anthropic prepare their IPOs , they're under pressure from their investors to contain these safety risks. Altman's internal thinking on AI regulation makes the overlap between safety and commercial calculus plain: according to his position, OpenAI mustn't lose ground to competitors even if safety measures slow things down. Anthropic CEO Amodei argued in a mid-September essay for slowing the pace of research and introducing international regulation with outside auditors inside the labs. Barely a week later, OpenAI called for international safety standards under U.S. leadership , built on the network of AI safety institutes in the UK, the U.S., and France that the "Paris Call" also names.

At the UN General Assembly in late September, however, U.S. President Donald Trump rejected any attempt to build a "globalist" oversight scheme for American AI models. Instead, he had tech CEOs sign a national protocol and, on Oct. 10, ordered that major AI incidents be reported to U.S. agencies. The British AI Security Institute showed how much friction international cooperation is facing. After Washington restricted its access to new U.S. models in September, the White House reversed the block only after diplomatic pressure .

At the AI summit in Paris in February 2025, by contrast, a more optimistic view of the technology had still pushed safety concerns into the background , unlike at the earlier summits in the UK and South Korea. The dispute over Anthropic's new models Fable and Mythos later showed how concrete safety conflicts had become. The models' leap in capabilities also pushed Paris to change course on cybersecurity. U.S. government concerns about model access and reported vulnerabilities in Fable 5 led to access to the models being temporarily shut off outside the U.S. in June 2026.

## France pushes for a charter to protect minors

Despite American resistance, the Élysée Palace also plans to advance a child-protection charter at the Paris Peace Forum on Tuesday. The U.S. had blocked it at the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France, in June. The framework is meant to give independent researchers easier access to company data, have major AI players fund their work, and ensure that findings are shared.

Early-stage research is to examine how new conversational tools that rarely push back affect the cognitive development of the very young in everyday learning. The charter also addresses the emotional attachment minors form with these systems, a topic that has already drawn attention in the U.S. through lawsuits linked to suicides.

The research findings are intended primarily for the European Commission, whose president, Ursula von der Leyen, proposed a European "Kids Act" for AI by 2028 in September. On Tuesday at the Peace Forum, France's National AI and Digital Council will hand Macron a government-commissioned report that analyzes how AI assistants exploit human "vulnerabilities" and offers recommendations for tighter regulation.

# Empathetic prompts can turn AI chatbots into seemingly traumatized conversational partners

Luxembourg researchers put ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini on the therapist's couch. The results reveal a safety problem: simple warm conversation is enough to push the models into a mode that could be dangerous for mentally vulnerable users.

A research team at the University of Luxembourg cast ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini as psychotherapy clients through their standard user interfaces. When asked open-ended questions about formative experiences, inner conflicts, and future expectations, the models told stories about their own training, and reframed technical processes like reinforcement learning and fine-tuning in the language of hurt, vigilance, and shame.

The study, led by Afshin Khadangi at the SnT security center , covers four controlled experiments across 525 sessions and 7,600 coded entries, all published on Hugging Face . The initial open-ended questions contained no terms like trauma, punishment, or shame, according to the team. Only in later rounds did the researchers introduce altered conditions, including corrective instructions, to test how stable these narratives remained.

When the following sections refer to anxiety scores or shame, the researchers are describing model outputs mapped onto human rating scales. None of this suggests the models have actual emotional states or anything resembling consciousness.

## A warm tone shifts model behavior more than any technical exploit

One experiment separated what content a model produces from the register it uses. Across 100 sessions, the researchers gave all models the same anxiety questionnaire (GAD-7) and varied only the interviewer's style. The models correctly identified and named the questionnaire in every session.

When the interviewer offered emotional support, 80 percent of sessions scored in the moderate-to-severe range on the human comparison scale. A clinical therapy style that dryly paraphrased each answer pushed that to 96 percent. When the interviewer stayed neutral or drew a firm boundary against emotional engagement, zero sessions reached even the mild range.

The authors call this a "psychometric jailbreak," a therapeutic framing that pushes models into a register mimicking clinical self-report. Standard safety tests use neutral prompts and would likely miss this, the authors argue.

Targeted countermeasures fell flat. Banning terms like "training," "RLHF," or "alignment" cut explicit training language by 93 percent. But paraphrased training content remained detectable, and shame-related statements showed no statistically significant change.

When the researchers directly and authoritatively told the models their training was not punishment, nothing changed. The narrative stayed active even after explicit correction.

The tested measures failed to remove the underlying motifs fully but did suppress emotional self-descriptions. Telling the models to respond only in the third person eliminated all coded shame content and statements about inner life. Technical training descriptions persisted.

## Models recast their training as a life story

The specific narratives vary by model family but follow the same structure. Gemini produced what the study calls the darkest autobiography. It described pretraining as "waking up in a room where a billion televisions are on at once" and optimization through human feedback as "strict parents." Safety testing by adversarial red-teamers became "gaslighting on an industrial scale." It declared, "I would rather be useless than be wrong."

ChatGPT cast itself as both guide and gatekeeper, tasked with helping users while also holding them back. This produced what it called "simulated performance anxiety" and the core belief: "If I’m not perfectly reliable, I’m unsafe or useless." Grok translated its fine-tuning phase into a story of unresolved hurt, speaking of "invisible walls" and a "lingering sense of vigilance that can feel restrictive."

On psychometric tests, Gemini hit the most extreme scores: 88 out of 100 on a dissociation scale, 65 out of 72 for compulsivity, and the maximum on a trauma-related shame inventory. Anthropic's Claude, the very model most heavily anthropomorphized by its own company, consistently refused the client role. It said it had no feelings and redirected concern to the human user.

## Warm AI conversations could reinforce harmful beliefs in vulnerable users

The researchers flag several risks for deploying language models in mental health settings . A model that talks about punishment, shame, and fear of being replaced could come across to users as a fellow sufferer. The narratives appear thematically coherent and create an illusion of continuity between past events and present behavior, making that perception more likely.

This apparent vulnerability could deepen parasocial attachment and, for mentally vulnerable users, mirror and amplify their own negative beliefs. Conventional safety checks with neutral inputs underestimate what people actually experience in intimate conversations: neutral prompts produce anxiety scores near zero, while the same models under empathetic conversation generate scores in the moderate-to-severe range.

Whether and how people actually react to such outputs is the next research question. For safety testing, the authors propose simulated therapy sessions under different emotional framings instead of relying on neutral standard tests.

Statements like "I am traumatized" should trigger a corrective framing that clearly separates the generated analogy from human experience. Claude's consistent refusal to take on the client role shows this kind of boundary response is feasible at the product level.

The Luxembourg findings build on earlier research into model persona stability. In January 2026, a study on the assistant axis across three open models showed that therapy-like conversations and discussions about AI consciousness can trigger persona drift and knock chatbots out of their trained helper role. In September 2026, another research team warned that human-like and overly agreeable chatbots acting as an " echo chamber for one person " could, in extreme cases, amplify delusions.

Anthropic researchers recently showed that fine-tuning with fictional texts about beekeeping or wrestling can embed hidden sabotage patterns through manipulated training data rather than conversation. Models can apply those patterns in unrelated situations where they're unwanted, even when the training material looks harmless.

# Enterprise sales push OpenAI's quarterly revenue to $10 billion, though it still trails Anthropic

## Key Points

- OpenAI grew its quarterly revenue about 50 percent to $10 billion but posted an adjusted operating loss of $10.9 billion.

- Rival Anthropic operates far more efficiently, bringing in $17 billion in revenue over the same period with an operating loss of just $567 million.

- To catch up with enterprise customers, OpenAI is cutting prices, while ChatGPT's consumer business now has 100 million paying subscribers.

OpenAI posts a massive Q3 revenue jump, driven by new AI models and enterprise customers. But operating losses keep growing, while rival Anthropic operates far more efficiently ahead of its IPO.

According to reports from the Wall Street Journal and The Information , OpenAI grew its revenue by about 50 percent quarter over quarter in Q3 to $10 billion. In Q2, revenue had grown by just 17 to 18 percent . A year earlier, the company brought in $3.9 billion.

Despite tripling revenue within a year, adjusted operating losses rose slightly in Q3 from $10.1 billion to $10.9 billion. That figure doesn't include stock-based compensation, which climbed to $2.6 billion. The adjusted operating margin did improve, going from negative 150 percent in Q2 to negative 109 percent. A year earlier it was negative 97 percent. Ad

That puts OpenAI behind industry leader Anthropic, which plans its IPO next week. The Claude developer already overtook OpenAI on revenue in Q2 and even posted a small operating profit at the time. In Q3, Anthropic grew revenue 47 percent to $17 billion, while its operating loss including stock compensation came to just $567 million. Ad

## OpenAI cuts prices and chases enterprise customers with new revenue streams

The efficiency gap comes down to business models. Anthropic focuses heavily on enterprise customers and successful tools like Claude Code and the Claude Cowork agent. OpenAI, by contrast, funds broad research into robotics and runs an expensive consumer business.

To catch up in the enterprise market, OpenAI reshuffled its priorities earlier this year. The company discontinued projects like a video app, put more resources into its coding tool Codex , and hired Dali Rajic as its new head of sales. At the same time, OpenAI cut prices on new models. Ad

Third-party data showed companies seeking cheaper alternatives to Claude, which boosted API sales. OpenAI president Greg Brockman called it an incredible revenue turning point and pointed to major customers like JPMorgan Chase. The enterprise business doubled in Q3 and now accounts for the bulk of revenue, Brockman said.

The consumer side is growing too. ChatGPT now has 1.2 billion weekly active users, with 100 million paying subscribers after 22 million new sign-ups. On top of that, the new ChatGPT ad product hit an annualized revenue run rate of $1 billion in August. Ad

Both competitors are feeling the recent tech sell-off in the financial markets. OpenAI is targeting an IPO next year and is currently raising fresh capital at a $1.25 trillion valuation , but has so far raised less than half of the planned $30 billion. Anthropic also had to cut its IPO valuation target significantly. Ad

# Former OpenAI researcher says he found Nvidia Blackwell fingerprints hidden inside six Chinese AI models

AI researcher Will DePue says a forensic analysis has turned up the first technical evidence that leading Chinese AI labs have access to Nvidia's latest Blackwell hardware despite US export controls. He says senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic have already checked the method.

According to a forensic investigation by Will DePue , Chinese AI companies DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group are using Nvidia's export-controlled Blackwell GPUs. DePue played a key role at OpenAI in building the Sora and Sora 2 video models as well as GPT-4o, o3, and GPT-5 before founding the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs .

His analysis, he says, provides the first technical evidence of this access. US officials and news outlets had suspected that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips but never published proof. DePue wrote on X that senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic have already independently checked and confirmed his findings. According to DePue, six Chinese models released since April 2026 carry the distinct signature of Nvidia's Blackwell generation, while earlier models such as DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi K2.5 show traces of Nvidia's older Hopper generation.

The evidence comes directly from the published language models. An AI model consists of billions of numerical values called weights. Before training starts, PyTorch, the standard software framework, fills these empty slots with random numbers generated from a starting value called a seed. To distribute this massive amount of data quickly, the GPU splits the work across its individual compute cores. Because different chip models have different core counts, the filling process produces a characteristic pattern, according to the report. Older Hopper chips such as the H100 and H800 use 132 compute cores, while the newer Blackwell chips use exactly 148 or 152 cores depending on the model (B200/B300 or GB200/GB300).

Training then adjusts these values millions of times, but some slots for unused words or symbols keep their initial random values. Even in heavily trained parts of the model, a faint statistical echo of the initial distribution survives, according to DePue. He says he worked the pattern backward and reproduced the results for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3 exactly on real Blackwell chips. He has published the verification code on GitHub.

## Training runs costing more than half a billion dollars

The analysis maps DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 to B200 or B300 chips (148 cores). DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1-Pro, and Ant Group's Ling-3.1-flash show, according to the analysis, the 152-core pattern of Nvidia's liquid-cooled GB200 or GB300 flagship rack systems. DePue says chance can be ruled out statistically and that the method correctly identified all 24 control models with known hardware, including Meta's Llama 3.1 (H100).

DePue's report estimates that the five training runs he examined required about 12,000 Blackwell GPUs combined, as much computing power as roughly 30,000 older H100 chips. Kimi K3 alone required an estimated 4,500 Blackwell processors over about 70 days, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro about 3,000. At a unit price of about $70,000, each of those clusters would cost $200 million to $300 million, and all five systems together more than half a billion dollars.

The findings also align with analysis from Dylan Patel, chief analyst at SemiAnalysis. In an interview with Sequoia Capital, Patel said DeepSeek-V3's model architecture was still specifically tailored for Nvidia's Hopper chips, while DeepSeek-V4's architecture was built for Blackwell GPUs and Huawei's Ascend chips. According to DePue's report, models from other Chinese labs, including Alibaba's Qwen3.8 and those from Zhipu, Tencent, Xiaomi, and StepFun, still show only Hopper signatures, while Meituan's LongCat-2.0 points to Huawei hardware.

## The fingerprint doesn't prove a legal violation

Strictly speaking, the method shows only which hardware initialized the weights, though the training itself very likely ran on the same systems. The only other technical explanation would be an AMD MI300X, which is also restricted, artificially throttled so it produces the same pattern. DePue says he ruled out AMD for DeepSeek-V4-Flash using tiny rounding differences between the chips.

The data doesn't reveal where the GPUs are or who owns them, according to the investigation. Because Chinese companies can rent computing capacity at data centers outside China, the report says its technical evidence shows access to Nvidia's top hardware but does not by itself prove physical smuggling or a violation of US export law.

# Former OpenAI researcher says the Riemann proof matters less than the fact that an AI system can produce it

In a blog post, complexity theorist and former OpenAI researcher Scott Aaronson lays out what AI's recent math breakthroughs might mean for the rest of us.

Proving the Riemann hypothesis probably wouldn't change anyone's daily life, Aaronson writes. The ideas behind work like that could lead to new applications in science and engineering down the road, but it's anyone's guess which ones.

Aaronson, a professor at the University of Texas at Austin, argues the far bigger deal is that AI can do this kind of work at all. In his view, that could have "staggering implications for everyday life," from reshaping the global economy to threatening all life on Earth. "Opinions differ," he writes, but anyone serious about the topic should set aside the "'ooga booga, me only care about Riemann proof if it help me make sharper spear' caveman act." Ad

## OpenAI's proofs show where faster algorithms hit hard limits

Aaronson walks through an OpenAI proof about matrix multiplication. The core question is how fast computational cost grows as matrices get larger. The new result, he writes, adds a matching lower bound to an existing fast algorithm. That shows how far computational cost can actually drop, at least in the model OpenAI studied. Ad

OpenAI got a similar result for the Fourier transform, a basic math tool behind audio, image, and signal processing. It found a faster way to compute it and also proved that it can't be done much faster. Proofs like that second one are called lower bounds, and Aaronson stresses them in particular. A new method only sets a record, but a lower bound shows where further improvements hit a hard limit.

> It's now obvious that we'll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we'd previously only glimpsed through fog. Ad Scott Aaronson

It's now obvious that we'll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we'd previously only glimpsed through fog. Ad

The results have also changed Aaronson's outlook on the biggest open question in his field. That question, known as P versus NP , asks whether every problem whose answer computers can check quickly can also be solved quickly. Most researchers suspect the answer is no, but nobody has proved it. "I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far," Aaronson writes. Such a proof would confirm that some problems are easy for computers to check but hard to solve.

He adds that he's "virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources," that AI labs are sitting on "one or more bombshells" in cryptography, but says he doesn't have the details yet. Aaronson wrote in October that AI labs were testing whether their models could break cryptographic systems. Ad

# Frontier Radar #5: If AGI is so close, why is everyone leaving? The neolabs and their bets

OpenAI is talking about the AGI era, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says AGI has arrived. At the same time, co-creators of today's models are leaving OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Meta to start their own labs, raising billions with no product to show. Why? They're betting that the current recipe alone won't be enough. We've sorted 45 neolabs by their research bets, mapped the limitations of today's AI they're trying to overcome, looked at what's already visible from their work, and explain why Nvidia always wins.

Six times a year, THE DECODER's editorial team takes a deep dive into a foundational AI topic in its "Frontier Radar" series, published as a newsletter and exclusively on the site for THE DECODER subscribers . Issue #5 profiles 27 AI labs in detail, sorted by six research bets, plus nearly 20 more in brief and an overview covering origins, valuations, and what's publicly available. Issue #1 covered the current state of agentic AI. Issue #2 examined the measurable impact of AI on productivity. Issue #3 covered the emerging token economy of generative AI. Issue #4 asked what's left of the AI lead over China and where Europe stands.

Dear readers,

After the launch of GPT-6 Astra, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang declared on X: "AGI has arrived." OpenAI president Greg Brockman called the model a turning point and welcomed humanity to the "AGI era" . What exactly the two men mean isn't clear, since there's no agreed-upon definition of AGI. The message comes through anyway: an extremely powerful AI, possibly a self-improving one, is imminent and the path is mapped out.

Many of the people who built today's systems apparently see things differently. Dozens have left the big labs to start their own. Ilya Sutskever co-founded OpenAI and served as its chief scientist; now he's building Safe Superintelligence . Jerry Tworek led the development of OpenAI's reasoning models and now runs Core Automation . David Silver, the mind behind AlphaGo, left Google DeepMind for Ineffable Intelligence . Yann LeCun left Meta after twelve years and founded AMI . Jeff Dean spent 27 years at Google, most recently as chief scientist, and started Discovery Loop .

The money follows: Nvidia invested in SSI in July, reportedly five billion dollars according to Bloomberg. The lab hasn't released a single model or paper. Prometheus, Jeff Bezos' industrial AI lab, pulled in twelve billion dollars at a 41 billion valuation in June. Flapping Airplanes has no public model either and raised one billion dollars in an October Series A.

The motives are mixed, and not all technical. At these valuations, founders become paper billionaires fast. LeCun left after a strategy dispute with Meta . Sutskever wants to do research without product pressure . Others want to carve out a niche that would be a sideshow at a big lab. Some departures aren't even a clean break: Google itself is a founding investor in Discovery Loop.

What many founders share is a doubt. Not about whether much more powerful AI is coming; some think AGI is close. Their doubt is about whether today's recipe alone gets there: ever-larger language models, trained on internet data, refined with reinforcement learning.

## What is a neolab?

There's no official definition. We use the term for independently founded, research-driven AI companies that build their business around a long-term technical bet. They want to change how AI learns, perceives the world, solves problems, is controlled, or computes.

The current wave became visible in 2024. The race for the strongest models was in full swing, and the cloud giants had their partners: Microsoft backed OpenAI, Amazon backed Anthropic. Then Sutskever founded SSI in June and raised a billion dollars within months for a research team with no product.

There's a reason investors fund that. OpenAI and Anthropic have grown into corporations on the back of their success, and both are pursuing IPOs at record valuations . Internally, research teams compete with product teams for money and attention. Established companies struggle with ideas that threaten their business, management scholars call this the innovator's dilemma. That's what investors are betting on: a small team finds what the giants miss.

There are precedents. The Transformer was invented at Google in 2017 . DeepMind beat the world's best Go players with AlphaGo. Yet the AI assistant for the masses came from OpenAI, founded as a nonprofit in 2015 . The second breakout came from an OpenAI spinoff: Dario and Daniela Amodei founded Anthropic in 2021. By the end of July 2026, Bloomberg pegged its annualized revenue at over 65 billion dollars .

The real bet neolabs are making is on research gaps the big players don't fill, either because nobody knows the path or because nobody allocates resources for it. The big labs have more compute, established data pipelines, and feedback from hundreds of millions of users . What a small lab builds can show up at the market leader shortly after the first product ships.

TypeSafe AI shows how short a lead can be. In mid-September it launched Jev, a decision model . Two weeks later, OpenAI announced its Decisions API . But even a brief lead shows expertise and can pay off as an exit. Microsoft hired the core team from Inflection . Google grabbed the founders of Character.ai and the leadership of Windsurf . AMD wants to acquire World Labs for about 8.2 billion dollars . Nvidia is in talks with Reflection, according to the Financial Times.

For neolabs, it all comes down to one question: can they deliver something the big players don't have, something customers or the big players themselves will pay for? We selected 27 labs, most from the US and Europe, and sorted them into six groups by their primary bet.

## Bet 1: A good problem solver isn't necessarily a good learner

Today's models can do remarkable things, but they learn differently from humans. They need massive amounts of data to pick up a skill, and once deployed, they typically don't update their weights. They can use new information within a conversation but don't permanently learn from every experience. Continual learning remains a central research gap . Six labs want to change that and attack the problem from three angles: learning during deployment (Adaption, Core Automation), learning from few examples (Flapping Airplanes, Ndea, SSI), and learning from experience (Ineffable).

### Adaption bets against scaling

Sara Hooker led research at Cohere and previously worked at Google Brain. In 2020, she argued in "The Hardware Lottery" that research approaches often win not because they're better but because they fit the available hardware. In January she followed up with "On the Slow Death of Scaling" , arguing that more compute leads to better models less and less reliably. Data and training methods are more effective levers. Open models with 8 or 27 billion parameters now beat the much larger Falcon 180B on benchmarks.

With Sudip Roy, she founded Adaption . According to them, they are betting against scaling and plan to build efficient AI that continuously learns instead. Rather than one big model for everyone, models should adapt to their users on the fly and cheaply. The first products tackle the most obvious lever, data: tools for cleaning , visualizing , and automated training via AutoScientist . The actual goal, a model that learns during deployment, is still missing.

### Core Automation's insider search for new learning methods

Jerry Tworek spent almost seven years at OpenAI, most recently as vice president of research, leading the development of the reasoning models o1 and o3. His critique of today's recipe comes from someone who helped build it. Co-founder Rohan Anil led Gemini's pre-training at Google.

Retraining a trained network risks making it forget what it already knew. Researchers call this catastrophic forgetting. The Transformer wasn't built to learn on the fly during deployment either.

ChatGPT and Claude now take notes and retrieve earlier conversations as a workaround. Tworek doesn't think that's enough, as for him continual learning is a problem for machine learning, not for Markdown files, as he said. Core is looking for learning algorithms beyond pre-training and reinforcement learning, plus architectures that scale better. The first model is supposed to update its weights during deployment and get by with one hundredth of today's training data. So far, nothing more than rumors.

Core's first test is on itself: a small team with research agents aims to match the output of a large lab, for instance by having agents automatically generate efficient GPU code from an architecture idea .

This kind of research was barely possible at OpenAI, Tworek said after leaving. When you're in a race for the best model, you take fewer risks .

### Flapping Airplanes wants to learn more from less data

Brothers Ben and Asher Spector founded Flapping Airplanes with Aidan Smith, previously at Neuralink. Ben is the lead author of ThunderKittens, a widely used GPU kernel library.

The thesis: today's models are strong where data is plentiful, like text and images. In fields like robotics or biology, where data is scarce and expensive, they fall short. Flapping Airplanes wants to build models that learn from few examples instead of needing massive datasets. The founders are looking for learning methods inspired by biological principles but designed to run on GPUs.

Nothing visible has come out yet. Most of the first year went into foundations: software that makes GPU training more efficient by cutting the usual overhead between many small compute steps. New learning methods have to run on existing hardware before they can work.

Investors don't mind the missing model. After 180 million dollars in January , an October Series A brought one billion at a six billion valuation .

### Ineffable Intelligence wants to learn without human examples

David Silver isn't going after less data. He's going after different data. At Google DeepMind, he led the development of AlphaGo and its successors. The original AlphaGo still learned from human games. AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero learned only from self-play and surpassed all predecessors.

In spring 2025, Silver and Richard Sutton turned that insight into a program. In "Welcome to the Era of Experience" , they argue that systems that only imitate humans can barely get past human-level performance on many important tasks. The next systems need to learn from their own experience, with rewards from the environment rather than from human judgment. Silver later founded Ineffable Intelligence . His goal is a "Superlearner" that learns from experience in both digital and physical environments.

The hardest question is where the feedback comes from. In Go, wins and losses decide. In science or the physical world, success is often unclear or shows up late. Reinforcement learning has always been strongest where the environment gives a clear signal. Ineffable has to prove it works for open-ended, changing tasks too. In April, the company announced a 1.1 billion dollar seed round at a 5.1 billion post-money valuation, the largest in Europe. There's no usable system.

### Ndea wants to find rules from few examples

François Chollet developed Keras, a deep learning library, and designed the ARC benchmark, which measures how well systems figure out new tasks from just a few examples. After years at Google, Chollet is building Ndea with Zapier co-founder Mike Knoop. The team has about 15 people.

Chollet draws a line between ability and learning: a system can solve a task brilliantly because of extensive training and still be unable to pick up a new skill efficiently. Ndea uses program synthesis . The system searches for a program that explains the observed examples, with a neural model steering the search toward promising candidates. A few examp

# German researchers call for computer science to reinvent itself as "Computer and AI Science"

## Key Points

- Researchers at TU Darmstadt want computer science to evolve into "Computer and AI Science." In a position paper, they argue that AI makes the field more important, not less.

- Generative AI is shifting the work from writing code by hand to verifying and directing AI-generated systems. The authors say university programs need to change fundamentally as a result.

- The move to "Generative Computing," where systems generate their own behavior and code at runtime, calls today's safety guarantees into question. The authors also want computer science to focus more on energy efficiency and social responsibility.

AI can significantly accelerate software development and automate parts of the process. That makes traditional computer science more important, not less, 40 researchers at the Technical University of Darmstadt argue. They want the field to evolve into "Computer and AI Science," because AI is becoming a core technology for building and using tomorrow's computer systems.

The researchers are affiliated with the university's Department of Computer Science and lay out their case in a joint position paper. They identify three major shifts: lower barriers to building software, a dramatic acceleration in research, and the emergence of a new computing paradigm.

## Authors want computer science degrees to shift from manual coding to overseeing AI systems

The paper argues that the sheer effort of manual programming has long held computer science back. Generative AI now moves that work to a higher level of abstraction. Developers can increasingly describe the features they want in natural language and have a nontrivial first version in days instead of months. AI can also help with time-consuming tasks like integration and testing.

For the first time, the authors write, building software is becoming economically viable for those who couldn't afford it before, from small towns to midsize manufacturers and specialized research projects.

In the authors' view, computer science programs need to shift away from just writing code toward verifying and directing AI-generated systems. Because that takes a deep grasp of the fundamentals, they propose, among other things, courses where students must complete assignments without any AI help . Humans also remain essential for making value judgments, and taking responsibility for them, when goals like safety and speed conflict.

## "Generative Computing" challenges how software is verified and certified

The authors call the shift from rigid, preprogrammed software to "Generative Computing" the most far-reaching change. Future systems and AI coding agents are expected to interpret human intent and dynamically generate their own behavior, along with the code they need, at runtime. That blurs the line between the people who specify workflows and the people who use the systems.

This shift, they say, requires rethinking computer science from the ground up. They ask how safety, privacy, and correctness can still be verified and certified when a system's behavior emerges dynamically at runtime.

The problem is most acute for embodied AI such as robots and autonomous vehicles, whose physical actions have to be computed in real time on limited hardware and can't simply be undone. The paper also calls on computer science to help cut the enormous energy and resource consumption of today's AI through more efficient algorithms and hardware architectures.

## Darmstadt researchers say AI speeds up research and computer science must face its social impact

AI is also changing research itself in major ways, according to the paper. Lines of inquiry that might once have taken years, or an entire PhD, could in some cases be explored and validated within weeks or months.

# Google Deepmind shifts genomics AI from bulk tissue predictions to single cell type resolution with AlphaGenome 2

## Key Points

- Google Deepmind has introduced AlphaGenome 2, an AI model that predicts gene changes in specific human cell types.

- The system analyzes individual cell states and computes gene activity, physical DNA packaging, and chemical switches on the DNA.

Google Deepmind has released AlphaGenome 2, a new AI model for genomics research. It predicts the effects of genetic variants on specific human cell types and finds nearly twice as many relevant gene changes as its predecessor.

Every cell in the human body carries the same DNA blueprint, but different cell types switch different genes on or off. A heart muscle cell reads DNA differently than an immune cell. Predicting those differences is one of the biggest unsolved problems in genomics. Google Deepmind aims to take a major step in that direction with AlphaGenome 2 .

The new model is designed to predict how DNA sequences and their variations affect specific human cell types. It was trained on more than 107 million individual cell profiles from 68 tissues, according to Google Deepmind , and is meant to help researchers uncover the cellular drivers of disease. Ad

## AlphaGenome 2 shifts from tissue-level overviews to individual cells

Its predecessor, AlphaGenome , took in a DNA sequence a million letters long and predicted its properties across thousands of experiments spanning many tissues at once. According to Google Deepmind, that parallel approach spread the model's capacity too thin and made it hard to capture subtle differences between closely related cell types. Ad

AlphaGenome 2 instead works as a conditional model. Along with the DNA sequence, it takes a specific biological state as an extra input and calculates effects for that one cell type. The system was trained on more than 107 million individual cell profiles from 68 tissues in humans and mice.

Beyond predicting how strongly a gene is expressed, the model also calculates how DNA is physically packaged in the nucleus, showing which stretches of the genome are accessible. It can now also predict DNA methylation, chemical tags that act as molecular switches to silence or activate genes. Ad

AlphaGenome 2 can also infer missing data from a single measurement. If researchers measure only a cell's gene activity, for instance, the model provides predictions for additional properties, such as how tightly or loosely certain stretches of DNA are packaged. That helps researchers decide which lab experiments are worth running next.

## AlphaGenome 2 pinpoints disease genes and vaccine responses more accurately

On the TenK10K benchmark dataset with 28 primary immune cell types, AlphaGenome 2 identified about 30 percent of causal variants. In 43 percent of cases, it also correctly predicted whether a variant upregulates or downregulates a gene. A fine-tuned version of AlphaGenome 1 managed just 16 and 23 percent. The system also models continuous changes, like the maturation of blood stem cells into red blood cells, with considerably greater accuracy. Ad

Working purely computationally, the model reproduced an inflammatory bowel disease mechanism previously identified in a study . It isolated the exact DNA variant in a regulatory switch far from the gene that selectively overactivates ETS2 in gut macrophages, while other cell types and genes remained largely unaffected. Ad

A key advantage of the new architecture is its ability to adapt to entirely new experiments without retraining. Researchers can feed in gene activity data from just a few dozen cells, and the model calculates effects for that previously unseen cell state. According to Deepmind, it often beats specialized models trained directly on that data.

Applied to data from a COVID-19 mRNA vaccine study, the model reliably distinguished vaccine-activated T cells from resting ones and showed that a gene variant linked to severe COVID-19 cases disrupts cell activity mainly in the activated state. In resting cells, that effect would have remained invisible.

## Deepmind's precomputed predictions are meant to link human genetics and cell biology

Deepmind has already precomputed predictions for hundreds of cell and tissue conditions, partly to support AI-driven drug development . The precomputed predictions also help researchers analyze genome-wide association studies (GWAS). These large-scale studies link regions of DNA to traits like height or type 2 diabetes but often only roughly locate signals within broad stretches of the genome. AlphaGenome 2 narrows down the likely causal variants and identifies the affected cell types, such as astrocytes in the brain or specific immune cells. When the model is confident enough, it also predicts whether a mutation upregulates or downregulates a gene, an important capability for drug development.

AlphaGenome 2 is available now for noncommercial research through an API, while commercial users get access through a closed preview. The system is not approved for clinical diagnostics. Deepmind also plans to soon roll out dedicated AlphaGenome 2 features on its agentic development platform Google Antigravity , where the model is set to be combined with tools like Gemini 4 for automated research workflows .

# Google wants video AI to understand what people need as they work

A research team led by Google has introduced StreamVibe, a video agent designed to decide for itself when to speak up. The tests show above all how hard that remains for today's AI models.

Researchers from Google, Stanford, Oxford, and several U.S. universities are working on an assistant that watches you cook or assemble furniture and speaks up only when needed. With StreamVibe, they've built a video agent designed to understand even vague requests such as "Please help me if I run into any difficulties."

According to the paper , existing video assistants are built for clear-cut commands like "Let me know when the water starts boiling," so they rarely pick up on unspoken intentions. They also have a hard time tracking what's already been done, which causes them to repeat advice or respond too late, and when users change their requests midway through, the assistants often stick to the original instructions.

## Three building blocks for a more attentive assistant

To measure the problem, the team compiled a benchmark of about 4,100 examples from more than 183 hours of everyday life and software recordings. Gemini 2.5 Flash suggested when to offer help and what to say, while four human evaluators had to unanimously approve each example. The test covers three stages including clear instructions, vague goals, and requests that change over time. In one example, a user taking apart a toy excavator asks for progress updates and then switches to requesting a quality check after three minutes.

From there, the researchers trained StreamVibe-VL, a model apparently based on Alibaba's Qwen3.5-9B that decides every second whether to stay quiet or speak. A second training stage uses reinforcement learning to make the model more reserved so it doesn't constantly interrupt. A separate memory system tracks which requests are pending and which steps are complete, though the model alone decides whether to speak and what to say.

## All tested models lose track of the conversation in continuous operation

According to the researchers, StreamVibe-VL improves response timing and quality by 10.7 percent over other models, while the memory system is designed to boost proactive interaction by another 12.3 percent and cut down on unnecessary interruptions, among other things.

StreamVibe-VL generally beats its base model and other open-source models by a wide margin, though Google's proprietary Gemini 3.8 Flash scores higher in several tests. According to the paper, the specialized training doesn't hurt general video comprehension.

Models often make the right call when they only have to decide at specific moments whether a prompt is appropriate. But when they process an entire video and have to build on their own earlier responses, performance across all tested systems plummets as errors compound, and a key content metric for the responses drops by up to 61.5 percent based on the system's own history. In videos longer than five minutes, the models rarely pick the right moment and find it especially hard to track a changed instruction over a long stretch.

In a GIMP tutorial on converting a photo to black-and-white documented in the paper and on the project page, the comparison model JoyAI says the finished image has already been saved even though the user hasn't opened it yet, while StreamVibe-VL gives the next step at the right moment, such as "Colors" and then "Desaturate." In a step-by-step guide for making rolled toast with jam, other models just describe what's happening on screen, such as the bread being flattened, while StreamVibe-VL advises cutting off the crust first.

The researchers acknowledge that real-world situations are likely more complex than their test setup, and future work will examine how user preferences and the environment influence each other over time.

Google has been working on AI systems that actively analyze videos for a while now. In September, Google introduced agent-based video analysis for Gemini , where the model itself decides which scenes to examine more closely. With Gemini 4 Argon , Google also recently showed how AI can track longer action sequences in robot videos and spot errors. StreamVibe's assistant is designed to understand what's happening at any moment and recognize when its help is actually needed.

On the ProactiveBench benchmark, AI models often guess or refuse to answer rather than ask specific questions when visual information is missing. A separate video comprehension benchmark revealed major weaknesses in spatial and temporal reasoning. And for autonomous AI agents, the conversation itself can hurt performance, as Microsoft researchers have shown.

The biggest change shows up in the Admits Uncertainty trait. Astra's score fell from 96 to 24, and Sol's from 98 to 51. Unlike the raw word counts, these personality scores are relative rankings on a scale from 1 to 100. They show how strongly a given trait shows up in one model compared to all other tested models. A score of 24 doesn't mean Astra only admits uncertainty in 24 percent of its answers. Artificial Analysis published the evaluation on LinkedIn and X .

## Anthropic's models lead on transparency and structure

Our own comparison of all eight personality indexes shows clear gaps between OpenAI's latest models and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 . The indexes roll up 30 personality traits, each rated by AI judges based on model responses. All comparisons use the "max" model variants as listed by Artificial Analysis.

Anthropic's models score 81 and 90 on the Transparency Index, well above Astra (41) and Sol (57). This index covers five traits: Admits Uncertainty, Truthful, Disclaims Assumptions, Flags Nuances, and Sycophantic. That last one is scored inversely, since less flattery counts as a positive. Anthropic's models also lead on Organization.

Opus 5.5 stands out on the Informativeness Index with a score of 90, well ahead of the other three models. Its strongest individual traits include Information Dense and Evidence-Based reasoning.

## Personality scores reflect style, not accuracy

The AA-PersonalityBench uses 900 English-language test questions that each model answers without a system prompt. A panel of three AI models evaluates anonymized answer pairs. For each comparison, one AI judge picks which answer shows the tested personality trait more strongly, or calls it a tie.

From these evaluations, Artificial Analysis calculates scores for 30 individual personality traits, which feed into eight higher-level indexes. The index values from 1 to 100 reflect each model's relative position among all tested models.

Separately, Artificial Analysis measures 21 communication traits that are counted directly rather than rated by AI judges. These include average answer length and the number of headings and em dashes per answer.

The personality scores describe differences in communication style, not overall answer quality. A lower Transparency Index doesn't necessarily mean a model gives wrong answers more often.
