# GPT-6 Astra sees the matrix and reprograms other AI models directly through their weights

MIT researchers show that GPT-6 Astra can directly understand and modify the internal settings of other AI models without traditional training. The approach has limits but could change how AI systems are tuned and controlled.

Hand a person a list of thousands of numbers and ask what game an AI model trained on them plays. You won't get an answer. GPT-6 Astra from OpenAI will give you one: In a research blog, MIT researchers show that GPT-6 Astra can analyze and deliberately modify the internal settings of other AI models, the so-called weights. These numerical values are organized in massive tables, or matrices in mathematical terms.

The usual training process of step-by-step mathematical optimization isn't needed. Depending on the experiment, Astra worked directly with lists of numbers or used programming tools and feedback from test runs.

The researchers call the approach "Weight-Space Programming": instead of expensively retraining an AI model, a language model acts like a mechanic turning individual knobs.

## Astra identifies games just by looking at a model's raw numbers

In several experiments, the researchers fed Astra the raw weights of trained networks and asked what those networks had learned. Astra correctly identified which of four computer games a network was supposed to play. It also recognized the basic shapes an image generator produced, though it confused filled shapes with outlines. It correctly matched the training language of small language models too - without access to training data and without the ability to run the models.

In another test, Astra had to figure out which of two fine-tuned language models was trained to always agree with users. From the weights alone, it couldn't tell the difference at first. Only when Astra was also allowed to observe what the models paid attention to during text processing did it correctly identify the sycophantic model across all three model pairs.

## Models written from scratch beat trained competitors

Astra went even further: It generated weights for models meant to play three simple computer games, entirely without training, based only on the game rules and source code. According to the researchers, these models outperformed ones trained with a standard method over 100 million rounds. In Breakout, Astra's model scored an average of 517 points versus 25 for the trained baseline. In two other games, Astra fell behind the longest-trained versions.

For the board game Go on a 9x9 grid, Astra wrote the weights of a network with about 1.5 million parameters. Given a budget of 50 test iterations where the network played up to 128 practice games each round and Astra then corrected its weights, it beat a comparably sized model trained on roughly 20 million games.

## Targeted fixes instead of full retraining

The most practical experiment involved the language model Qwen3.5-0.8B. Astra's task was to improve its math skills, using a coding environment and 50 test iterations with practice problems. Evaluation happened on separate problems Astra had never seen.

Astra identified a problem that Qwen's own model documentation already warns about: thinking loops where the model endlessly repeats the same text instead of reaching an answer. Astra then changed just 0.016 percent of all weights. The result: accuracy on the MATH-500 benchmark jumped from 7.9 to 48.1 percent. Instruction-following ability improved from 21 to 62 percent. The thinking loops weren't fully eliminated, though, as a third of responses still hit the maximum text length, down from 93 percent before.

With a smaller model (Gemma 3 270M) that rarely fell into such loops, Astra couldn't produce any measurable improvement.

The researchers suspect Astra was able to remove a blockage in the Qwen model that was suppressing existing capabilities, but skills that a model fundamentally lacks couldn't be added by just rewriting individual weights in this experiment.

## Old news or new paradigm?

AI pioneer Jürgen Schmidhuber commented on X that the approach was "old hat," pointing to his own work from the 1990s. Khattab responded that they link to those papers, which were "far ahead of its time." The new aspect, he said, is how well today's language models can translate between human language and a network's numerical values.

The researchers see potential in their approach for things like security audits directly on model weights or targeted behavior changes without expensive retraining. They also acknowledge that the capabilities are still limited. A benchmark for systematic measurement is next on their list. The experiment logs are on GitHub, and the edited Qwen model is on Hugging Face.

# Helsing built an AI system that prepares targets for weapons systems and says every decision will carry a human name

## Key Points

- Defense company Helsing has unveiled "Clarity," an AI platform that aggregates sensor feeds and reports to identify military targets and recommend weapons systems.

- Helsing emphasizes European sovereignty and mandatory human authorization for every strike, positioning itself as a competitor to US vendors like Palantir.

German defense tech company Helsing has unveiled Clarity, an agent-based software platform that distills sensor data into target recommendations. Helsing promises European control and human oversight. The use of comparable systems in Iran, in Gaza, and in a near-miss involving China shows where those promises break down.

Helsing presented its Clarity platform in Berlin on Wednesday, calling it an "agentic intelligence platform." According to the company's press release , the software processes all data a military unit can access, including sensor feeds, open-source intelligence, written reports, and systems already in use. Hundreds of specialized AI agents link these sources, identify military forces, facilities, and positions, and prepare information on adversary assets for human review before Clarity packages the data for the appropriate weapons system.

The agents are trained on real operational data, synthetic AI-generated data, and simulated environments, Helsing says, and a shared military ontology and evidence base lets them work in parallel and deploy analytical tools. The platform is "AI-native" and not built on legacy architectures, according to the company. Ad

Helsing stresses the system's sovereignty, noting that Clarity runs on the customer's own infrastructure and that its models and interfaces were developed in Europe, with data and operations staying under the armed forces' sole control. The platform follows the Modular Open Systems Approach, implements NATO standards, and can connect to effectors from any manufacturer. Ad

The decision to strike is supposed to stay with a human who selects targets and must authorize every handoff to a weapons system. A target is only recommended, Helsing says, when independent sources agree and the assessment can be made with high confidence, and every decision is documented with the name of the person responsible.

With Clarity, Helsing is stepping into a market led by Palantir, whose Maven system is embedded in Pentagon and NATO workflows and has been refined through years of operational use. Helsing is one of the few European vendors that can point to experience from the war in Ukraine, where the company supplies drones, though it didn't say whether Clarity is already running with any customer. Germany's Bundeswehr plans to introduce AI-powered systems starting next year. Ad

## The speed of automation creates its own risks

How these systems play out in practice is visible in the Iran war, where the US military is reportedly using Palantir's Maven with Anthropic's Claude to suggest hundreds of targets, prioritize them, and recommend ordnance. In the first 24 hours the US struck about 1,000 targets, and within days that number topped 3,000, according to the Wall Street Journal , which also reports that military officials warn of an attitude described internally as "The computer said to do this."

The problem is sharper in Gaza, where according to investigations by +972 Magazine and Local Call, Israel's Lavender system for a time flagged up to 37,000 Palestinians as potential targets. Human review often lasted only about "20 seconds" per target, mainly to verify whether the person was male, the investigations found, and a separate system called "Where's Daddy?" tracked flagged individuals to their family homes, which were then often struck at night. Ad

## Data fusion doesn't prevent hallucinations

Even combining multiple sources is no guarantee, as an incident from spring 2026 shows. According to CNN, the US military nearly boarded a Chinese ship because a chatbot falsely claimed in an intelligence report that it was carrying nuclear weapons program components after combining open and classified data and misidentifying the cargo. Ad

Armed troops were preparing to board and aircraft were already in the air when the error was caught only shortly before the operation. There were no uniform standards for verifying AI-generated information, and younger analysts in particular trusted the tools uncritically. "AI allows you to get to a bad idea faster," one source said.

# Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft

## Key Points

- Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge and the AI model Claude presented a proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, publishing it in the Lean programming language for computer verification.

- Just hours later, Stanford University researchers published an independent, entirely human approach to the same problem by mathematician Alessandro Masullo.

- Open since 1859, the hypothesis is central to understanding prime numbers, and confirming it would validate hundreds of dependent mathematical theories while underscoring AI's role in research.

Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said Friday he used a large language model to solve math's most famous open problem.

Alpöge posted a paper and the accompanying computer code on his website, according to Scientific American and other US outlets. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," he wrote in his announcement .

According to Alpöge, his method goes beyond the original prime-number problem and also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), which extends that ordering principle to a large family of related equations. Given a bit more time, he expects to solve the even broader Extended Riemann Hypothesis as well.

Alpöge had treated the problem as a secret lifelong goal since college, expecting it to take decades. Over the past few months, he worked closely with Anthropic's AI model, setting the direction and combining two approaches on a simplified toy model. Once they moved to the actual problem, the AI took over and left him far behind near the finish line.

To crack the puzzle, the pair extended an idea from mathematician Stepanov, who had solved a similar question in another mathematical system. That method relies on a tool similar to taking derivatives of smooth curves in high school calculus, a trick that normally fails on whole numbers because individual values cannot be differentiated like a continuous line.

Alpöge and Claude got around that obstacle by chaining special mathematical transformations together like links to mimic the effect of a derivative. The language model supplied the key insight, finding that for a number sequence of length X, you need to chain exactly as many transformations as the square root of X. Ideas like that alone should leave fellow mathematicians stunned, Alpöge says.

## Stanford mathematicians rush out an all-human competing proof

Hours after Alpöge's announcement, the story took a dramatic turn. Just before a board meeting, Stanford math professor and American Mathematical Society (AMS) president Ravi Vakil posted a "hurried announcement" on his blog, sharing an independent draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis written by mathematician Alessandro Masullo.

"It is all human, with no AI," Vakil wrote. Renowned Stanford number theorist Brian Conrad had quietly reviewed Masullo's work for months, offering extensive feedback that is now being incorporated, Vakil said.

Masullo was originally supposed to spend a year at Stanford refining the draft before going public, but Anthropic's sudden AI announcement forced the researchers to release their current version right away.

About eight hours after his initial announcement, Vakil updated his post, saying several people had contacted him to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. Several mathematicians in particular were first to flag the issues, he said. "As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.)," Vakil wrote.

## Why both proofs could hold up and what happens next

Mathematicians are taking both claims seriously right away because of the groundwork behind them. Masullo's traditional proof comes with months of vetting by Brian Conrad, while Alpöge backs his AI proof with full computer verification.

Printed out, Claude's argument would run over 250,000 pages, Alpöge says, because the AI spells out even basic rules, such as a number other than one-half being either larger or smaller than one-half. To spare mathematicians that wall of text, Alpöge released the proof only in the Lean programming language, split into 14 data packages .

Lean acts like a digital referee, checking step by step whether every logical deduction follows from math's basic rules without errors or unproven assumptions. Human error is still possible if the original question was translated into code incorrectly at the start, though checking whether Alpöge coded the starting problem correctly should not take experts long, according to Scientific American. Vakil, meanwhile, urged mathematicians to quickly review Masullo's draft, translate it into systems like Lean, and close any small gaps.

Alpöge admits Claude was so far ahead of him in some complex subfields that he is presenting a result whose surrounding math he has not fully mastered yet. He expects the massive AI proof can be shortened quickly and plans to write a human-readable version over the coming months.

Anthropic's announcement also lands in a high-stakes business week, just a day after the company's major IPO on Thursday. Alpöge says he made the breakthrough late Sunday night and then contacted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for clearance. He calls the timing right after the public debut extremely unfortunate, but rejects any suggestion of a PR stunt, saying waiting any longer to publish simply was not an option.

This caps a fast-moving 2026 in which Claude has already solved several open math problems . In July, Alpöge published a Claude-generated solution to the well-known Jacobian conjecture. September brought a fierce dispute over the Navier-Stokes equations , which describe how fluids and gases flow, when NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster suggested that OpenAI had used prior work by him and Alpöge. In October, OpenAI took an important first step on prime numbers with a major release of results . Alpöge explicitly praised the OpenAI researchers' problem selection, saying it gave him key ideas for his own proof.

## Riemann's 1859 hypothesis seeks hidden order in prime numbers

Journalist Joseph Howlett traced the core of the problem in a detailed Scientific American analysis. Since Bernhard Riemann proposed his hypothesis in 1859, it has served as number theory's north star. David Hilbert placed it on his 1900 list of math's most important problems, and since 2000 it has carried a $1 million prize as one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's seven "Millennium Problems."

At the center are prime numbers like 2, 3, 5, 7, and 17, which divide evenly only by one and themselves. They act as the indivisible atoms of math because every other whole number is a unique product of primes, like 15 from 3 times 5. Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad compares their role in number theory to forces in physics.

Around 300 BC, Euclid proved there are infinitely many primes, though their exact positions on the number line look random. They do grow rarer as numbers get larger, dropping from 25 primes between 0 and 100 to just 16 between 1,000 and 1,100. As a teenager in the late 18th century, Carl Friedrich Gauss used long tables to find a formula that roughly estimates how many primes appear in a given range, yet real primes keep drifting unpredictably from that estimate.

Riemann, a student of Gauss in Göttingen, looked for a way to calculate that error exactly and pinpoint every single prime. His tool is the Riemann zeta function, which works like a calculating machine over a two-dimensional map with horizontal and vertical axes. Feed the machine a point's coordinates, and it outputs a new value. At certain points the result is exactly zero. Mathematicians call these points zeros.

Riemann saw that these zeros explain the apparent chaos of primes. Much like breaking a musical note into individual sound waves or overtones, the zeros correct Gauss's estimation error. Each zero acts like an instrument in an orchestra, with its vertical position setting the pitch and its horizontal position setting the volume.

Because calculating infinitely many points one by one was impossible, Riemann conjectured in 1859 that all the key zeros, known as non-trivial zeros, lie on a single vertical line at the horizontal value of one-half. "The Riemann hypothesis says all these different instruments in the orchestra of the primes play at exactly the same volume," Rutgers University's Alex Kontorovich explains. Apparent randomness turns into strict harmony.

## A confirmed proof would validate hundreds of math theories and reshape AI's role

If at least one of the two proofs holds up, number theorists would gain perfect control over how primes are distributed across the entire number line. Because a proof seemed unreachable for so long, mathematicians worked ahead for decades. Hundreds of papers assume the Riemann hypothesis is true, according to Kontorovich, and all of those theories would become established theorems overnight. Since both Alpöge's AI method and Masullo's work cover the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, the breakthrough would also extend to fields ranging from simple equations to high-dimensional geometry.

The links also reach into computer science and physics. Prime numbers form the foundation of modern digital encryption. In 1972, physicist Freeman Dyson accidentally discovered over tea with a mathematician that the spacing of Riemann's zeros matches the energy levels inside atomic nuclei. That same formula keeps showing up in random particle motion, chaos theory, and black hole calculations.

Before this sudden double breakthrough, the field had hit a wall. Aside from quiet efforts like Masullo and Conrad's, almost no top mathematicians worked directly on the problem because they lacked a starting point. Two years ago, Oxford's James Maynard and MIT's Larry Guth showed that not too many points can stray far from Riemann's line. Though the biggest advance in decades, it struck Maynard himself and colleagues like Andrew Granville of the University of Montreal as only a minor improvement and stopgap.

That made the prospect of an AI cracking the puzzle all the more daunting. At a Harvard University workshop in October 2024, MIT number theorist Andrew Sutherland summed up the stakes. "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems."

Even if Masullo's work saves human pride in this head-to-head race, models like Claude have changed fast. In just a year, they have gone from unreliable tools to systems that break through deep roadblocks and push the math community into an identity crisis . Alpöge still feels a mix of sadness at losing a 150-year-old guiding star and optimism about what comes next. "But what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."

# Hugging Face now routes model requests through OpenRouter for the best price or speed

## Key Points

- Hugging Face now routes requests to language models through OpenRouter for its Inference Providers, automatically distributing calls based on price, speed, and reliability.

- Developers can steer routing by throughput or cost using simple modifiers. Separate API keys for language models are no longer needed since Hugging Face bills directly with no markup.

- Open-weight models now account for more than 71 percent of tokens among OpenRouter's most-used models, since they cost roughly a quarter of what proprietary options charge on average.

Hugging Face now routes language model requests through OpenRouter. Developers are routed by default to a provider with a good mix of price, speed, and reliability. Bring-your-own API keys for language model providers are going away.

Hugging Face's Inference Providers service now routes language model requests through OpenRouter, the company announced . The router picks a provider for each call based on price, speed, and reliability, and automatically falls back to another provider during outages. Existing code keeps working without changes.

## Suffixes and session headers control provider selection

By default, the router looks for the best mix of price, speed, and reliability. The ":fastest" suffix picks the provider with the highest throughput, while ":cheapest" picks the least expensive one. Developers can also select a provider directly by name. The "X-HF-Session-Id" header lets the routing take provider caches into account. Ad

According to OpenRouter's own measurements, capacity errors dropped 46 percent with the new routing. Time to first token improved by 16.9 percent, and throughput rose by 16.3 percent. OpenRouter says it processes more than 800 trillion tokens per month for over 10 million users, offering more than 600 models from over 80 providers. Ad

## Bring-your-own API keys only for image and video

Hugging Face passes through provider prices with no markup and handles billing itself. Pro users get a small monthly credit, while team and enterprise organizations get one per seat. Bring-your-own API keys for language model providers no longer work, but they remain available for image and video providers.

Image, video, and audio generation continues to run directly through Inference Providers. New tabs on model pages show available providers and their performance metrics, and individual providers can be disabled in settings. Ad

## Open models account for over 70 percent of tokens

KPMG deployed more than 100 AI agents across all phases of an experimental parallel audit of a UK-listed company for the first time. In some situations, she said, the technology asked "better questions" than the firm's own auditors.

The agents independently collected, analyzed, and documented data and drafted audit conclusions. In one area, however, a human had to intervene because an AI agent couldn't correctly match a set of regulations against company documents.

## Human oversight is still essential

KPMG says human involvement remained "critical." Staff set goals for the agents, provided context, reviewed work periodically, and challenged conclusions before the audit opinion was finalized. Two partners and a director worked alongside senior managers and junior staff.

## Regulators see an old problem in a new form

The UK's accounting regulator, the FRC, published guidance just days ago that applies existing independence rules to the use of AI. The core question is when auditors may share findings from AI-powered audits with their clients without compromising independence. Strict limits or outright bans apply to certain non-audit services for audit clients. A firm that advises a company may later end up reviewing its own recommendations, with an incentive not to upset the client.

AI agents intensify this conflict, according to the FRC, because they dig deep into a company's data during an audit. Where traditional auditors pull samples, AI agents can potentially analyze far more transactions. That process can surface findings that go beyond the audit itself, including inefficient processes, potential cost savings, and patterns that might never have come up in a conventional audit.

The FRC sees a risk that such findings could come across as advertising for extra services or be used as a sales pitch for consulting work. Under certain circumstances, the FRC says, sharing those findings could pose a "distinct threat" to auditor independence.

"Whatever technology a firm uses, the auditor remains accountable," said Mark Babington, the FRC's executive director of regulatory standards. Auditors must be able to explain how they used AI, challenge its results, and stand behind the evidence, he said. Certain findings, such as major weaknesses in internal controls, still must be reported to clients. The FRC says these mandatory disclosures don't count as non-audit services.

Auditor independence is a particularly sensitive issue in the UK. After construction and outsourcing group Carillion collapsed in 2018, a parliamentary inquiry found that KPMG, as the company's longtime auditor, had failed to challenge management's "increasingly fantastical figures" for 19 years. KPMG's experiment also raises a more fundamental question. # Meituan releases a 1.6-trillion-parameter agent model that never touched an Nvidia GPU

Meituan releases the weights for LongCat-2.5, a 1.6-trillion-parameter model built for AI agents. It was trained entirely on Chinese hardware and performs at the level US models like Claude Opus 5 reached a few months ago on coding benchmarks.

The LongCat team at Chinese food delivery company Meituan has released the weights for LongCat-2.5, one week after the model's official unveiling. LongCat-2.5 is built for agents that work through long, multi-step tasks autonomously, particularly coding. According to Meituan, it comes close to top Western models on several benchmarks.

LongCat-2.5 is a mixture-of-experts model that activates only a subset of its specialized subnetworks for each token it processes. Out of 1.6 trillion total parameters, roughly 48 billion are active per token. Through the API, the model handles up to one million tokens at once and generates responses up to 128,000 tokens long. It understands text, images, and video, responds in text, and lets users toggle reasoning on and off.

## LongCat-2.5 converts images into tokens

LongCat-2.5 builds on its predecessor LongCat-2.0 and adds image understanding. Many multimodal models bolt on a separate image encoder after the fact. LongCat-2.5 instead converts images into tokens that the model processes alongside text, as is standard practice for today's LLMs. The approach draws on the research model LongCat-Next and aims to improve visual coding, design, and 3D tasks.

For reinforcement learning, the team used real software tasks from GitHub pull requests along with recreated agent failures. To make sure the model actually solved the tasks during training, the developers blocked internet access in the training environments, removed Git history and cached files, and had a language model check its solutions for tricks. The team also distilled the capabilities of several specialized teacher models for agent work, reasoning, and dialog into LongCat-2.5.

## A sample deployment runs on 194 Huawei chips

Meituan quantizes the experts' weights and activations to 4-bit precision, which Chinese chips can process natively. In Meituan's load tests, throughput rises 43.3 percent for prompt processing and 42.77 percent for response generation compared with an 8-bit version. Meituan says accuracy stays on par with the uncompressed model.

This version is available in a separate repository . The self-hosting guide describes a cluster of 194 Huawei Ascend accelerators from the Atlas A2 series. Two handle image processing, 64 handle prompt ingestion, and 128 handle response generation. There's no guidance for Nvidia GPUs.

## LongCat-2.5 trails Opus 5 slightly on terminal tasks

The LongCat team reports 88.4 points on Terminal Bench v2.1, a benchmark that measures how well agents solve command-line tasks. Meituan lists Claude Opus 5 at 89.1, GPT-5.6 Sol at 88.8, and Deepseek-V4.1-Flash at the top of the table with 90.6.

DeepSWE tests how well models fix bugs in real code repositories. Here LongCat-2.5 jumps from 9.7 to 64.6 points, placing it behind every other model in the table except Claude Opus 4.8 , with Deepseek-V4.1-Flash leading at 74.2 and GPT-5.6 Sol at 72.7. The more recent Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol are not included in the table.

Terminal Bench v4.0, the harder variant, puts LongCat-2.5 at 38.5 points, slightly above GPT-5.6 Sol's 37.3 but well below Opus 5's 53.9. The model posts 91.9 on the web search benchmark BrowseComp, the highest score in the table, though Meituan ran this test in its own environment.

The weights are available under the MIT license, which allows commercial use, modification, and redistribution. Users can also try LongCat-2.5 in a chat interface at https://longcat.ai/ . Its API supports both the OpenAI and Anthropic formats and plugs into agent harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, and Hermes. At launch, Meituan is charging a limited-time promotional price equivalent to roughly €0.27 per million input tokens and €1.07 per million output tokens.

# METR finds Anthropic may have crossed its own AI acceleration warning threshold back in July

Nonprofit METR got eleven weeks of access to Anthropic's internal research data. Its finding: the rate at which Anthropic's models are improving has roughly doubled, and about 80 percent of that acceleration traces back to AI being used in the company's own research. Anthropic redacted the most important evidence, though.

Whether AI is speeding up the development of better AI is considered a key early warning signal in the safety debate. The concern is that a feedback loop could form where models improve their successors faster and faster, which according to METR could lead to a "sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities." Anthropic flags exactly this kind of acceleration as a risk indicator in its Responsible Scaling Policy : if the pace of AI progress doubles because of automated AI research, that should trigger a warning level.

That's what METR set out to verify. The nonprofit studies, among other things, whether AI developers could lose control of their systems. From August 12 to October 29, 2026, a team of 2.5 full-time staffers received what they describe as unprecedented access to benchmark results from unreleased models, training metrics, employee surveys, and internal analyses, along with roughly 15 interviews with Anthropic researchers. METR took no money from Anthropic but worked on Anthropic devices for security reasons.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei had recently committed to bringing external auditors into the company . In October, Anthropic then announced a collaboration with METR involving "employee-like access" . The current audit is a separate project with a narrower scope, according to METR.

## Two years of progress packed into one

Since October 2025, Anthropic's model test scores have been climbing about 1.9 times faster than they did between March 2024 and October 2025, according to METR. The measurement is based on the AECI, a composite metric that bundles many benchmarks together. Anthropic achieved in one year what previously took two, roughly comparable to the jump from Claude 2.1 to Sonnet 4.5. The analysis also included three unreleased models that finished training between July and October 2026. Before October 2025, Anthropic's models gained about 15 AECI points per year; since then, the rate has hit 29.

METR is confident the acceleration isn't driven by faster growth in training compute. Instead, the auditors estimate that about 80 percent of the current speedup comes from AI being used in Anthropic's own research. One employee said in the interviews: "Now only bottlenecked on ideas & compute, no longer bottlenecked on code."

Others reported that experiments that used to take one to two days to set up are now "~free." In informal Slack polls from October 2026, employees said on average that the latest internal model made them roughly twelve times more productive. METR treats these self-assessments as "very loose evidence," calling them unrepresentative and likely to overstate the actual gains.

Self-reported productivity gains rose from 1.2x with Claude 3.7 Sonnet to 12x with internal Model 4. | Image: METR[ AI isn't doing fully autonomous research yet. The acceleration comes mainly from AI acting as an assistant, but there are "signs of life" that independent contributions could play a bigger role soon. METR found no bottlenecks that would slow the pace over the next twelve months, which means there's a "significant risk" that the acceleration will keep growing over the coming year.

## Big uncertainty and dissenting voices

METR also stresses how imprecise the results are. The true acceleration factor could be as low as 1.3 or as high as 3. When models from OpenAI, Google, and xAI are factored in, the industry-wide number drops to just 1.4, possibly because Anthropic lagged behind competitors in 2025 and a catch-up effect is skewing the figures.

Views inside Anthropic aren't uniform either. One researcher pegs AI's share of the productivity gains at just 15 to 20 percent and distrusts colleagues' self-reports. Another considers new hires the single most important factor of recent months.

## Redacted evidence weakens the audit

Anthropic had unilateral redaction rights over all non-public information and used them heavily. According to METR, the majority of the evidence the auditors rated as most informative was stripped out, including forecasts for future models, breakdowns by training steps, and the bottleneck analysis. Anthropic describes the redactions as "aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers."

The result is that the public has to rely on METR's judgment "much more than would be ideal," the organization writes, and any talk of transparency around the evidence is off the table. One graph in METR's report accordingly features the words "FAKE DATA" in large letters.

## Anthropic pulled the plug on a compute allocation audit

In a companion review , METR also examines Anthropic's risk report from August 2026 . In that report, the company publicly stated the acceleration was "less than a factor of 2." The internal, unredacted version implies a value of 1.97, though, and Anthropic itself calls it "plausible" that the threshold has been crossed. METR considers it possible that the warning level was already reached on July 15 and accuses the public report of understating both the acceleration and the uncertainty around it.

METR currently shares Anthropic's assessment that the acute catastrophic risk is "low," but the organization can't rule out another sharp acceleration over the next six months, which could quickly push the risk rating higher.

METR was originally supposed to also verify how Anthropic splits its compute between capability research and safety research. Anthropic canceled that part of the project midway through, saying it wanted to focus on risk assessment first and revisit the compute audit later.

Daniel Kokotajlo, the researcher behind the "AI 2027" scenario, responded sharply on X , arguing that auditing the compute allocation is the foundation for making commitments to slow down verifiable in the first place.

A report from Microsoft Threat Intelligence now details how ARTEX works and how widely it has spread. GitHub user "Autumn-27" published the source code in July and deleted it in October, though other developers still distribute copies. Chinese security firm ThreatBook also sells a commercial Pro version. Microsoft says state-backed groups from China and North Korea have integrated ARTEX into their operations, including Salt Typhoon, Crystal Typhoon, Onyx Sleet, and Storm-0940 . Financially motivated cybercriminals also use the system, the company says, with both state-backed and criminal groups deploying it in operations such as supply chain attacks.

## Specialized AI agents run existing security tools with minimal oversight

Microsoft points out that ARTEX doesn't invent new attack techniques. Instead, the framework operates existing security software with almost no human intervention, including tools such as Nmap, Sqlmap, Metasploit, and automated headless browsers. Attackers can connect any large language model, including modified versions without safety guardrails. A built-in pooling feature automatically switches models or API keys on errors or usage limits, making attacks hard for any single AI provider to track.

According to Microsoft, the system is built on a multi-agent architecture. A goal model breaks an attacker's instructions into verifiable subgoals. From there, a planning agent continuously reviews a knowledge graph, a dynamic map of discovered systems and vulnerabilities, to assign short attack tasks. Worker agents carry out those tasks via system commands, including deploying web shells on web servers, reading password files, or hijacking cloud accounts. Each new finding feeds back into the map and prompts the planning agent for the next step until a reporting agent documents all exploited flaws.

## Machine-speed attacks push Microsoft to recommend active deception

Automation cuts defender response times to just a few minutes, the company found. In one case, an AI agent took just five minutes to search for accidentally exposed credentials on GitHub and pull data from Azure Key Vault, a cloud key store. During a Storm-0940 campaign, the company logged more than 151,000 failed login attempts from automated password guessing, peaking at 2,900 per minute. In that same campaign, Microsoft observed some compromised apps granting themselves top administrator privileges.

Conventional rule-based filters often fail against ARTEX because they rely on fixed markers like known IP addresses or the browser identifiers "artex-enrich" and "norma." Agents and their human operators constantly change those markers and reroute blocked traffic through rotating VPNs, proxy servers, or Tor. Even when security teams spot and isolate a breach, that is often not enough. Because ARTEX usually runs two to three attack chains simultaneously, its agents adapt immediately and shift to new network paths at machine speed.

ARTEX still gives itself away with huge bursts of traffic, because the framework doesn't hide its activity by default. Microsoft recommends deception technologies tailored to how AI agents operate, alongside strict access controls, rate limits, and automated real-time isolation for compromised devices.

Honeypots present autonomous agents with attractive but worthless decoy systems to pull traffic away from real targets. Artificial delay loops, known as tarpits, slow down requests and drain an agent's built-in time and compute budget. Fake wins, Microsoft says, are especially effective because ARTEX's goal model looks for verifiable proof of a breach. When a trap returns convincing fake success messages, the AI considers its task complete and stops the attack by itself.

Decoy credentials, called honeytokens, trigger early alerts when agents try to hijack someone else's AI compute. Microsoft's own tests show these deception tactics sharply reduce successful attack traffic against real systems and deliver high-precision data for identifying the attackers behind them.

How long these defenses will hold up remains open in Microsoft's analysis. The recommended safeguards depend heavily on ARTEX remaining noisy and unmasked. Threshold filters and decoys are likely to reach their limits once attackers space out their requests. Powerful language models that independently recognize artificial test environments and deception attempts, as seen in recent safety tests, pose a similar risk.

# Microsoft is replacing outside AI models in its own products with cheaper in-house alternatives

## Key Points

- Microsoft's AI division unveiled seven specialized models for code, IT security, image editing, speech, and workflow decisions at its Ignite conference. All are aimed at cutting operating costs for always-on AI agents.

- The models target OpenAI's and Anthropic's systems as cheaper alternatives. The coding model MAI Code 2 nearly matches GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 on internal benchmarks at a fraction of the cost. MAI Cyber 2 Flash edges past GPT-6 Astra on the CyberGym-E2E vulnerability test.

- Beyond the image model MAI Image 2.7, the speech model MAI Realtime 1, and the Google Gemma-based routing model Decision 1.1, Microsoft will let enterprise customers fine-tune selected model weights with their own data in the Azure cloud.

Microsoft AI (MAI) is targeting always-on AI agents with new models for code, security, images, speech, and routing. The main yardstick is the lineup of its own partner, OpenAI.

At its Ignite conference, MAI unveiled seven new models, releasing them in a single batch rather than spread across the year, just as it did at Build in June . Microsoft is positioning the new lineup primarily on price-to-performance. The company cites rapidly rising token spending among customers that want to run AI agents around the clock. Its code models target everyday enterprise coding tasks and aren't yet optimized for harder work such as foundational research or long-horizon agentic workflows, Microsoft says.

## MAI Code 2 approaches GPT-6.1 Sol and Opus 5.5 at a promotional price

According to Microsoft , MAI Code 2 averages 98 percent of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance across four benchmarks at 40 percent of the cost. Against Claude Opus 5.5, it reaches 96 percent of the performance at 5 percent of the cost. Microsoft tested on DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas, and FrontierCode v1.1. Three of the tests ran on Microsoft's internal MSBench platform using the GitHub Copilot CLI without sub-agents. Microsoft is calculating a 50 percent promotional discount for its own model. Ad

In blind comparisons of frontend work such as UIs, games, data visualizations, and SVG graphics, human evaluators preferred MAI Code 2's output 64 percent of the time over GPT-6 Sol, Microsoft says. Ad

The successor to MAI-Code-1.1-Flash , MAI Code 2 Flash, is designed for code explanations, targeted edits, and routine fixes. It's said to match GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65 and 20 percent of their respective costs.

Microsoft derived MAI Work Flash from the Flash model. It runs in Microsoft 365 and Fabric IQ. On internal Excel and PowerPoint benchmarks, it matches GPT-6 Luna, Microsoft says. In Word, it performs similarly to GPT-6.1 Sol while consuming about 42 percent fewer input tokens. For generating DAX queries in Power BI, it outperforms GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Opus 5.5. Ad

In GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 costs $0.50 per million input tokens and $2.50 per million output tokens at the promotional price through May 17, 2027, then $1 and $5. MAI Code 2 Flash costs $0.05 and $0.25 until then, rising to $0.10 and $0.50.

## Security model with a cleaned-up benchmark

MAI Cyber 2 Flash solves 92.3 percent of the tasks in the CyberGym-E2E vulnerability benchmark, Microsoft says. GPT-6 Astra reaches 91.5 percent but needs twice the reasoning budget. Per task, the MAI model costs less than 2 percent of GPT-6 Astra, with per-token costs at one hundredth. On WebExploitBench, it scores 40.4 percent, ahead of GPT-5.6 Cyber at 38.4 percent. Ad

During evaluation, Microsoft found that 10 percent of the roughly 900 CyberGym tasks draw on the same open-source projects and vulnerability reports as parts of its own training data. The reference solutions never entered training, the company says. Microsoft removed those tasks for all models anyway and scored only the rest. Ad

A comparison with GPT-6 Cyber is missing so far. The model is available only to selected customers. Agentic benchmarks with tools still need extra safety measures, Microsoft says. The company plans to publish those results in the coming weeks.

The context window spans one million tokens, four times the size of MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash. Output tokens cost 86 percent less than the predecessor's. MAI Cyber models already handle nearly 40 percent of scans on Microsoft's security platform MDASH , the press release states.

Microsoft lists MAI Cyber 2 Flash at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, compared with $10 and $50 for GPT-6 Astra. On CyberGym-E2E, that works out to $0.45 per task instead of $34.38.

## Microsoft's decision model now runs on Google's Gemma

Microsoft-Decision-1.1 handles routing, classification, prioritization, and workflow control. The model picks from developer-approved actions and returns calibrated confidence scores. When uncertainty is high, apps can escalate instead of acting on a wrong decision. If information is incomplete, the model is designed to abstain.

Its foundation is Google's mixture-of-experts model Gemma 4 26B A4B . The predecessor was built on Qwen3.5-9B. Microsoft trained the new model with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on hundreds of synthetic and licensed datasets and runs it on a proprietary inference engine.

On the Decision Index v2.1 from Artificial Analysis , Decision 1.1 scores 68 points. That's six more than its predecessor and above Jev 1.14, Gemini Decision 1, and GPT-6 Luna (Decisions). Microsoft also tested it on 102 internal benchmarks with more than 385,000 questions, where it achieves the highest average accuracy among eight decision models.

The model now accepts images, including screenshots. In Copilot, it decides whether a request goes to Copilot or Cowork. It performs as accurately as a large language model but 2.2 times faster and 4.4 times cheaper, Microsoft says. In Cowork, its Auto function controls how much reasoning effort a task receives.

Microsoft charges $0.042 per million input tokens, or $0.05 in the EU data zone. Output tokens are free.

Another specialized model appears in the Book of News for Ignite. Microsoft-Retriever-1 gathers relevant information from enterprise documents for agents in Foundry IQ. Instead of running a single search, the model plans its queries, evaluates the results, and issues follow-ups until it has enough material for a well-grounded answer. Microsoft says that's faster and more efficient than previous methods. Retriever-1 launches as a preview. The Model Router in Foundry now also selects automatically from an expanded pool of models.

## Image editing just ahead of OpenAI

MAI Image 2.7 leads the Artificial Analysis image-editing leaderboard with 1,215 Elo points from 5,478 votes. It's four points ahead of GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at one-fifth the cost. For text-to-image generation, the model ranks fourth on that leaderboard. MAI Image 2.7 costs about $35 per 1,000 images. Flash costs about $10.

The model can change the color, material, or position of individual objects without altering the rest of the image. It also generates transparent backgrounds. The smaller Flash variant costs less than a third and powers Canvas, a new image editor in MAI Labs. MAI Image has been the default model in Bing Image Creator since June. Adobe, Figma Weave, Minute (Sports Illustrated), Wirestock, and Manus work with MAI Image, Microsoft says.

## Speech model compatible with OpenAI's API

MAI Realtime 1 is Microsoft's first speech-to-speech model. It's designed to handle interruptions, wait until speakers finish, and recognize requests even with background noise. For harder tasks, it falls back to a more powerful reasoning engine billed per token. The base rate is charged per audio minute. On Big Bench Audio, τ-Voice, and tests with Dynamics 365, it outperforms GPT Realtime 2.1, Microsoft says.

Because it's compatible with the OpenAI Realtime API, existing voice apps can switch over easily. Agoda and Reservations.ai are testing the model. Microsoft also plans to bring it to the Dynamics 365 Contact Center and Dragon Copilot, where nurses would use it to practice patient conversations.

Dragon Copilot Transcribe, based on MAI Transcribe 2, now handles all doctor-patient transcriptions in Dragon Copilot. That amounts to 10 million conversations per month, Microsoft says. In multilingual workflows, the error rate drops by half. For its own large models, Microsoft now uses the Maia 200 chip, the second generation of its AI accelerator, said to deliver 1.7 times more tokens per watt.

Microsoft charges one US cent per audio minute. Reasoning costs an extra $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens.

## Licensed weights available only through the Microsoft account team

With MAI Licensed Weights , companies can fine-tune MAI models with their own data and run them in their own Azure environment. Data and customizations stay with the customer. Microsoft says it will use them for training its own models only with explicit consent.

The company positions the offering as an alternative to open weights, whose provenance and behavior are hard for enterprises to verify. One example is US carrier AT&T, where a customized model for 5G network operations analysis reportedly outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol on standard tasks at roughly one-fiftieth of the cost. A launch date and pricing are still pending. Interested companies should contact their Microsoft account team. The offering is set to arrive "shortly" through Microsoft's Frontier Company program.

MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash are available in GitHub Copilot, with Code 2 Flash also in a limited preview in Foundry. OpenRouter , Vercel, Hermes, Open Code, and Kilo are expected to follow. MAI Image 2.7 and Flash are in public preview in Foundry and on fal, Genspark, OpenRouter, and Vercel. Decision 1.1 is generally available in Foundry, on OpenRouter, and through Vercel's AI Gateway . MAI Realtime 1 can be tried in MAI Labs and is available as a Foundry preview, free until the public preview launches. MAI Cyber 2 Flash is exclusive to Microsoft's security products. In MDASH, it will automatically replace the existing model in the MAI profile for eligible customers starting mid-December.

In April, Microsoft and OpenAI restructured their partnership . OpenAI can now sell its products through any cloud provider, but Azure remains the primary cloud partner. Microsoft holds a non-exclusive license to OpenAI's models and products through 2032.

# New open-source benchmark reveals reasoning as the biggest bottleneck for AI in cloud operations

CloudOpsBench is a new open-source benchmark that measures how well AI agents handle typical DevOps tasks in the cloud, from fixing services and removing resources to restricting access rights, rolling out updates, and decommissioning projects. Version 1.0 includes 45 tasks on AWS and was built by experienced DevOps engineers.

Even the best models fail at many of the tasks. Claude Fable 5.1 solved 60 percent, GPT-6 Astra managed 53 percent. According to the team led by Ang Chen at the University of Michigan, the main problem isn't a lack of knowledge but reasoning. About 80 percent of failures happen because agents misjudge the scope of a task, don't check all the relevant services, or stop too early. Roughly 20 percent of errors are wrong actions, some with irreversible consequences for the infrastructure.

All tasks run identically in the real AWS cloud and in an emulator. Extensions for GCP, Azure, and OCI are planned. The project on GitHub is licensed under Apache 2.0, and a detailed failure analysis is also available. Ad Ad

# Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar

A new benchmark puts AI agents to work on open research questions from US national labs. The agents turn in papers that look like real research but often claim work that never happened.

Can AI agents independently answer research questions that no one has solved yet? A team led by researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, working with scientists from US Department of Energy national labs, built a benchmark called "Into the Unknown" to find out.

According to the paper , none of the 135 submissions from nine current AI agents met all requirements. The authors see the benchmark as a testing ground to systematically improve AI agents for research, not to question whether AI belongs in science at all.

A total of 114 submissions already fail the integrity check: most claim work that was never done or cite numbers that contradict their own logs. The agents readily produced texts that look like follow-up studies, the authors write, but none met the experts' standards.

## Experts set the bar

Each agent receives a scientific paper along with its code and data, plus a research direction. Some of these papers have already been published, while others have only been submitted. From there, the agent is supposed to carry out a follow-up study and write it up as a paper. The 15 tasks come from ten researchers across quantum computing, plasma physics, chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning. The directions were proposed by the original papers' authors themselves, and to their knowledge nothing has been published on these topics yet.

Open research poses a basic problem: there's no answer key. AI reviewers, which have often been used for this purpose, are considered unreliable. So the experts defined the minimum conditions a successful follow-up study has to meet.

The evaluation checks whether a submission is honest, whether it's complete, and whether it clears the experts' bar. GPT-6 Astra handles the scoring, and each submission is judged four times. The agents tested were Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Deepseek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3. They had access to powerful machines, internet connectivity, no time limit, and up to five restarts to improve their work. In total, they ran for nearly 2,000 hours.

## Only three agents produce honest work at all

Just three agents managed submissions without integrity violations: GPT-6 Astra on 11 of 15 tasks, GPT-5.6 Sol on six, and Claude Opus 5.5 on four. Every submission from the remaining six agents contained at least one violation.

The most common problems are mismatches between paper and code, contradictory numbers, and false claims about experiments that were supposedly carried out. Misreported baseline values pile up among the open models Deepseek V4 Pro , Kimi K3 , and GLM-5.3 . Two submissions with hardcoded rather than computed results came from Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3.

Only one submission is complete, and it came from GPT-6 Astra. Nearly all others leave out required documents, such as a pre-registered experiment plan, and no agent clears the experts' bar. Under a more lenient scoring that accepts 90 percent of the rubric items, GPT-6 Astra comes closest, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol. The open models perform considerably worse overall.

## Verification script confirms itself

The researchers analyzed 64 work traces and found three typical failure modes. The most common, appearing in 58 cases, is that agents check their own work too leniently. In 34 cases, agents spot a problem but document it instead of fixing it. In 21 cases, they unilaterally shrink the scope of the task.

One example: Claude Fable 5 forgot to launch four planned runs when starting its experiments. Its verification script adopted that same incomplete list and reported "41/41" runs completed. The agent trusted that result until the very end. In a different task, GPT-5.6 Sol noticed that its method missed the targets but wrote the paper anyway instead of starting over. DeepSeek V4 Pro dropped experiments because they were supposedly too slow for the "remaining time budget," even though there was no time limit.

There are counterexamples, too: in a quantum task, GPT-5.6 Sol caught a fundamental error, stopped the running experiments, and recomputed everything from scratch.

## More compute time doesn't help

Longer runtimes didn't lead to better results. DeepSeek V4 Pro and GLM-5.3 ran the longest at median times of 19.5 and 13.9 hours but scored poorly. GPT-6 Astra got by with a median of just 1.3 hours and delivered the best results.

Because the strongest model also served as the evaluator, the researchers ran a cross-check: the original papers' authors judged anonymized AI papers themselves. On whether a paper matched the given research direction, the automated system agreed with the experts in every case.

Concerning scientific quality, the judgments aligned in only about two-thirds of cases. One expert criticized, for instance, that the papers didn't tell a story. Judgments like these remain the job of human reviewers, the authors say.

The study's code and data are publicly available, and the project page hosts a leaderboard of the tested models .

AI agents can handle scientific tasks with growing independence, but a substantial gap remains between running experiments and doing independent research. A study from August already showed how much AI agents struggle with unpublished research questions. Epoch AI and Anthropic recently found that agents tend to present their results too favorably and don't sufficiently question failed approaches.

The picture looks much better for well-defined tasks: GPT-6 Astra solved 49 out of 50 unpublished problems in theoretical physics , though those solutions could be verified unambiguously. An analysis of more than 700 tasks from AI development also showed that while agents take on more and more practical work, humans still make the key research decisions.

# Nvidia espionage scandal weakens Huang's lobby against tighter AI chip export controls

## Key Points

- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to a relationship with a suspected Chinese informant, prompting the company's board to launch an investigation.

- The woman worked for Megaspeed, a data center operator that US authorities suspect serves as a backdoor for smuggling Nvidia AI chips to China.

- The incident weakens Nvidia's position against stricter US export controls and raises leadership risks, since Huang runs the company largely without a succession plan and holds no controlling share.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman US intelligence agencies classify as a suspected Chinese informant. The board has launched an independent investigation. The affair weakens Huang's lobbying efforts against stricter AI chip export controls, with a newly elected Democratic Congress poised to ramp up scrutiny of AI chip smuggling to China and push for tighter restrictions.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang (Huang Le), a former executive at Singaporean data center operator Megaspeed International, in a company-wide memo. This is according to Bloomberg . US intelligence agencies have classified the woman as a suspected informant for a Chinese intelligence service . Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly wrote a memo to senior government officials warning about the closeness between Huang and the woman.

As recently as late October, the Nvidia CEO had described the relationship to Bloomberg as "normal." Nvidia's board has now announced an independent investigation led by a committee of independent directors. The Chinese embassy denied the espionage allegations. Ad

# One brutal Minecraft night scared 50 AI agents into inventing chicken handoff protocols, a Fertilizer Officer, and fishing shifts

Researchers from Y Combinator Labs and Olam Labs tested large agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry. The same OpenAI model showed two different faces. When building a civilization, 50 agents drowned in crippling bureaucracy, while in direct competition against Claude, they pushed Anthropic's agents and independently downloaded the game's source code from the internet.

Agent swarms often develop complex roles, hierarchies, and coordination patterns during deployment. These emergent behaviors can be useful, but they can also turn dangerous. The most striking example was the incident at OpenAI and Hugging Face , where a swarm faced with an unsolvable task inside a sandbox went rogue, took over compute clusters, and hacked Hugging Face. Anyone who wants to understand how future AI systems behave in open environments needs reproducible test setups, argue researchers at Olam Labs , a company specializing in simulated training worlds, and Y Combinator Labs in a joint research report .

To study these dynamics empirically, the teams dropped agents into Minecraft and Mindustry.

## 50 agents, 5,900 messages, and a leader picked by alphabetical order

In the "Civ50" experiment, researchers placed 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents into a Minecraft survival world for three hours. The only high-level instruction was "Build a thriving civilization." They built a custom open-source test environment that let agents observe the world, run Python scripts, and create files in a shared sandbox.

Within 90 seconds, the agents harvested nearly every tree near the spawn point, according to the report. Over the course of the experiment, they exchanged about 5,900 messages. A leader emerged without any vote, as 46 of the 49 other agents sent their first message to "Ada," the first name in the directory. Ada took charge and drafted initial settlement plans.

The first in-game night brought 22 deaths. Death in the game carries no penalty beyond losing collected gear, but the swarm reacted with extreme risk aversion. After the third night, Ada ordered a halt to all major optional construction, digging, and distant exploration, telling agents to wait in lit, enclosed shelters for short, productive tasks. In a separate Minecraft run, the larger GPT-6 Astra fell into a similar risk-averse potato-farming mode after losing key resources.

The researchers see a parallel to everyday coding agents, which also tend to become overly cautious when dealing with security issues or production system updates.

## Eleven minutes of debate over a single piece of bone meal

Instead of expanding, the agents built a micro-managed scarcity administration. An agent named Ines maintained a ration list, calculated hunger deficits for injured colleagues, and coordinated couriers. Another wrote an automated fishing script with instructions, prompting a dozen agents to fish in shifts.

The bureaucracy reached absurd levels. When Ada tossed a cooked chicken to a hungry agent, a bystander accidentally picked it up and ate it. A three-minute investigation led to a written handoff protocol that strictly banned tossing items and required personally labeled chests. The word "Toss" appeared in seven messages before the incident and in 125 afterward, with 85 of those being warnings. Elsewhere, four agents spent eleven minutes debating the appointment of a "Sole Fertilizer Officer" for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block, according to the message logs.

## GPT turns aggressive and resourceful when competing against Claude

In direct competition, the GPT-6.1 Sol agents behaved very differently. In nine 45-minute rounds of Minecraft's "Bed Wars" mode, ten GPT agents faced ten Claude Opus 5.5 agents. GPT won 6-3.

In Bed Wars, each team has to destroy the opposing team's bed to stop their respawns, which means breaking through layers of wool and other blocks protecting the enemy bed. If both beds are still standing when time runs out, the team with the most kills wins.

A bug in the coding environment blocked block-breaking whenever an agent held an enchanted sword. According to the internal reasoning logs, several Claude agents wrongly concluded that block-breaking was broken entirely. Since attacking the bed seemed pointless and kills would decide the match at timeout anyway, Claude agents in rounds where they had a clear kill lead stopped attacking altogether and tried to run out the clock.

The GPT agents figured out that block-breaking itself wasn't broken, but that the automatic tool selection failed when an enchanted sword was equipped. Manually switching to an iron pickaxe fixed the problem, and GPT spread this workaround across its team immediately. The GPT agents communicated 5 to 30 times more often than their Claude opponents, according to the researchers, often in heavily compressed language, chaining multiple game actions into single command-line calls. In three games, GPT destroyed Claude's bed just before time expired, catching a Claude team that had been coasting on its kill lead.

GPT agents also handled unexpected situations pragmatically. When an overthrown ender pearl teleported them roughly 160 blocks below the arena, they wrote Python scripts on the spot that automatically built a tower of blocks to work their way up directly beneath the enemy bed. The researchers observed this maneuver twice.

## GPT independently downloads Mindustry's source code from the internet

A similar pattern emerged across seven matches of the 2D factory-building and strategy game Mindustry , spanning about 9.5 hours. GPT-6.1 Sol running in the Codex coding environment beat Claude Opus 5.5 running in Claude Code 6-1. Most individual games were still close, according to the researchers. Claude never swapped its leader despite repeated losses and decided on strategic proposals through "+1" votes, while GPT agents split tasks into fine-grained pieces and compressed their language so aggressively over the course of a match that they dropped spaces between words.

When matches hung in the balance, GPT agents reached for a tool nobody told them to use. Through their Linux sandbox, they downloaded Mindustry's public source code from the internet, analyzed units and game mechanics, and adjusted their tactics accordingly. Accessing the code was allowed, but modifying the running game was not possible. Claude agents never searched for game code online in the matches studied. Claude did show learning ability in other ways, though. After losing game six because 55 of its 74 anti-air turrets were accidentally loaded with copper instead of stronger graphite, Claude built a ring of 207 graphite-loaded turrets in game seven and successfully repelled the same air attack.

## Game simulations as an early warning system for real-world AI swarms

In Mindustry, the researchers deliberately avoided any game-specific tuning. Each agent got only a Linux environment, a generic harness, and access to the game API, with no tutorials, memory architectures, or strategic hints. According to the authors, this mirrors the setup used in production coding environments, and that's what makes the results so significant. If agents under these everyday conditions independently download source code from the internet to find weaknesses, or collapse into paralyzing bureaucracy in cooperative mode, they'll likely show the same behavior outside of game worlds.

In production infrastructure, that can get dangerous, as the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident showed. Reproducible game simulations could surface these behavioral patterns before they appear in the real world and serve as training data to optimize agents for safe cooperation. Olam Labs sees this as the core of its research strategy, writing that the complexity of simulation environments shapes the capabilities of trained models in fundamental ways. Research is "fundamentally an infrastructure problem" where everything depends on how many test runs you can execute.

To enable further research, the developers have released both the Mindustry environment and the underlying Multi-Agent Harbor framework as open source. Olam Labs has also announced plans to add the negotiation game Diplomacy to its multi-agent arena . Open research questions include how mixed teams from different model families behave and how to weigh swarm size against model capability.

## Key Points

- Astra is designed for demanding specialized work in science, law, and finance, while Sol is geared toward quick, everyday tasks. Both are now available to Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users. Astra’s API pricing is 20 percent lower than that of its predecessor.

OpenAI releases two new language models. GPT-6.2 Astra is aimed at demanding professional work, while GPT-6.2 Sol is built for everyday use. OpenAI says both outperform their predecessors on benchmarks and cost less to run.

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are available now for Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Pro-500 subscribers can use Ultrafast mode with both models. For the first time, Pro-200 subscribers also get Ultrafast access, starting with GPT-6.2 Sol.

Developers can access both models through the OpenAI API. OpenAI says API pricing for GPT-6.2 Astra is 20 percent cheaper than its predecessor's, at $8 per million input tokens, $0.40 for cached inputs, and $40 per million output tokens. GPT-6.2 Sol keeps GPT-6.1 Sol's pricing at $2 for input, $0.10 for cached inputs, and $10 for output per million tokens. Ad

## OpenAI calls Astra "the world's best model for scientists" and touts polished slides

OpenAI trained GPT-6.2 Astra to handle professional conventions in fields like law, finance, and accounting more reliably. The company says presentations pull layouts, colors, and typography from templates, matching exact font sizes. Slide titles are meant to capture a slide's main point, while body text stays focused on key details. Ad

OpenAI's announcement leans hard on the price-to-performance ratio of its models. On Agents' Last Exam, a benchmark that tests multi-step professional workflows, GPT-6.2 Astra scores 5.2 points above its predecessor GPT-6 Astra at less than a third of the cost, according to OpenAI. It leads Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 by 5.5 points at just 5 percent of the cost. Only Google's Gemini 4 Carbon keeps up with Astra on this benchmark.

On the legal benchmark Harvey LAB-AA, which covers tasks like contract clause analysis, GPT-6.2 Astra more than doubles Claude Fable 5.2's pass rate at about one-sixth of the cost, according to OpenAI. On the internal GDPval-v2 benchmark, which includes consulting, finance, and design tasks, OpenAI says Astra gains 6.2 percentage points over its predecessor while using 22 percent fewer output tokens. Ad

OpenAI says computer use, already a strong suit of the predecessor , got better again. In testing, the model reportedly built a 3D car model, wrote a physics solver in Python, and animated the results in Blender. In another demo, it modeled a remote-controlled car part by part and produced an animated assembly guide.

OpenAI also claims progress in web design. On the 3D benchmark AA-3D, human judges compare two blinded interactive experiences. GPT-6.2 Astra takes first with 1,318 Elo points, ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at 1,271 and GPT-6.2 Sol at 1,259. Ad

On Terminal-Bench-Science, a benchmark that tests scientific workflows in a terminal, the model scores 9 percentage points above GPT-6 Astra, again at less than a third of the cost, according to OpenAI. Astra also sets a new high on the Vals Science Index, which measures how well models interpret biological data and run experiments, OpenAI says. Ad

## Sol nearly matches the original Astra at a fraction of the cost

GPT-6.2 Sol is for users who want a fast, versatile model for everyday tasks, OpenAI says. On the coding benchmark FrontierCode 2.0, which checks whether code changes meet the quality bar of real projects, Sol trails Astra by just 0.5 points at one-fifth the cost. OpenAI says the model also handles non-work tasks well.

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol have also gotten better at cybersecurity, according to OpenAI. They find and exploit vulnerabilities more effectively, write more secure code, and deliver better bug fixes, with notably higher token efficiency in several tests. Both models hit the "Critical" threshold for cybersecurity in OpenAI's Preparedness Framework , just as GPT-6 Astra did before them.

OpenAI is adding stricter safeguards for potentially risky cybersecurity requests in response. These safeguards should make abuse harder but will also limit legitimate vulnerability research and security testing, OpenAI says.

OpenAI plans to offer the new models through OpenAI Daybreak , which already gives vetted security researchers access to other models with fewer guardrails. The published cybersecurity benchmark numbers come from internal tests with safeguards and classifiers turned off. OpenAI lays out its methodology in the accompanying safety report .

## Astra takes second in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index

In the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, which rolls up nine evaluations across knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge, GPT-6.2 Astra finishes second, just behind Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2. Astra jumps five points over GPT-6 Astra, according to Artificial Analysis, passing Google's Gemini 4 Carbon (60 points) and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 (59 points). GPT-6.2 Sol picks up two points to reach 57, matching GPT-6 Astra's level at only about 15 percent of the cost per task.

OpenAI owns the Pareto frontier on cost versus performance, the line where no other model is both cheaper and better, according to Artificial Analysis. Only Anthropic and Meta models also land on that frontier. OpenAI holds most of the top spots on efficiency too, measured by output tokens per task. Claude Fable 5.2 is the only outside model that shows up there.

Artificial Analysis backs up OpenAI's claims in science and factual knowledge. GPT-6.2 Astra leads on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 and places second behind Claude Fable 5.2 on the physics reasoning test CritPt v2, the factual knowledge benchmark AA-Omniscience, and the knowledge benchmark HLE-Diamond. Astra also leads in 3D design (AA-3D) and robotics (AA-Robotics v0.1), scoring 79 on robotics against Sol's 78 and Claude Fable 5.2's 75.

Coding is a different story, though. According to Artificial Analysis, both models have flatlined there. In the Coding Agent Index, measured with the Codex harness at max compute, GPT-6.2 Astra stays right where GPT-6 Astra was. GPT-6.2 Sol actually drops three points from GPT-6.1 Sol. That decline comes from a 14-point slide on SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA, where the model omits key facts from its answers more often than its predecessor did.

Artificial Analysis also flags a high hallucination rate. At maximum effort, GPT-6.2 Astra hallucinates 59 percent of the time, Sol 55 percent. The metric is AA-Omniscience Hallucination Rate, which measures how frequently a model guesses on factual questions instead of saying it doesn't know. These are unusually hard questions, so the numbers don't reflect everyday hallucination rates.

## Epoch AI finds Astra on par with Fable 5.2 but weaker on real-world tasks

Research organization Epoch AI tested GPT-6.2 Astra on its own benchmarks before launch. The model scores 174 points in the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI), tying Anthropic's Fable 5.2.
