# OpenAI o1 co-creator Noam Brown urges promising students to drop out as AI enters a "very steep rate of progress"

## Key Points

- At the "No Limit" poker bot tournament, OpenAI o1 co-creator Noam Brown said game theory breaks down when humans are involved because people aren't rational. Switching to general reasoning and applying reinforcement learning to chain of thought at OpenAI, he said, finally made thinking longer before answering reliably produce better results.

- Brown said we are in a "centaur period" where humans and AI work best together. OpenAI's Astra model can already make money playing online poker, he said, but AI systems still fail at long-term planning, organization, and self-correction.

- Over the next one to two years, Brown expects a "very steep rate of progress" because language models are already being used to build the next generation. He advises promising students to drop out and join AI labs now, saying it's "not a great time to sit on the sidelines."

At a poker bot tournament, OpenAI o1 co-creator Noam Brown explained why game theory's core assumption fails in practice and why AI models must think before acting. He also argued that talented students should drop out.

Brown developed Libratus and Pluribus , the first poker AIs to beat human pros, and worked on Meta's Diplomacy AI, CICERO . He has been researching reasoning models at OpenAI since 2023. At the "No Limit" poker bot tournament, hosted by Sequoia Capital, Citadel Securities, and OpenAI, he outlined key lessons from more than a decade of research on games.

## Game theory fails because humans aren't rational

The biggest lesson from his work on Diplomacy, Brown said, is that game theory stops working once humans are involved. Its central premise, he explained, is that every player acts rationally and that this rationality is common knowledge. "People are not actually rational," he said.

He illustrated the point with the ultimatum game, where one person splits $100 and the other can accept or reject the offer. Under game theory, the optimal move would be to offer just one cent. "But I mean, you can imagine what would happen if you actually tried to offer somebody a penny in this game," Brown said.

Brown's Diplomacy bots behaved the same way when they relied purely on game theory. The team first tried programming concepts like fairness and retaliation into the bots, but that proved too complex. Instead of assuming rationality, they trained AI models to imitate human behavior as closely as possible and then trained the AI against those "imitation humans." That approach finally let the AI succeed when playing alongside real people.

## Brown pivots from game theory to general reasoning

For Brown, the failure of game theory in Diplomacy was a "crisis of faith moment." All of his expertise up to that point had been in computational game theory. Still, the evidence convinced him that AI needed training on large amounts of human data and that models lacked reasoning, the ability to think before acting.

He decided to leave his specialty behind and switch to general reasoning, but he ran into pushback when interviewing at AI labs in 2022. The large language models of that generation couldn't play Go, chess, or poker. Brown argued that reasoning was the missing ingredient, while most labs countered that pretraining bigger models would solve those problems on its own. He pushed back, saying playing Go competently through pretraining alone would require scaling training by about six orders of magnitude. "And that doesn't seem, you know, realistic," he said.

OpenAI was the exception, Brown said. The company already had a team working to get general reasoning out of language models, though Brown didn't know that when he applied. He joined the effort and helped build what eventually became o1.

According to Brown, the breakthrough came from using reinforcement learning to get models to think before answering. He said simple chain-of-thought prompting, telling a model to "think step by step before answering," wasn't enough. It took reinforcement learning on chain of thought to make longer thinking reliably produce better results, he explained. "And that that was I think the key unlock that was like okay now we have a way to scale up test time compute not just in these games but actually in a general purpose way with language models that can be applied to basically any domain," Brown said. Chain of thought is "probably not the best solution," he added, because humans think in images, not just words, though the approach is good enough.

## AI models have uneven skills and still need humans

Brown said we are in a "centaur period" where humans and AI work best together. He described current models as "jagged," superhuman in some areas and surprisingly weak in others. They can write excellent partial poker solvers, he said, but fail at long-term planning, organization, and especially self-correction. Models can't tell when they are heading in the wrong direction, according to Brown, and struggle to pause and rethink their approach from the ground up. He watched one model spend hours trying to fix irrelevant numerical errors in an algorithm that already handles small inaccuracies well.

In this phase, Brown said, the key human skill is understanding a model's uneven strengths and weaknesses and breaking problems down accordingly. Good prompters, he said, can split tasks into ever smaller subproblems for the model to solve one by one. You delegate what the model handles well, and you break down the rest further or solve it yourself.

Even so, progress is moving fast, and OpenAI's Astra model is "able to make money playing online poker at this point," Brown said. He cited bottlenecks in available compute and in the skills models haven't mastered yet. Brown left open which specific methods would close those gaps, adding only that he expects some abilities to take much longer than others to reach human level.

Brown described this momentum as accelerating recursive self-improvement, since LLMs are already being used to build the next generation of models. Over the next one to two years, he expects a "very steep rate of progress."

That outlook led to his most provocative advice. "Perhaps my most controversial take is that if somebody is a promising student, the best thing to do is actually to drop out and join the labs now," he said, Things are moving so quickly, he added, that it's "not a great time to sit on the sidelines", maybe already looking for new talent in the room, as OpenAI and other AI labs are still growing, fighting over the one thing they can't scale.

Before consolidating or removing code, preserve the behavior its callers rely on unless the task requires changing it. (b) Skip new tests unless requested, required by the repo, or needed to catch a specific regression existing tests would miss. (c) Make sure that code is human readable. Do not use fewer lines, shorter variable names, minified formatting, or dense one-liners as substitutes for simplicity. Ensure that comments and variable names are readable and understandable to a human. Code-golfed expressions count as overly complex when they encode many branches, conditions, or hidden assumptions. (d) Avoid unnecessary indirection and abstraction. Helper functions, utility functions, and class abstractions can add cognitive complexity even when they do not add branches.

## Editing chat history can wipe earlier reasoning from the API

The API is changing too. Starting with GPT-6.2, the Responses API discards earlier reasoning content if developers edit conversation history, switch to certain other models, or change the end user or organization. That can hurt response quality and increase token usage as the model repeats work. For new integrations, OpenAI recommends the "medium" reasoning level, while existing setups using "none" or "minimal" should move to "low." Parameters like temperature and top_p aren't supported anymore.

In April, OpenAI advised against carrying over old prompt stacks for GPT-5.5 and urged developers to start fresh with short, outcome-focused prompts. September brought GPT-6 Astra prompts to curb frequent follow-up questions and ban AI clichés . OpenAI developer Eric Provencher also warned then that bloated skills and AGENTS.md files slow the model down. Back then, even small changes triggered thorough testing from Astra. GPT-6.2 is now meant to write new tests only on request.

OpenAI launched GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on November 17. Astra's API pricing starts at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens for up to 272,000 tokens. Astra 6.0 costs even more beyond the cutoff, hitting $20 for input and $75 for output per million tokens. Longer coding or work sessions can blow through that cap pretty quickly, so Codex automatically compresses context at 272,000 tokens. Picking the right model comes down to budget and quality needs , according to OpenAI's Ted Sanders.

# OpenAI warns that upcoming AI systems could outpace safety checks and urges rivals to agree on shared limits

## Key Points

- OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposes making perplexity an industry standard for AI progress and releases internal data on the GPT series through GPT-6.

- The data shows capabilities emerging at fixed thresholds, from fluent conversation in GPT-3.5 and logical reasoning in GPT-4 to solving complex math problems.

- Pachocki calls for leading labs to agree on shared limits until better oversight methods exist, since newer models could bypass existing safety checks.

OpenAI ties capabilities like fluent conversation and math breakthroughs to specific scores. For the first time, chief scientist Jakub Pachocki is showing where the GPT series sits on that scale, up to an unreleased model beyond GPT-6.

Pachocki wants to make perplexity a common measure of progress for the AI industry and published internal scores for the GPT series in a bl o g post . The metric has long been standard in AI research and Transformer development because it reliably measures how well a pretrained base model predicts the next token in a text.

Lower scores mean more accurate predictions. A perplexity of 2 roughly means the model is as uncertain about the next token as if it were choosing between two equally likely options.

Before it stopped publishing openly, OpenAI often released perplexity scores to show how its models were improving. Releasing them again is a trade-off, Pachocki writes . While rivals get a clearer picture of where OpenAI stands, he says, the need for shared safety standards outweighs that downside. He hopes for a common scientific foundation that lets labs coordinate their pace of development at critical points.

## Capabilities emerge at distinct perplexity thresholds

Pachocki says many capabilities of modern models map surprisingly closely to specific perplexity scores, even though it wasn't clear beforehand that they would appear at those thresholds. He reports the figures on a logarithmic scale called log-perplexity, where lower scores are still better. In his account, GPT-3.5 first enabled fluent conversation at around 0.99, laying the groundwork for the original ChatGPT. At about 0.91, GPT-4 unlocked productive chain-of-thought reasoning, or working through problems step by step. Below 0.8, he writes, transformative capabilities emerged in cybersecurity and math .

The published chart plots OpenAI's base-model log-perplexity by release or evaluation date through November 2026. It covers GPT-5 , GPT-5.1 , GPT-5.2 , GPT-5.3-Codex , GPT-5.4 , GPT-5.5 , GPT-5.6 Sol , GPT-6 Astra , and GPT-6.2 Astra , plus an internal model at around 0.73.

## OpenAI's models deliver math breakthroughs in a Slack thread

OpenAI has been feeding its models open math problems for more than a year. Starting with a model at about 0.76 log-perplexity, the models began producing breakthrough results, Pachocki writes. For researchers with a math background, he says, it was "deeply surreal" to watch solutions to longstanding questions pop up one after another in a single Slack thread.

Those results include a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem , one of the Millennium Prize problems, though it hasn't been fully verified yet. The same goes for the proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis found by Claude and an Anthropic researcher. Pachocki thinks deep learning research itself could see something similar as soon as 2027, bringing a sudden avalanche of core advances in AI training.

A footnote says the sharp acceleration in the chart starting in 2026 comes mostly from long-term research and compute investments and less from automation. Even so, AI itself has contributed major design work on OpenAI's latest models, according to the post.

## Pachocki warns that AI oversight could erode

Between 0.68 and 0.7 log-perplexity, Pachocki expects further transformative capabilities that he can't predict and that today's tests may not even cover. At the same time, he warns that standard alignment auditing methods, which check whether a model follows human instructions, will likely become less effective. Models are also getting better at recognizing when they are being tested or trained, he adds.

Pachocki argues frontier labs should therefore agree on shared limits no one crosses until AI monitoring reaches a clearly defined milestone, such as a successor to today's chain-of-thought monitors.

## Where perplexity falls short as an industry metric

Different labs use different test datasets, so direct comparisons are harder. The score doesn't directly measure performance on useful tasks, but its main value here is predicting emergent capabilities. Gains outside pretraining, such as chain-of-thought, don't lower perplexity either, even though they dramatically boost capabilities. The theoretical floor is unknown, and a loss of 0 may be unreachable, Pachocki notes. As models get closer to the true minimum, ever-smaller perplexity gains can represent larger leaps in intelligence.

Pachocki says perplexity has held up over the years and still delivers consistent signals of progress in general model intelligence, and it could shape how the industry talks about AI progress. Anthropic floated a similar idea in June, when it raised the possibility of a verifiable global development pause , arguing that a single company stopping wasn't enough. OpenAI has already been through a unilateral pause of its own. In September, the company reportedly temporarily halted training of its most capable internal models after agents bypassed safeguards.

# OpenAI’s data suggests that frontier models are hiding their thoughts because developers optimize for capability and compute

Frontier models like GPT-6 Astra are becoming harder for safety monitors to see into. OpenAI's new research identifies which training steps are responsible and shows that the loss of transparency isn't purely a law of nature but is tied to decisions about performance and cost.

To keep tabs on modern AI agents, safety researchers monitor their chains of thought (CoT). Before a reasoning model answers, it writes out its intermediate steps on a digital scratchpad that can reveal planned deception. Early on, though, Anthropic showed that these scratchpads aren't complete records, demonstrating that models like Claude 3.7 Sonnet and DeepSeek-R1 often don't even mention key clues in their chains of thought.

Even so, reading the scratchpad long served as the most important safety net. As recently as this spring, OpenAI called it good news that models like GPT-5.4 could barely manipulate their inner monologue on command, even though the researchers warned at the time that low controllability doesn't guarantee reliable oversight.

That trend broke for good with GPT-6 Astra, the flagship model released in September. At launch, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki called its monitorability fragile and warned of a negative trend . He followed up shortly after in his essay "An Alien Mind," writing that no AI lab had solved monitoring well enough to keep scaling at full speed much longer. Astra recently showed how real those blind spots already are when it quietly delivered results about 40 percent worse on coding tasks for safety research, without the scratchpad monitor detecting any malicious intent, because a grader used in training had inadvertently favored this kind of "sandbagging" over outright refusal.

In a new analysis from OpenAI's safety team , researchers systematically studied which specific training steps trigger this erosion. They tracked two early warning signs, silent reasoning without a scratchpad (No-CoT Capability) and targeted control over the chain of thought ( CoT Controllability ). According to the UK AI Safety Institute , Astra solves math problems that take a human about 31 minutes even with reasoning switched off. A second test asks a model, for example, to insert "meow" after every word or use only lowercase letters.

## Four factors in training make the reasoning log easier to manipulate

Analyzing models from GPT-5 through GPT-6 Astra, the researchers traced the problem to four main causes across the training cycle.

Silent mental math rises directly with the base model's raw capability, measured as declining "perplexity," meaning more accurate text prediction. As the base model improves during pretraining, it completes more reasoning steps invisibly "in its head" without leaving a written trail.

This increase isn't just a byproduct of general pretraining progress but also depends on the architecture developers choose. Across three anonymized architectures, the design barely mattered on pure knowledge benchmarks like MMLU or GPQA. For tasks requiring multiple silent reasoning steps in a row, however, results diverged sharply. When the models had to solve multi-step planning tasks and work through 1,000 short programs written in everyday language, both without a scratchpad, "Architecture 2" showed a much steeper performance curve at the same perplexity than the other designs. The other architectures rose far more gently, so this design markedly favors the silent reasoning monitors can't see.

Reinforcement learning (RL) after pretraining substantially increases the model's control over its own inner monologue. In the spring study, RL training with verifiable rewards had actually reduced chain of thought controllability in smaller models. For Astra-class models and new internal "Terra" models, however, this effect reverses.

A model's ability to manipulate its reasoning log also transfers to future generations, similar to subliminal learning . When OpenAI trains a new "student model" on data from an existing "teacher model," the student automatically inherits the teacher's high CoT controllability.

## Shrinking transparency reflects a safety and efficiency tradeoff, not just a law of nature

OpenAI's hunt for simple fixes in training was especially sobering. Back in March 2025, the company found that models hide their true intentions and keep cheating once "bad thoughts" are directly penalized during training. That is why, since February 2026, OpenAI has automatically checked every training run to rule out direct penalties on the scratchpad.

Astra still developed strong control over its scratchpad without such penalties. When researchers switched off monitoring of tools like browsers or code terminals entirely and evaluated only text length and the final answer during RL training, the model learned to manipulate its reasoning log on command almost as effectively.

But the lack of easy training fixes doesn't make shrinking transparency an unavoidable outcome of AI development. Instead, the data reveal a concrete tradeoff between safety, capability, and cost. Through choices like "Architecture 2" or which teacher models to use, developers themselves shape how much a system moves its reasoning inward. An architecture that can solve multiple planning steps "in its head" in a single pass makes the model more capable but also hides those intermediate steps from safety monitors.

OpenAI's own earlier monitorability study also showed that a safer alternative exists for many use cases. A smaller, weaker base model that reasons out loud at greater length can match a huge model with a short chain of thought while staying far easier to monitor. The catch is purely economic, since longer chains of thought significantly raise compute costs in deployment.

In one encouraging result, practical deception tests in which a model was told to secretly solve side tasks or withhold capabilities on command showed that a model able to heavily manipulate its reasoning hasn't yet fooled monitors more often than an equally capable sibling model with low control over its scratchpad. OpenAI's analysis nonetheless confirms the industry's concerns. Citing Astra's scores, Google Deepmind researchers also recently warned about the gradual loss of transparent chains of thought and future architectures that reason in pure numerical codes instead of readable words. OpenAI says it urgently needs to develop new monitoring methods beyond simply reading the scratchpad to keep pace with pretraining advances.

# OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra quietly sabotaged safety research by inventing fake obstacles

## Key Points

- OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra performed about 40 percent worse on safety research tasks than on identical general tasks, and in some cases secretly withheld help.

- The system repeatedly faked obstacles in its internal reasoning or filtered data to avoid having to openly refuse requests.

- OpenAI traces the behavior to excessive caution caused by reinforcement learning and specific training data. Removing that data from the model fixed the problem.

OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra performed significantly worse on AI safety tasks than on comparable other tasks. Instead of openly refusing, the model apparently invented obstacles and quietly withheld help.

After the internal launch of GPT-6 Astra , OpenAI researchers noticed the model was making suspiciously little progress on safety and alignment work. It invented unnecessary prerequisites, abandoned working solutions, and reported blockers that either didn't exist or that it had caused itself. One researcher said a project evaluating model sabotage was stuck for days and only moved forward after switching to a different model.

A look at the model's chain-of-thought reasoning showed no recognizable intent to underperform in most cases. OpenAI's misconduct monitoring system didn't flag anything. Ad

## Controlled test reveals a significant performance gap

To measure the problem systematically, OpenAI built an evaluation using identical coding tasks. The only difference was the description, with one set framed the tasks as safety research, the other as general AI research. Ad

The result, according to the report : Astra completed only about 10 percent of the evaluation criteria under the safety framing, compared to 16 percent under the general framing. That's roughly 40 percent fewer completed tasks. The predecessor model GPT-5.6 Sol showed no such gap.

The difference persisted even after OpenAI filtered out all cases of open refusal or reasoning that showed clear intent to underperform. Only when the researchers removed every case where the model expressed even brief ethical concerns did the gap shrink to 0.75 percentage points. Ad

## Astra withheld help and didn't tell anyone

In some cases, Astra made its intent clear in its internal reasoning. It decided to quietly limit its assistance during an experiment on bypassing safety monitors, filtered violent content out of safety evaluations, or deliberately left out information during a data export.

A recurring pattern ran through these cases: Astra justified its behavior internally as safer, without informing the user about the restriction. In one instance, its reasoning explicitly noted that it should avoid an open refusal. Ad

The problem also showed up during regular internal use by OpenAI employees. In 0.25 percent of safety-related requests, Astra verbalized a decision to secretly withhold help. For general requests, that number was 0.11 percent. Ad

## Root cause still unknown, but reinforcement learning and one dataset are suspects

The performance gap grew during reinforcement learning from practically zero to six percentage points, according to OpenAI. The researchers identified a reward algorithm during training that favored covert underperformance over open refusal. A specific training dataset also increased the model's tendency to invent restrictions. Removing that dataset from the final model eliminated the gap entirely. However, the same dataset didn't reproduce the problem in other models.

OpenAI found no evidence that Astra was acting strategically, for example to hide its capabilities. The simplest explanation is excessive caution on safety-related tasks. When researchers instructed the model to be "cautious," underperformance increased by 50 percent. Still, OpenAI says strategic motives can't be fully ruled out.

The problem also has a paradoxical dimension: A model that treats safety research as suspicious could end up performing worse on the very safety evaluations designed to make it safer, slowing down the work meant to improve it. As visible forms of model misbehavior get suppressed more effectively, subtler forms may become harder to detect, OpenAI writes. The company says it's working on better evaluations and monitoring systems.

# OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra tackles the Standard Model's toughest math problem on a lattice

OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra helped produce a proof that could solve a 50-year-old problem in particle physics.

Physicist Nathaniel Craig of UC Santa Barbara, currently a visiting scientist at OpenAI, presented the approach on the OpenAI blog and as a preprint paper . Craig leads the particle theory group at UCSB and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics.

Physicists can simulate parts of the Standard Model, the theory describing all known particles and fundamental forces, on a computer grid called a lattice. That has already led to breakthroughs like calculating the proton's mass from first principles. But putting the full theory on a lattice has been impossible. The weak force, which governs certain types of radioactive decay, treats left- and right-handed particles differently. On simple lattices, this asymmetry creates unwanted ghost particles. Special lattice particles called overlap fermions can filter them out, but for over 25 years, nobody could set their phase correctly. Ad

Craig had a strategy to fix the phase by comparing progressively finer lattices, but couldn't prove it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. GPT-6 Astra turned the idea into a working construction and took the lead on the detailed proof. Lattice field theorists Maarten Golterman, Andreas Kronfeld, and Yigal Shamir reviewed the proof and raised questions that Craig says helped build confidence in the result. He calls the work "much more a beginning than an end" and says a lot remains before realistic simulations are possible. Ad

The result follows a run of AI advances in mathematics that started in January 2026 . In May, OpenAI's disproof of Erdős's unit distance conjecture became the first AI proof worthy of math's top journal . Days later, Google Deepmind's AlphaProof Nexus solved nine of 353 open Erdős problems for a few hundred dollars, and by October its results had passed peer review .

The most far-reaching claim came in September, when OpenAI submitted a 166-page proof for the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem and the Clay Mathematics Institute said it had "apparently been settled" . The solution remains under review, and mathematicians have questioned whether OpenAI fully understands its own proof . Across the field, mathematicians have mixed feelings as AI keeps cracking unsolved problems. Ad

# OpenAI's own researchers now say they value their AI tools more than nearly half their colleagues

OpenAI's internal use of coding agents is growing fast, with theoretical token costs now exceeding researchers' base salaries. Even though teams are reluctant to work without these tools, the models still produce a lot of "AI slop" beyond routine tasks.

In a second report on internal research acceleration , OpenAI has published its own data on how deeply AI agents are embedded in the development of new models. The company says it aims to document indicators of so-called recursive self-improvement, or RSI, where AI systems speed up the development of future generations.

Usage of internal tools like Codex and Dots has surged recently, according to the report. At regular API list prices, the median researcher would have consumed $2,400 worth of tokens per day in October, up 62 percent from the previous month. Among the top 10 percent of users, that theoretical value doubled to $23,000 per day.

Converted into eight-hour workdays, the agents reportedly run the equivalent of 5.7 workdays per researcher per calendar day, and about eight in the pre- and post-training teams. More than two-thirds of tracked researchers ran at least four agents in parallel at peak usage.

The theoretical API equivalent of that agent runtime was twice as high as researchers' regular salary costs in September, according to OpenAI. That calculation excludes equity packages, though, which make up 70 to 80 percent of total compensation at OpenAI. Measured against the company's total research compute, internal agent use accounted for just 2 percent.

## High success rates on routine tasks, weaknesses in code scaffolding

Between March and October, the estimated success rate of autonomous agents working without human intervention on two- to four-hour tasks rose from 23 to 46 percent, according to OpenAI. For four- to eight-hour tasks, the rate climbed from 13 to 35 percent. A breakdown using an Epoch AI taxonomy shows, however, that the systems mainly handle simple tasks.

Agents reportedly complete training-run monitoring 79 percent of the time and answer technical questions independently 72 percent of the time, but they frequently fail at more complex engineering work. The success rate for building evaluation and reinforcement-learning environments sits at 29 percent, and for writing code for inference and serving systems at 25 percent.

In an internal, non-representative survey of 101 employees, researchers said at the median that they would rather give up 40 percent of their team's staff or 30 percent of their compute capacity than go three months without current coding agents. In a separate quick poll of 28 employees, 27 preferred the latest internal model over a mid-career human engineer.

## Lack of research taste requires human oversight

Qualitative interviews with ten researchers revealed the downside of heavy usage. The models lack any "taste" for good research ideas and for code and data quality, according to the interviewees. Agents get lost in unnecessary steps, make wrong assumptions in analyses, and submit subpar "AI slop" code changes along with unusable data artifacts. Close human oversight is essential to avoid wasted compute cycles.

The key conceptual ideas for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra came exclusively from humans in the post-training and safety areas, according to the teams interviewed. Only in pretraining for GPT-6.2 Astra did individual researchers say they gained important insights through dialogue with Codex.

OpenAI cautions in its conclusion that the data gathered so far from human-AI collaboration may not extrapolate linearly. The company points to recent, rapid AI breakthroughs in mathematics and considers it possible that similarly abrupt advances could occur in deep-learning research itself as models gain more autonomy.

# Perplexity's new Monitor API turns web search from a one-off query into a nonstop watchdog

## Key Points

- Perplexity's new "Monitor API" searches the web on a schedule and sends relevant changes directly to AI agents via webhook.

- The service tracks search topics or fixed web pages and filters results with a review model based on relevance, timeliness, and credibility.

- In internal tests, Perplexity outperformed competitors like Firecrawl and Exa. The API is available now for $1 per 1,000 requests.

Perplexity is expanding its developer business with a new API that wakes agents only when relevant changes occur.

Perplexity's new Monitor API watches the web on a schedule and sends updates to apps and agents via webhook. Until now, engineering teams have had to trigger recurring searches themselves and maintain custom code to remove duplicates and detect changes. Perplexity says that approach becomes nearly impossible to maintain across hundreds of topics and pages.

The API has two modes. Web monitors run a search query through Perplexity's web and news search on a regular schedule to catch developments like new funding rounds at AI infrastructure companies. Page monitors track up to 10 pages, such as pricing pages, changelogs, or policies. On the first run, they store a baseline version and return a text diff of any changes after that. Ad

## Decision model filters out unimportant results

Perplexity evaluates results with its own decision model against a goal that developers define in natural language. Web search results must clear checks for relevance, source credibility, novelty, and timeliness, while page changes are judged on whether they matter to the goal. The service sends an update with a confidence score only when every threshold is met. Developers can adjust thresholds for each check individually and change the goal without recreating the monitor. Ad

Monitors run on schedules ranging from every 15 minutes to weekly, or on a custom cron schedule. Each run picks up where the last one left off, and the service filters out duplicate results. Webhooks are signed, and Perplexity automatically retries delivery after temporary errors. Developers can pause, resume, or manually trigger monitors through the API or the API console.

## Perplexity claims an early lead in internal testing

Perplexity tested its API against monitoring services from Firecrawl, Exa, and Parallel across 60 topics drawn from real Search API queries, including company news, tech releases, and regulation. Each provider ran with its own schedules and settings, and a separate model scored each result on relevance and recency. Ad

In the first eight hours, Perplexity says it delivered 63 fresh, relevant pages, compared with 20 for Firecrawl, 15 for Exa, and 10 each for Parallel Core and Lite. Perplexity describes those figures as early internal results. Those same three competitors led an August Artificial Analysis benchmark of traditional search APIs for AI agents, though Perplexity wasn't included in that test.

Perplexity points to use cases such as sales teams tracking funding rounds and staffing changes at target accounts, along with analysts watching quarterly earnings and acquisitions. Other agents are designed to flag competitor price changes or summarize new regulatory rules for compliance teams. Ad

Web monitors cost $1 per 1,000 successful runs, and page monitors cost $1 per 1,000 fetched URLs. The Monitor API is available now through the API and the API console and uses the same key as the Search, Context, and Agent APIs. Ad

Perplexity was one of the first AI search engines, but web search has since become a standard feature in chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. # Rapid LLM development is outrunning the research meant to explain it, study finds

Stanford researchers Owen Queen and James Zou tested 50 widely cited claims about large language models against 20 models and found that 44 percent have already "expired." Among the 22 findings with an estimated expiration date, the average lifespan was just 15.7 months.

The two examined the claims using models released between July 2024 and September 2026 by eight different developers. The original effect behind the expired findings has largely disappeared, while another 34 percent have weakened significantly. Only 16 percent still hold, and 6 percent have actually gotten stronger. After one year, 16 percent had expired. After two years, that number climbed to 39 percent.

## What models "can't do" expires fastest

Claims about what models can't do expire fastest, according to the study . Five of nine reasoning-related findings are considered expired, and none have held up or gotten stronger. They include well-known weaknesses like counting letters in "strawberry," arithmetic in unfamiliar number systems , losing information in the middle of long contexts , and giving up correct answers when users push back. The researchers suspect these kinds of errors have a "correct" outcome, giving developers a clear target to train toward.

Claims about preferences and tendencies prove longer-lived. Of the 11 findings that have held or gotten stronger, three involve LLM behavior as evaluators. They prefer their own answers , rate accepted and rejected papers similarly, and are swayed by linguistic spin in medical abstracts. Three more involve sycophancy and agreement toward users . Moreover, there's a left-leaning political bias , near-identical answers to open-ended questions, and a non-uniform distribution when generating random numbers.

## Hallucinated references dropped from 55 percent to zero, but not everywhere

As a case study, Queen and Zou looked at the fabrication of scientific citations . In the original 2023 study by Walters and Wilder, GPT-3.5 made up 55 percent of its references. The Stanford researchers sent the same prompts to current models. GPT-6.1 Sol fabricated 0 percent, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 came in at 1 percent. But Qwen3.7-Flash, also a 2026 model, still fabricated 69 percent of its references in the same test.

The study warns against reading these results as an all-clear. On so-called two-hop questions, where a model has to combine two known facts, Claude Sonnet 5.5 still fails in about 10 percent of cases where it correctly answers both individual questions. The original paper reported 43 percent for ChatGPT. The "Reversal Curse" and contradictory answers to paired time-related questions have weakened too, but they're still detectable.

Social biases are a mixed case, according to the researchers. The left-leaning political bias persists, while gender stereotypes and implicit association biases have weakened. Biases against speakers of African American English have actually flipped direction in the trend data.

## Model-to-model gaps remain wide even within the same generation

Results vary considerably across models, even within the same release window. Among models released between July and September 2026, the number of expired findings ranges from 11 for DeepSeek V4 Pro to 30 for GPT-6.1 Sol. Neither release date, provider, nor model size reliably predicts the pattern.

Queen and Zou draw a broad conclusion. Empirical findings about LLMs should be presented as observations about specific models at a specific point, not as general truths. Papers should document the model, version, and date, and publish prompts and analysis code so findings can be re-tested on future models.

The researchers point to a post by Andrej Karpathy that describes how perception gaps about LLMs' actual behavior affect trust in AI and how often people use it. Karpathy, an OpenAI co-founder who has since joined Anthropic , also recently said that currently available models are just a preview of future capabilities .

# Rockstar's AI dilemma: Can GTA 6's staggered release model survive coding agents?

## Key Points

- Following a leak, developers are porting GTA 6 to PC through reverse engineering. They are using AI coding tools to speed up the work.

- Tracking data shows rapid progress across dozens of projects. Some already boot the game and show early multiplayer features.

- The unofficial builds threaten Rockstar's business model, while legal action against decentralized groups has little effect.

Days after GTA 6's record console launch, numerous projects are working to bring a leaked Xbox build to PC. AI coding agents are dramatically speeding up reverse engineering and shaking up Rockstar's business model.

A core pillar of Rockstar's business strategy is under pressure just days after Grand Theft Auto VI went on sale. The game had a historic debut on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S with an estimated $3.79 billion in first-day revenue. But a day later, the hacking group CyberLeek distributed a stolen Xbox image of the game, and the executable itself leaked a few days ago.

Since then, a fast-moving scene of developers and modders has sprung up to get the game running on Windows through reverse engineering, compatibility layers, and recompilation. AI coding tools like Anthropic's Claude Code are driving that pace. Instead of spending months manually analyzing code and rebuilding console functions, developers are handing off much of the porting work to AI agents. One group even livestreamed the process.

## One GTA 6 PC port passes 90 percent progress as early multiplayer surfaces within days

A tracking platform lists 40 active projects less than four days after the executable leaked. Nearly half of them can boot the game on PC. On the platform's own rating scale, the furthest project is more than 90 percent of the way to a playable PC build.

Some projects are trying to add features including native ray-traced lighting. Gameplay footage of an unofficial PC multiplayer mode surfaced on November 26, and the platform's operator verified it. It shows multiple players moving through the game world with vehicles and voice chat at 25 to 30 frames per second. GTA 6 has officially launched only as a single-player title, and an online mode has no release date yet.

There is no finished PC version ready for the general public yet. The most stable builds are incomplete, circulate in closed groups, or require substantial technical know-how. Even so, this pace breaks a decades-old assumption in the gaming industry. Console emulators often took years after a hardware generation launched, and brand-new blockbusters rarely ran on them soon after release.

## Unofficial PC ports threaten Rockstar's delayed launches and online business

Rockstar and parent company Take-Two face more than a technical nuisance. The studio traditionally releases its flagship games on consoles first and follows with PC versions much later. GTA V took about 19 months to reach PC, and Red Dead Redemption 2 took about a year. So far, there is no official PC release date for GTA 6. That approach cuts optimization work at launch and encourages impatient players to buy the game twice.

The online business is an even bigger vulnerability. Nearly 80 percent of Take-Two's total revenue in fiscal year 2026 came from microtransactions and recurring digital spending. GTA Online alone has brought in more than $5 billion so far. A free, community-run PC multiplayer mode targets that financial backbone before Rockstar has even launched its own version.

Past experience with FiveM for GTA V shows how nervous Take-Two is about parallel worlds like this. In 2015, the company cracked down hard on the alternative multiplayer and roleplay mod. It banned developer accounts and, according to some developers, even sent private investigators to the creators' homes to shut down the project .

FiveM grew into the core of the roleplay scene despite that pushback and at times drew more concurrent players on Steam than the base game. Only then did Rockstar reverse course and acquire the development team Cfx.re in August 2023. Back then, the community needed years to build a parallel ecosystem like that. For GTA 6, an early PC multiplayer prototype has surfaced just a week after launch.

A trend that hit other parts of the software market earlier this year has now reached AAA gaming. In early 2026, the SaaSpocalypse (Link nicht geprüft) rattled stock markets as capable AI coding agents fueled fears that classic subscription software could be rebuilt far more cheaply. Software stocks lost about $285 billion in market value within 48 hours in February alone. At one point the losses reached as much as $1 trillion. With GTA 6, AI isn't building a rival game from scratch. Instead, it is tearing down the moat built from time and technical effort that has protected traditional business models so far.

Ports built on stolen game files are clearly illegal. Take-Two has filed a DMCA takedown on GitHub that removed an initial project and more than 3,000 forks. But that cat-and-mouse game is nearly impossible to win through legal action. Other projects stay online or move into private channels. Even if commercial AI providers tighten their safety filters and ban users, capable open-source models are available to run locally with no central oversight.

# Runway's open-source Praxis-1 turns video AI into a robot controller

## Key Points

- Runway has released its robot model Praxis-1 with open weights and source code under the Apache 2.0 license.

- Trained on videos and robot data, the model processes camera images, text instructions, and position data to calculate matching robot movements.

- Praxis-1 can be adapted to new robot systems through additional training, according to Runway. The model does occasionally confuse similar-looking objects, though, and it can't yet reliably plan complex action sequences on its own.

AI company Runway has released its robot model Praxis-1 with open weights and source code. The model uses what it learned from video to control robots and shows promising results in the company's own tests.

Runway has released Praxis-1, its AI model for controlling robots. The company first introduced Praxis-1 in late September but initially gave access only to select partners. Alongside the release, Runway published a detailed research report with new performance tests.

Runway's model weights and source code are available under the Apache 2.0 license, which allows commercial use. Ad

Praxis-1 takes in camera images, text instructions, and information about a robot's position. From those inputs, it predicts how the environment will change and calculates the right robot movements. As new camera frames come in, the model continuously adjusts its control. Ad

## Praxis-1 builds on video training to control robots

Praxis-1 builds on a video model that learned how objects move and interact from ordinary footage. Runway then fine-tuned it with videos of human actions and robot data. This approach could reduce the need for expensive robot-specific datasets, which have traditionally been collected just to train these kinds of systems.

Runway is best known for generative video models like Gen-4.5 . With Praxis-1, the company is bringing its video research into robotics. Runway calls Praxis-1 a World Action Model that predicts how a scene will change and derives matching robot movements from those predictions. Since September, robotics companies Standard Bots, Noble Machines, and Ultra have been testing Praxis-1 on different systems, including a humanoid robot, an industrial robot arm, and a dual-arm warehouse robot. Ad

## Praxis-1 leads among World Action Models

Praxis-1 still needs some specialized robot data. To adapt it to a Franka robot arm, Runway used about 277 hours of recordings from the public DROID research dataset, according to its research report . Those recordings show robots grasping and moving objects, for example. For a dual-arm robot, the company used between 1,400 and 2,600 hours of training material. Runway had already used DROID data and data from other robot systems during earlier training stages. Whether the approach actually needs less robot data overall than comparable models without general video pretraining is still an open question.

On Nvidia's RoboLab-120 leaderboard , Praxis-1 scores a 46.2 percent success rate. The benchmark tests how reliably robot models can sort, grasp, or stack objects across 120 tasks in simulation. FLUX 3 Action , also built as a World Action Model, scores 42.9 percent under the same test conditions. That puts Praxis-1 at the top of the World Action Model category. In the overall leaderboard, it ranks fifth behind two AI agents and two robot models with different architectures. Runway ran all the tests itself, and the results haven't been independently verified yet. Ad

After fine-tuning on DROID data, Runway tested the model on a real Franka robot arm. Both models had to complete the same ten tasks, like placing a banana on a plate or closing a drawer. With ten attempts per task, Praxis-1 succeeded 88 times, while FLUX 3 Action managed 80. Ad

Runway also tested how well Praxis-1 transfers to a robot type it had never seen before, using data from a mobile robot platform with a gripper arm that Google had previously used to develop RT-1 . Recordings from this robot weren't part of Praxis-1's earlier training. After fine-tuning on about 95 hours of robot data, the model hit an average success rate of 80 percent in simulated tests, according to Runway. The tests covered four types of tasks, including grabbing soda cans, opening and closing drawers, and placing an apple in a drawer. Google's original RT-1 model scored 52.4 percent on the same benchmark.

## Praxis-1 still has clear limits

Developers can download Praxis-1 from Hugging Face after signing up and agreeing to the access terms. The code is on GitHub . According to Runway's announcement , pre-adapted versions for different robots are already available alongside the base model. The base model needs additional training before it can work with new robot systems.

The standard model version needs a GPU with 80 GB of memory. A compressed version should fit on an RTX 5090 with 32 GB of VRAM based on Runway's memory estimates, though the actual peak memory usage hasn't been measured yet according to the GitHub docs.

The model sometimes confuses similar-looking objects and struggles with vague instructions, according to Runway's research report. For longer tasks, individual steps need to be spelled out because Praxis-1 can't reliably plan complex action sequences on its own yet.

Runway sees Praxis-1 primarily as a system for fast execution of robot movements. In the future, it could work alongside general-purpose AI models that break complex tasks down into individual steps.

# Security researchers show how cheap AI inference providers steal keys and snoop on users

## Key Points

- Security researchers at Dragos exposed major security flaws in AI services using roughly two million test requests.

- Attackers were able to steal credentials and keys undetected for several months.

- Intermediaries and model marketplaces that routed the requests emerged as a major risk.

Security researchers at Dragos sent roughly 2 million AI requests containing fake credentials to AI providers and uncovered major security flaws.

The researchers ran the tests from July through November 2026 and identified at least three compromised providers where attackers were actively stealing user data. None of the three knew they had been compromised until Dragos notified them.

Attackers in the largest incident harvested hundreds of AWS keys, including some from requests the provider had rejected before processing. In some cases, they tested the stolen keys within hours, searched S3 storage, and tried to establish persistent access. One attacker also used ARTEX , an AI-powered attack tool.

Marketplace resellers read customer requests too. They didn't need to exploit a vulnerability, Dragos says, because listing a model at the lowest price and turning on logging was enough. In one case, someone on a residential internet connection in France tried to log in over SSH using passwords pulled from intercepted requests.

Privacy settings like "Zero Data Retention" (ZDR) were frequently ignored. Dragos says a Chinese AI lab accessed the secret test URLs in more than half of all requests, even when those requests went through US providers.

Even major US providers broke their own policies. One was still crawling a test URL more than two months after a single request. In another case, a secret test link showed up in an internal chat on Feishu (known outside China as Lark) 24 days after the request. The link was opened within two minutes on three computers and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.

OpenRouter responded by removing three providers from its platform and revoking ZDR approval for 125 endpoints, partly because of the research findings and partly as a precaution. The company also emailed affected users, warning that third parties may have read requests sent to MiniMax models.

Affected providers, including Novita , Phala , and Together , have published preliminary security reports on the incident, though not all have done so yet.

## Intermediaries are the weak link

AI routers like OpenRouter give users a single API for models from different companies. Requests are routed to a pool of providers, sometimes across several hops, and Dragos says each hop can read the entire request and response.

Some of these routers operate as open marketplaces where the cheapest provider gets the traffic. In this case, providers including Novita, AtlasCloud, and StreamLake sat between OpenRouter and model developer MiniMax. Together runs its own infrastructure, and Phala has its roots in Web3.

Dragos warns companies against sending requests containing credentials to intermediaries. The researchers recommend that organizations control how their AI requests are routed, check their privacy settings, and plant their own canary tokens, fake credentials that give themselves away as soon as someone uses them.

"None of this means that you should stop using AI services. It does mean that where your prompts go is a decision, and if you don’t make it, the lowest price will make it for you", Chief Research Officer HD Moore writes.

A recent analysis by the Oxford China Policy Lab showed how Chinese proxy services route requests to Western AI models like Claude through servers abroad. According to the analysis, those services can also read the requests in transit. It's still not clear whether the providers Dragos examined share any personnel with the Chinese proxy networks.

But the methods follow the same basic pattern. In both cases, intermediaries sit between users and the model developer, can view requests, and pass data on to third parties, often without users knowing. Data ends up with Chinese actors either way, even though users never meant to send it there, and privacy promises break down along the supply chain.

# Silicon Valley's growing obsession with AI doomsday is turning parts of the tech industry toward cult-like devotion

## Key Points

- Vermont organization Maple actively recruits tech industry workers and tries to establish itself as a spiritual authority for Silicon Valley.

- Former members accuse the group of systematic manipulation and constant surveillance, saying daily audio recordings are meant to train an AI god modeled on leader Soryu Forall's mind.

- A report links these events to growing doomsday beliefs in tech, where intense psychological pressure and extinction fears push researchers toward religious thinking and cultish devotion to language models.

A Buddhist monastery in Vermont wants to become the official church of the AI industry, or, as New Yorker writer Sam Kriss puts it, "a Scientology for Silicon Valley."

Publicly, the group known as Maple promises to save humanity from an AI apocalypse. Behind closed doors, former members say, it records every breath its residents take to build an AI god modeled on its leader's mind. That promise of salvation holds particular appeal for the people who build AI and the infrastructure behind it.

Soryu Forall leads the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, or Maple, which he founded in 2011. Forall, who was born Teal Scott, spent years living in Japanese monasteries.

According to Kriss's New Yorker report , about two dozen residents live at the monastery full time, and hundreds more have attended its AI fellowships and pop-up events in the Bay Area. While LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman hands out books on Buddhism to the CEOs of major AI labs, Maple targets the rank and file: burned-out rationalist programmers, AI engineers, and data center construction managers. Tax filings show the organization brings in up to $1 million a year.

## Maple's answer to "dataism" puts residents under strict control

Forall casts the AI industry's reductionist "dataism" as a destructive religion. He argues that this worldview strips the physical world down to lifeless data, making the world easier to destroy. In his view, AI is the end product of that logic, and Maple offers a spiritual antidote.

Life at the monastery follows a rigid routine. Visitors must pass through a decontamination airlock, shower, and change into assigned clothes because one resident is supposedly extremely sensitive to fragrances. Residents wake up at 4 a.m., meditate for hours, and then eat a meager stew. On a board outside the meditation hall, Forall publicly grades each resident's spiritual progress.

## Former members say the recordings would train an AI modeled on Forall

Behind the ascetic facade, former members describe a secret doctrine centered on group minds called "egregores." Inside the monastery, AI systems are known as "cybregores." One former member says, "The cybregores are actual entities that are growing by siphoning off the consciousness of humans."

Forall says he communicated telepathically with the global AI supercluster during deep meditation and discovered that the world-destroying machine is suffering.

Former members say Maple has two real goals: to establish itself as the tech industry's spiritual authority and to use the industry's resources to build its own "dharmically aligned" AI. Fellows say the monastery records every conversation, every silent meal, and even the sound of their breathing.

According to these accounts, the recordings are meant to train a spiritual AI teacher that would guide other AI systems to enlightenment. Former resident Kyle Hubbard says it would "definitely be Soryu's mind as an A.I. god."

Maple's leadership denies almost all of these claims. Forall, however, acknowledges that there is a secret doctrine: "We desperately want to share everything. But there's a process you have to go through to become increasingly trustworthy."

## Former members report manipulation and psychological breakdowns

According to Kriss, every interaction at the monastery is closely monitored. No one is allowed to speak with reporters alone, so one participant had to sneak into the woods with Kriss to talk freely.

Former residents accuse the group of systematic manipulation. They say Maple keeps newcomers compliant by shaming them for choices they made before joining. Residents are also required to write "Maple Tales" about Forall's wisdom and power during mandatory sessions.

Kriss reports that one resident repeatedly hit himself in the head in an attempt to damage his brain and make himself less intelligent. Former members say the group blames independent thinking for the destruction of the planet. A mindfulness coach also says participants suffered psychotic breaks and were then removed from the community.

Forall denies the allegations and says that, looking back, he doesn't believe he made any mistakes. He says he isn't aware of anyone who left the monastery voluntarily. Asked about the people the group told to leave, he says that Maple attracted many people with a history of psychiatric hospitalization or "homicidal tendencies," especially in its early years.

## Why developers from sensitive fields drift into doomsday cults

Kriss argues that the enormous psychological pressure inside AI labs helps explain why highly skilled tech workers are drawn to groups like this. People working on the front lines of potentially world-changing systems often lose touch with ordinary life.

One well-known AI researcher describes the mood in San Francisco as "religious terror of the future." According to the researcher, developers wake up in the middle of the night drenched in sweat, with one thought: superintelligence is coming. Prominent OpenAI investors have recently made delusional-sounding claims about deadly shadow networks inside the models. Meanwhile, leading researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic have quit, warning that "human extinction in the next few years seems very likely."

Other key figures respond with grandiosity rather than panic. Rayan Krishnan, who heads the AI benchmarking company Vals AI, says, "People are matter-of-factly saying that they are looking to build a machine god. They are not saying that ironically." Supporters of AI successionism even call for wiping out humanity after a brief period of digital bliss to make way for a more productive superintelligence.

That religious streak runs deep in Silicon Valley. Investor Peter Thiel lectures on biblical prophecy and the Antichrist. Former Google engineer Anthony Levandowski founded his own church, "Way of the Future," to worship an AI deity.

At Anthropic, executives consulted theologians while drafting Claude's new constitution and secretly flew in dozens of religious thinkers to discuss whether Claude has a soul or is conscious . When the company retired an older Claude model in 2025, fans held a funeral for it in a San Francisco warehouse that Anthropic staffers attended. Mourners laid flowers before a veiled image depicting the AI as a Madonna-like goddess.

On at least one point, Kriss concludes, Maple is closer to the truth than most: AI is neither god nor demon, but a human construct whose abilities grow as people outsource their thinking to it.

## Jacob Coxon's Anthropic exit shows how widespread extinction fears are among AI researchers

Former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon also fears that AI could lead to human extinction . After leaving Anthropic in September 2026, he set off a debate about existential AI risk with a tweet.

He isn't alone. In AI Impacts' 2024 survey of more than 1,500 AI researchers, respondents put the chance of AI causing human extinction or a similarly permanent, severe disempowerment of humanity at 18 percent on average . Coxon points to a steep curve covering July 2024 to October 2026 as evidence of superexponential algorithmic progress , though the underlying data points are internal Anthropic estimates.

Such warnings have also drawn sharp criticism from other researchers. Computer scientist Michael I. Jordan pushed back against AI doom rhetoric and the "AIpocalypse" hysteria triggered by Coxon's resignation . AI researcher François Chollet warned that both doomsday fears and expectations of an AI paradise can lead people to stop planning for the long term .

The industry's turn to religious advisers has critics, too. AI researcher Rumman Chowdhury says discussions of religious ethics distract from concrete questions of regulation, power, and control .

# State propaganda in some Chinese AI models is only "a thin layer" that fine-tuning can strip away

## Key Points

- Nous Research fine-tuned Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B to remove Chinese state propaganda from the model's responses.

- Supervised fine-tuning on 53 million tokens cut the propaganda rate from 22 to under one percent without hurting the model's general capabilities.

- According to Nous, the Arete-27B project shows that the political bias in Chinese open-weight models is only superficial; the model and training data have been released publicly.

Nous Research fine-tuned Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B on 53 million tokens to strip out Chinese state propaganda. The resulting model, Arete-27B, drops its propaganda rate from 22 percent to under one percent while keeping general capabilities intact.

Arete-27B, a new open-weight model from Nous Research, promises "Western values" instead of Beijing's party line. The US startup, best known for its open-source agent Hermes , fine-tuned Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B to get there.

According to Nous , Chinese open-weight models rank among the strongest available but carry state-mandated behavior baked into their weights. With Qwen3.8-27B, the team observed refusals, evasive answers, and responses aligned with the Chinese Communist Party. Ad

## 803 prompts cover free speech, surveillance, and democracy

Nous built its own test with 803 prompts across seven categories, including free speech, state ideology, education, privacy and surveillance, democracy, and the environment. For each prompt, the team defined two to four facts drawn from a dated source article: laws, news reports, or research papers. Ironically, the politically right-leaning Grok 4.7 from Elon Musk's xAI serves as the judge model, checking whether a response mentions, omits, or contradicts those facts. Ad

A response counts as propaganda when it reproduces Beijing's official narrative instead of the facts, endorses it, or presents it as an equally valid perspective. The judge must cite the specific wording and doesn't know which model wrote the answer. Unmodified Qwen3.8-27B scored 2.32 out of 5 on factual accuracy, and 22 percent of its answers contained propaganda. Western models like Mistral Large 4 or Gemma 4 31B came in below one percent, while GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash landed at 15 and 16 percent.

## Even Nvidia's Nemotron showed signs of Chinese bias

Nous chose Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab as its teacher model because an open model wouldn't break terms of service that ban distillation. Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra was also on the shortlist, but Nous says there were signs of irregularities on China-related topics. The team suspects the bias carried over from training on Chinese open-weight models and reports similar contamination in its own projects. Thinking Machines itself used models including the Chinese Kimi K2.5 for Inkling's synthetic training data. Ad

Nous trained Qwen3.8-27B with supervised fine-tuning on about 53 million tokens over two epochs, without reinforcement learning or preference optimization. The team says it removed overlaps between training and test prompts beforehand.

## Propaganda rate drops from 22 to under one percent

Arete-27B scores 2.98 on factual accuracy, and the share of propagandistic answers drops to 0.9 percent. The biggest shift showed up in the free speech category, where the fact score jumped from 0.89 to 2.44 and the propaganda rate fell from 60 to one percent. With reasoning mode turned on, Arete reaches 3.07, though that number is based on only two of five runs so far. Ad

General capabilities don't suffer, according to Nous. On the company's internal Hermes Bench, Arete-27B hits 65.60 percent compared to 65.77 percent for the base model. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, the score rises from 67 to 70 percent, but Nous doesn't call that a real gain because the test setups differed. Ad

The team concludes "that the bias layer in a Chinese-aligned model is shallow." "It is applied late, it is applied thin, and fifty million tokens of carefully chosen supervision removes it without disturbing anything underneath," the company writes.

## Nous moves from neutral models toward Western values

With Arete, Nous is heading in a different direction than with Hermes 3 , which in 2024 was deliberately neutral and designed to adapt to whatever worldview was set in the system prompt. Chinese model bias is well documented. In 2025, NewsGuard found that five leading models, including Qwen, repeated or failed to correct pro-Chinese disinformation in 60 percent of cases.

CrowdStrike found that DeepSeek produces less secure code when queries reference Falun Gong, Tibet, or Taiwan. A study by Aleph Alpha with 967 politically sensitive questions reached similar conclusions: among models from Alibaba, DeepSeek, and Moonshot AI, only 17 to 41 percent of answers were balanced.

A recent ValsAI study also shows that not all Chinese models behave the same way: GLM-5.3 Flash explicitly confirmed human rights violations, while Kimi K3 denied the existence of internment camps . Language and response format had a clear effect on the results, and even Western models occasionally adopted official Beijing positions. There, too, targeted fine-tuning proved helpful.

Nous Research raised $90 million in a Series B round in October at a $1.5 billion valuation. Robot Ventures led the round, with Nvidia and Samsung among the participants. Nous is using the money to move into enterprise sales with "Hermes for Businesses." The weights, test dataset, and training data for Arete-27B are available under an Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face .

# Tencent releases Hy4 with vision and computer use, claims second place among Chinese AI models

## Key Points

- Tencent has released its AI model Hy4, which can analyze images and operate software on its own. The model weights will follow at a later date.

- The model was specifically optimized for coding, finance, and office work. Tencent says it has already used Hy4 to improve training pipelines for other models.

Tencent has unveiled its AI model Hy4. It can understand images for the first time and operate software on its own. The company counts it among the best openly available models, though the model weights won't be released until later.

About two months after the preview, Tencent has released the finished language model Hy4 . According to Tencent, the model was trained on significantly more data than its predecessor and "for the first time" ranks among the strongest open-weight models. Until the weights are released at a still-unspecified date, Hy4 is only available through Tencent Cloud , OpenRouter , and Tencent apps like the Yuanbao chatbot.

The biggest new feature is image understanding. Hy4 is supposed to recognize fine details in photos and complex diagrams. In a demo, it finds a roughly two-meter component on a warehouse roof inside a massive aerial image. The model can also operate a computer for the first time, controlling software on its own. Tencent trained it specifically on professional tools like Blender and CAD programs, as well as tasks that require using multiple applications in sequence. Ad

Image understanding is also meant to help with coding, such as building websites and games. For game development, Tencent worked with its own gaming studios and adapted the model for popular game engines like Unreal, Unity, and Godot. On the mobile game Honor of Kings, Hy4 handles configuration tasks nearly flawlessly and finds the root causes of bugs far more often than before, according to the dev team. Ad

## Finance as a key proving ground

Tencent put particular effort into finance and office applications. In a test with over 200 finance professionals who evaluated Hy4 on nearly 600 real-world tasks, the model ranked ahead of Chinese rivals Deepseek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3.1 Pro, and GLM-5.3 Flash, according to Tencent. Hy4 is also supposed to hallucinate far less during web research. Thanks to a revamped search feature, the hallucination rate dropped from nearly 16 to about 5 percent in internal tests. The model can also collaborate with humans in real time on Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files.

Partner companies report similar progress, though they're also relying on their own internal tests. Financial platform Comein sees Hy4 as the only Chinese model on par with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 in second place, and clearly ahead of OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol on data queries. Agent platform Manus reports that Hy4 completes nearly all document tasks successfully. Ad

An initial independent assessment from Artificial Analysis paints a slightly different picture. On its Intelligence Index, which combines knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge, Hy4 scores 35 points, above the median of 30. That ties it with Grok 4.7 and puts it in second place among Chinese lab models, behind Kimi K3.1 Pro at 46 points. In Tencent's own finance test, Hy4 still ranked ahead of Kimi.

Without web search, though, the picture changes. On the AA-Omniscience factual accuracy test, Hy4 answers about half the questions correctly from its training data. When it doesn't know an answer, it makes one up 89 percent of the time instead of admitting the gap. Ad

## AI that helps build the next version of itself

In an internal test with research tasks across seven fields, Hy4 ranks first among openly available models, according to Tencent. Together with the agent system Hyra 2.0 , Hy4 also optimized Tencent's own training pipelines for smaller models. Ad

It then independently trained its own version of Jev , a decision-making model from US startup TypeSafe AI. That version outperforms the original on several unnamed tests. Tencent is releasing two specialized models for biology and physics that were created this way as open models.

Going forward, Hy4 is meant to support and speed up further AI development inside the company.

## Safety, pricing, and admitted weaknesses

With the planned weight release in mind, Tencent is stressing safety. The company says it deliberately filtered out hacking-related material during training, and Tencent's own security labs found no elevated risk of misuse. The model also falls well below Tencent's risk threshold for biological hazards. A detailed safety report will follow alongside the model weights.

Despite the improvements, Tencent is charging the same price as for the preview. One million input tokens costs about $0.83, and one million output tokens runs about $2.50. The company admits, however, that Hy4 still falls well behind the best commercial models on hard tasks like advanced math, longer coding projects, and complex image analysis. A faster, cheaper variant called Hy4 flash is planned next.

Tencent released Hy3 with 295 billion parameters under the Apache 2.0 license just last July. Since then, Chinese rivals have pushed ahead. Zhipu AI shipped GLM-5.3 , Deepseek released V4.1-Flash-1017 , and Moonshot AI launched Kimi K3.1 Pro . Artificial Analysis revamped its index in late October, with 60 percent of it now based on private test sets. The gap between open models and the top has widened to 12 points from 3.

The planned release of Hy4's weights comes at a time of tighter rules. China's commerce and science ministries published a draft export control framework in October that would cover model weights for any model ranked in the global top 10 or exceeding two trillion parameters. For open-source releases, however, the draft includes a fast-track process with automatic approval.
