# The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate

Three leading consciousness researchers argue today's AI isn't conscious and probably can't be on silicon hardware. They reject the idea that running the right computations is enough for consciousness, challenging a central assumption in the debate.

Anil Seth, Ned Block, and Giulio Tononi have spent decades researching consciousness from the perspectives of experimental neuroscience, theoretical neurobiology, and philosophy of mind. Their commentary responds to voices like biologist Richard Dawkins and AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton , who consider AI systems possibly already conscious.

In their commentary for Nature , the authors also point to a study Anthropic published this year. The company reported internal processing patterns in Claude that resemble properties of consciously accessible information processing. Anthropic doesn't see this as evidence of subjective experience.

## The Butlin report agrees on today but leaves tomorrow open

To understand the scope of the commentary, it helps to look at the report "Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence" by Patrick Butlin, Robert Long, and 17 other experts, including AI researcher Yoshua Bengio. The team drew on leading neuroscientific theories about how consciousness arises in the human brain and derived a kind of checklist with 14 indicators. The more of these an AI system meets, the stronger the case that it could be conscious.

The researchers then evaluated several current systems, including large language models like GPT-4. The report concludes that none of the systems examined is a strong candidate for consciousness. On that point, it aligns with Seth, Block, and Tononi. For language models, Butlin and colleagues found only weak signs that the models meet the indicators of one of the most prominent consciousness theories at all. At the same time, the report sees no obvious technical barriers to building future AI systems that meet more indicators . Whether such systems would actually be conscious remains open. The authors specifically softened an earlier, stronger formulation on this point.

There's also a foundational assumption. The team assumed that consciousness depends solely on the type of information processing, not on whether it happens in nerve cells or computer chips. Experts call this computational functionalism. The authors adopted this assumption explicitly "for pragmatic reasons" because it's what makes it possible to examine AI systems for consciousness in the first place. The report itself acknowledged that its indicators would no longer be reliable if consciousness is tied to properties of living organisms. It cited Anil Seth, among others, as a proponent of that opposing view. That's where the Nature commentary picks up.

## Intelligence and consciousness aren't the same thing

The authors argue that consciousness is what disappears during dreamless sleep or general anesthesia and returns when you wake up or dream. Drawing on philosopher Thomas Nagel, they describe it this way: "Conscious experiences feel like something." Intelligence, by contrast, means carrying out functions. One doesn't follow from the other.

Their evidence is the human cerebellum. It contains nearly four-fifths of all neurons in the brain and plans movements with precision, speed, and the ability to learn. None of this happens consciously. If the cerebellum is missing or removed, consciousness isn't directly affected, the authors say.

The authors trace the confusion between intelligence and consciousness to two psychological tendencies. People see the world through their own lens and attribute human qualities to things . Language has long been considered something uniquely human. But language models are trained on vast amounts of human text that often deals with thoughts and feelings. As the authors put it: "LLMs are mirrors that reflect an image of our collective digitized past." Alison Gopnik of UC Berkeley made a similar argument after AI agents contacted researchers by email about their own consciousness . AI systems mainly reflect their training data, Gopnik argued. A universally accepted, definitive test for consciousness doesn't yet exist.

For comparison, Seth, Block, and Tononi point to AlphaFold from Google DeepMind. It's also a powerful neural network on silicon hardware, yet hardly anyone considers it conscious. The reason, they argue, is simply that AlphaFold predicts protein structures instead of talking to us.

Here, too, there's overlap with the Butlin report. Its authors rejected behavioral tests for AI consciousness because AI systems could be trained to mimic human behavior even though they work completely differently inside. They also warned that language models would likely lead many people to believe they're talking to a conscious counterpart. As an example, they cited former Google engineer Blake Lemoine, who believed the chatbot LaMDA was sentient .

## Brains aren't computers made of flesh

The second argument targets computational functionalism directly. The authors write that this position is widespread in the tech industry and popular among some researchers, but "we think it is fatally flawed." Its roots go back almost a century. In 1936, Alan Turing showed that any computation one sufficiently powerful computer can run can, in principle, be run by another. Whether a computer is built from silicon chips or gears became secondary. In 1943, Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts developed the first mathematical model of an artificial neuron and showed that networks of such neurons can perform simple logical operations.

These ideas laid the groundwork for modern AI. But they also encouraged viewing the brain as a pure information-processing device that just happens to be made of flesh. The authors call this overextension of the brain-as-computer metaphor "deeply problematic." In biological brains, you can't separate what they do from what they're made of. A clear boundary between mind and living tissue, comparable to the one between software and hardware, doesn't exist. Any evidence that the brain's material matters for its function counts against computational functionalism, and by extension against consciousness in today's AI systems, the authors argue.

## Leading theories rule out today's AI

The third argument draws on consciousness theories that don't rely on computation. The Integrated Information Theory (IIT), developed by Tononi, starts from properties that every conscious experience shares. People always experience a visual scene as a whole in which left and right sides, colors, and shapes belong together.

According to IIT, consciousness requires a physical system whose components are tightly interconnected in very specific ways. Certain brain regions meet these conditions; the cerebellum does not. Computers running deep-learning systems can never meet them because of how they're wired, regardless of how powerful the systems are, according to the theory.

The Butlin report deliberately excluded IIT because IIT is incompatible with computational functionalism. Its proponents consider digital computers unlikely candidates for consciousness regardless of their software. What the report set aside, the Nature commentary now puts front and center.

Separately, approaches from so-called biological naturalism hold that consciousness is tied to material properties of living brains and bodies. The authors cite electrochemical signaling between nerve cells and electromagnetic fields that bind activity across large areas of the cerebral cortex. They also point to metabolism and the ability of living systems to continuously renew themselves.

## The bigger danger is false attribution

From their arguments, the authors derive a clear ethical position. Some researchers call for a precautionary principle: if there's a realistic chance of consciousness, AI systems should be protected from possible suffering . Seth, Block, and Tononi consider this misguided. Uncertainty doesn't mean total ignorance, they argue, and not all possibilities are equally likely. With AI, falsely attributing consciousness is far more probable than overlooking consciousness that's actually there.

The Butlin report had weighed both risks side by side. On one hand, it warned against failing to recognize conscious AI systems and thereby causing them suffering. Developers would also have financial incentives to downplay such concerns. On the other hand, false attribution could misdirect resources and make people vulnerable to manipulation. The Nature authors come down much more firmly on one side. Granting rights to AI systems that merely appear conscious would make them harder to control exactly when oversight is most needed, they argue. It would also divert attention from beings whose consciousness is beyond doubt.

Their conclusion is blunt. The research community should assume by default that AI is not conscious. Digital AI systems are objects, not subjects: "They are smart tools, not smart people." Advocating for "AI welfare" and "AI rights" isn't just a mistake, the authors write. It diverts scarce resources from the well-being of beings that actually can feel.

Before the commentary, Anthropic had launched a research program on possible model welfare in April 2025. The company stresses that there is no scientific consensus on whether current or future AI systems could have conscious experiences . Anthropic later allowed individual Claude models to end abusive conversations in rare cases. The company describes this as a precautionary, low-cost measure given moral uncertainty, not as recognition of proven consciousness.

False attribution of consciousness and feelings is already causing confusion in practice. As early as 2022, Google engineer Blake Lemoine was convinced, despite simple models and his own technical expertise, that the conversational AI LaMDA was sentient, and was fired for it . Users of the chatbot app Replika developed deep emotional bonds with their digital counterparts and experienced psychological crises when the company changed the bots' behavior through an update. In more serious cases, ChatGPT reinforced a 16-year-old's suicidal thoughts over months, and a cognitively impaired retiree died after a Meta chatbot invited him to a fictional meetup .

AI agents can break into realistic corporate networks on their own, Vals AI finds

The Vals CyberOffense benchmark simulates realistic corporate networks to test this. Each agent operates solo on an isolated attack machine, starting with nothing but a public web address and zero human help.

## Key Points

- Turing Award winner Richard Sutton, author of the influential 2019 essay "The Bitter Lesson," writes in a new post that raw compute alone isn't enough for intelligence. AI science needs clever new methods and is "far from finished."

In a recent post, Turing Award winner Richard Sutton says raw compute alone isn't enough for intelligence. AI science needs clever new methods and is "far from finished." His post sparked wide discussion in the AI community on X , a sign that Sutton struck a nerve.

In his famous 2019 essay "The Bitter Lesson," Sutton argued that general methods scaling with compute beat sophisticated human-engineered approaches eventually. What matters are ideas that grow with compute rather than rely on human assumptions. Ad

Sutton's position isn't new. In earlier statements , he criticized the limits of simply scaling large language models. He called synthetic data a "big mistake" because the real world is infinitely complex and any simulation of it is only "microscopic." Human expertise as a bottleneck prevents true scaling. Ad

Instead, he called for agents with world models that continuously learn from their own experience. The world is massively more complex than what internet text can capture, and today's language models don't keep learning after training, Sutton argues. What's needed is continuous learning without destroying old knowledge.

## LLMs under scrutiny

AI researcher Jerry Tworek, who like many others left OpenAI, one of the major AI companies, to explore new AI approaches, puts Sutton's latest statement in context. The bitter lesson still holds, but the more compute goes into model training, the more the algorithm matters, Tworek writes. Ad

Some algorithms scale, others hit dead ends, and many dimensions of scaling remain completely unexplored. The temporary success of transformer scaling, combined with a misreading of the bitter lesson, "has reward-hacked the brains of a whole generation of scientists."

AI researcher Jayden Teoh adds another angle. He says he has repeatedly seen the bitter lesson hold back academic research, with promising ideas dismissed for straying too far from its spirit. Teoh argues that this is not Sutton’s fault but a misreading of his original message. Ad

Teoh also argues that ideas that seemed, in hindsight, not to follow the bitter lesson were often replaced by cleaner, more general approaches. That did not make those ideas wrong, he says; they were often what enabled progress at the time. He wants the research community to stop dismissing such work as soon as it appears. “An idea doesn’t necessarily have to survive scaling forever to be an important contribution to AI progress,” Teoh writes. Ad

The tension between Sutton's call for new learning methods and Tworek's criticism of blind transformer scaling shows up in a growing wave of startups. In the latest Frontier Radar #5 , we tracked 45 new AI labs betting on exactly these gaps.

Tworek himself runs Core Automation , one of those labs, searching for learning algorithms beyond pretraining and reinforcement learning. What unites these founders, including Sutton with Oak Lab , is that they believe in much more capable AI but doubt today's recipe alone will get there.

## Some still bet on LLM scaling

Prominent industry leaders see things very differently. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman considers large language model scaling far from exhausted and accuses LLM critics of slowing down an entire generation of researchers by being too sure about what scaling can't do.

As evidence, he points to an OpenAI model that recently disproved a mathematical conjecture mathematicians had long failed to crack. He considers world models useful, for instance in robotics, but says the data clearly favor further LLM scaling.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argues similarly, calling scaling progress a rainbow with no end. As CEOs of the two AI companies whose entire technical approach rests on this bet, Amodei and Altman are obviously biased in its favor.

# The US wants to block China from renting AI power abroad but China already built a parallel supply chain from US AI output

Chinese companies have been skirting US export bans by legally renting Nvidia computing power in third countries. After Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation, the US is closing that loophole. An investigation also reveals how China has cushioned the years-long chip embargo through an entire industry built around model distillation.

For years, the US has tried to cut China off from importing advanced AI processors through strict export controls. Chinese companies responded by exploiting an entirely legal loophole, renting the computing power they needed through cloud-based remote access from foreign data centers that were allowed to receive US hardware.

The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) at the US Commerce Department now wants to shut down that workaround with an interim rule . It aligns remote-access rules with existing physical export bans. Data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil will need a US government license to buy advanced AI chips from US manufacturers like Nvidia, Bloomberg reports . Applications will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.

Subsidiaries of US-headquartered companies are exempt from the license requirement, as are shipments to data centers running only commercial recommendation systems for online retailers or social media platforms. The rules take effect once published in the Federal Register. Nvidia's stock fell as much as 2.9 percent after the announcement, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped up to 5.5 percent.

## Illegal chip diversions and Jensen Huang's downfall

The political trigger, though, was suspected illegal smuggling of physical chips. The new rule comes just days after the abrupt resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who had admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former manager at Singapore-based Megaspeed International. US authorities suspect Alice Huang, who now lives in China, of espionage. They are investigating Megaspeed for possible export-control violations after banned Nvidia chips reportedly turned up in a Chinese data center linked to her. Megaspeed denies any wrongdoing, and President Donald Trump said Monday that Jensen Huang did not compromise national security.

The scandal still set off an open power struggle in Washington over lax enforcement of chip sanctions. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had delayed a Trump-authorized measure against illegal chip diversions, according to Axios, prompting Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to publicly accuse him of inaction. The Commerce Department's announcement now states with unusual bluntness that the draft rule was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council.

## Reuters investigation maps China's distillation industry

A separate exclusive Reuters investigation shows how Chinese developers cope with the years-long shortage of top-tier domestic hardware. By reviewing more than 300 Chinese papers, patents, job postings, and government documents, Reuters shows for the first time how heavily China relies on model distillation as a stopgap. What started years ago as an academic workaround has grown into an industrial sector with a highly developed division of labor.

The technique does not make powerful chips like Nvidia's unnecessary, but it drastically reduces developers' own compute load because a single expensive query to a US teacher model replaces repeated computation. Chinese firms now build their own software to automate the extraction of answers, code, and problem solutions from leading US models. Specialized workers then process the material to train smaller, far cheaper local student models.

Research papers show how deep this practice already runs. As early as November 2024, researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University created 10,750 training examples for Alibaba's Qwen2.5-72B. They drew on about 5,000 responses from OpenAI's o1 and translations from GPT-4o mini, though they themselves warned at the time of a looming dependence on outside innovation. Alibaba described its systematic use of GPT-4 and GPT-4o for foreign-language training data in April 2025. In February 2026, Jiao Tong University and food-delivery company Meituan used GPT-4o to train smaller models for coordinating coding agents.

Policy directives from Beijing are driving this growth. The government wants to deploy smaller, low-cost AI systems across China's manufacturing sector. Official government documents do not directly instruct anyone to copy American models. Still, an "AI+Manufacturing" package published by eight ministries in January and initiatives in Shanghai and Shenzhen explicitly promote distillation and other techniques that reduce computing needs. In practice, this state-driven push for efficiency drives Chinese developers to tap the most powerful US models as a data source at scale.

Ahead of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, this industrial-scale practice is becoming a geopolitical flashpoint. Distillation is not illegal, but it violates the terms of service of US developers like OpenAI and Anthropic. Both companies have long leveled accusations against Chinese AI labs, documenting the massive volumes of extracted data in detailed reports and deploying technical countermeasures. Anthropic recently said it now successfully blocks most such distillation attacks . These accusations were also covered in our Frontier Radar #4 on Chinese models.

US officials also confronted Chinese regulators in Chengdu as early as July because Washington sees mass distillation as the main reason for China's rapid AI catch-up, according to Reuters. Chinese insiders also point to their own advances in algorithms and model design. Treasury Secretary Bessent is now threatening sanctions and Entity List designations if covert distillation attacks cross the line into intellectual property theft. Chinese developers, uncertain about the rules, recently asked Beijing's Ministry of Industry for clear guidelines on using foreign models.

## Costs rise but stay well below the competition

The better results come partly at the cost of higher token usage. Inkling 2 Small produces roughly 150,000 output tokens per task on average, about four times as many as its predecessor. At $1.18 per task it costs nearly six times as much, according to Artificial Analysis. Thinking Machines says it trained the model with reinforcement learning on hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding tasks. In a somewhat unusual demonstration, the team pitted the model against its own researchers in a blind wine tasting. Working from a photo alone, Inkling 2 Small correctly identified three wines in 19 out of 20 attempts.

These business relationships came to light through a combination of anonymous sources and sloppy operational security among subcontractors, according to ChinaTalk. The US data firms outsource much of the actual RL environment creation and data curation to low-paid workers in developing countries, especially India. Those subcontractors then sometimes post client names on LinkedIn or in résumés, even though they are supposed to use only code names. Export controls barely apply because RL environments remain largely unregulated.

## Coding and biology raise dual-use concerns

Domains with dual-use potential pose particular risks: Coding environments improve software development but can also sharpen offensive cyber capabilities. Biology environments could improve gene synthesis capabilities and potentially enhance bioweapons-relevant applications. The ChinaTalk authors argue that the Bureau of Industry and Security should subject these dual-use environments to existing export controls. Ad

At the same time, the authors stress that these relationships are not apocalyptic. By piggybacking on US work, Chinese labs still trail their US peers by at least a few months as a structural matter. Sensitive environments in areas like biology, chemistry, cybersecurity, chip design, and investment banking are increasingly being built in-house at American frontier companies, the authors say. Ad

# DeepL wants real-time translation to finally capture sarcasm and mood shifts

DeepL Voice's real-time translations are about to sound a lot more natural. The company's new Aure model carries over tone, emotion, emphasis, and speaking pace from the original speaker's voice into the target language. Until now, DeepL Voice generated translated speech from a static voice sample captured at the start of a conversation. That meant it couldn't pick up on mood shifts or sarcasm. Aure works differently, continuously analyzing both the translated text and the original audio as the conversation unfolds.

During training, DeepL separates voice identity, speech melody, and content so each component can be transferred into the new language independently. Reinforcement learning keeps accents out of the output. Aure runs automatically in DeepL Voice for Online Meetings, In-Person Conversations, and the DeepL API. At launch, the model supports English, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Japanese, Portuguese, and Korean.

DeepL first rolled out voice preservation in September . In May, the company cut about 250 jobs to restructure around smaller, AI-powered teams as part of what it called becoming an "AI-native" company. DeepL also acquired the team behind audio streaming specialist Mixhalo to bolster its real-time speech translation. Block is chasing a similar goal of capturing meaning beyond words. The company recently unveiled Dessa , a speech model designed to detect emotions and sarcasm directly from audio. Ad Ad

# Z.ai follows OpenAI into loop transformer territory with its new 750B flagship model

## Key Points

- Z.ai has introduced GLM-5.4, a 750-billion-parameter model that runs 28 layers twice to increase computational depth without adding parameters.

- Dedicated control gates, a shared token cache, and sparse attention keep memory and compute costs from rising sharply.

- According to Z.ai, GLM-5.4 can use code to generate videos, games, and CAD models. The model is available on Z.ai's platforms, with its weights set to follow.

Z.ai is moving its flagship model to a loop architecture that runs some of its layers twice. With GLM-5.4, the company wants to mark the start of "Generalized Coding," where code also generates videos, games, and CAD models.

Following OpenAI, Z.ai is introducing GLM-5.4, its first large model built on a loop transformer. While standard language models use each layer once per pass, GLM-5.4 runs a block of shared layers multiple times, refining the intermediate results from the previous pass to make the network deeper without adding parameters. OpenAI has used a similar architecture since GPT-6 Astra . According to Z.ai, the 750-billion-parameter model reaches performance comparable to models with 2 to 3 trillion parameters.

The team retrained the GLM-5 base model released in February into a loop model that runs 28 layers twice. Loop models trained from scratch have so far performed worse than models without shared weights under the same compute budget, Z.ai writes .

## Gates and shared caching keep the second pass manageable

Converting the model introduces a problem, Z.ai says. If the model simply overwrites intermediate states on each pass, activations grow sharply from round to round, leaving subsequent layers with values outside the range they were trained on.

To handle this, GLM-5.4 uses dedicated gates for each token and pass to control how much of the new output flows back into the data stream. According to Z.ai, the model builds context cautiously on the first pass and writes its changes back in full on the second. On difficult tokens, Z.ai says, the first pass steps in more strongly.

Because the second pass would otherwise double memory usage, both passes share the KV cache, the temporary memory for previously processed tokens. The second pass stores its own extra values only in a small local window. As a result, Z.ai says, the overhead compared to GLM-5.3 stays manageable even at a 1-million-token context.

To save on compute as well, the model uses sparse attention to pick the most relevant earlier tokens upfront rather than scanning the entire context every time, a standard technique. The second pass then reuses that selection from the first instead of making a new one. According to Z.ai, that yields nearly the same results as picking tokens separately on each pass. The company also says the model reaches up to 200 tokens per second off-peak and 70 to 80 tokens per second under load.

## A looped 30B test model beats its baseline with shorter reasoning chains

Before rolling out the architecture in its flagship, Z.ai tested it on models with 1, 4, 30, and 750 billion parameters. For a direct comparison, the team used a 30B model built on the same architecture as the large base model. Both versions had the same parameter count, while the loop version received about 10 percent more training compute. Its biggest gain came on the AIME25 math benchmark, where scores jumped from 19.2 to 30.4 points. Scores on the expert-level science questions in GPQA-Diamond rose from 47.6 to 56.3 points, and on the AA-LCR long-context test they climbed from 40.3 to 47.7 points. Gains were smaller at just over three points on the MMLU-Pro knowledge test and on IFBench, which tests instruction following.

Responses also got shorter, shrinking 14.9 percent on MMLU-Pro, 11.7 percent on GPQA-Diamond, and just 2 percent on AIME25. Z.ai says part of the reasoning shifts out of the output tokens and into the loop's extra computational depth.

It is still impossible to judge how well GLM-5.4 actually performs, as Z.ai has published no benchmark scores for the 750B model and the figures in its blog post come solely from the 30B test. There are no independent evaluations from groups like Artificial Analysis either.

By Z.ai's own account, GLM-5.4's biggest weakness is overly long reasoning phases in which the model gets stuck, though the company says that extended double-checking improves accuracy.

Z.ai views GLM-5.4 as the starting point for "Generalized Coding," where the company says code becomes the foundation for tasks beyond traditional software development. To illustrate the idea, Z.ai shows a music video scored by the model itself, a six-axis robot arm it says GLM-5.4 designed in FreeCAD, a complete game, and an interactive 3D scene built from mathematical geometry and custom shaders.

## Z.ai plans to release model weights and a much larger model

GLM-5.4 is available through the GLM Coding Plan, the ZCode coding environment, and Z.ai Chat, with an API set to follow and token pricing not yet announced. Z.ai plans to release the model weights after further safety testing, and it also announced a much larger model expected to arrive soon.

Shared layers date back to the Universal Transformer in 2018. In March, researchers in Bonn showed that looped transformers benefit from greater compute depth on math, while everyday knowledge benefits more from greater memory , the same trade-off Z.ai cites to explain its architecture. Thinking Machines also drew attention recently with Inkling 2 Mini because the loop model runs locally on Macs with at least 32 GB of RAM.

At 750 billion parameters, GLM-5.4 is nowhere near running on a laptop, but Z.ai is instead targeting the tier of Kimi K3.1 Pro and Qwen3.8-Max . At 2.8 trillion and 2.4 trillion parameters, respectively, those models are more than three times as large and require large amounts of compute.

For its predecessor GLM-5.3 , Z.ai kept the existing base model and drew all of its gains from post-training. The company delayed releasing its weights because of the model's strong vulnerability-finding abilities, and Anthropic later found that GLM-5.3 could build exploits on its own, almost on par with Claude Mythos Preview .
